=== PÁGINA 13 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Getting Started
Getting Started
Introduction to the Johns Hopkins ACG® System
This document is divided into four volumes.
• Volume I: Installation and Usage on page 17 provides basic instructions on how to prepare input
data files, select model options with which to process the data, and describes how to validate the
output produced by the ACG System software. The listing of risk factors assigned within the
software is in ACG System Output Data on page 405.
• Volume II: Technical Reference on page 115 provides additional detail on the theoretical and
conceptual basis of each of these markers as well as how they are combined and evaluated for
modeling purposes.
• Volume III: Applications on page 262 describes how the ACG System is typically applied and
provides numerous examples for population health monitoring, clinical screening, performance
assessment and financial applications.
• Volume IV: Social Determinants of Health (SDoH) on page 353 describes ACG GeoHealth
components for assessing differential needs based on patient geography.
Customer Commitment and Contact Information
Technical support is available during standard business hours by contacting your designated account
representative directly. If you do not know how to contact your account representative, please e-mail
acgsupport@jh.edu.
As part of our ongoing commitment to furthering the state-of-the-art of risk-adjustment methodology
and supporting users of the ACG System, we will continue to perform evaluation, research, and
development. Please register on our website at https://www.hopkinsacg.org/ to join our mailing list to
learn about new developments and upcoming events and to gain immediate access to our
bibliography, webinars and presentations.
We thank you for using the ACG System and for helping us to work toward meeting the ACG System
team's ultimate goal of improving the quality, efficiency, and equity of health care across the United
States and around the globe.
Nomenclature and Citations
The following represent categories of output produced by the ACG System:
• Diagnoses-based Markers: Aggregated Diagnosis Groups (ADGs), Adjusted Clinical Groups
(ACGs), Resource Utilization Bands (RUBs), Expanded Diagnosis Clusters (EDCs), Social Need
Markers, Chronic Condition Count, Hospital Dominant Morbidity Types, Frailty Conditions,
Compassionate Care Allowances (CAL-SSA), Pregnant, Delivered, Pregnancy without Delivery &
Low Birth Weight (less than 2500 Grams).
• Pharmacy-based Markers: Rx-Defined Morbidity Groups (Rx-MGs), Active Ingredient Count,
Proximal Active Ingredient Count, Medication Complexity, and High Caution Medication.
• Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based Markers: Condition Markers, Pharmacy Adherence & High Risk
Prescription Opioid Use.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Getting Started
• Laboratory-based Markers: Laboratory Markers.
• Utilization and Resource Use Markers: All Cause Inpatient Hospitalization Count, Inpatient
Hospitalization Count, Inpatient Hospitalization Days, Unplanned Inpatient Hospitalization
Count, Readmission 30 Day Count, Unplanned Readmission 30 Day Count, Observation Stay,
Observation Days, Emergency Visit Count, Emergency Visits with All Cause Inpatient
Hospitalization, Emergency Visits Leading to Observation, Emergency Department Visit
Classification, Outpatient Visit Count, Dialysis Service Marker, Nursing Service Marker, Major
Procedure Marker, Cancer Treatment Marker, Mechanical Ventilation Marker, Psychotherapy
Service Marker, & Resource Bands.
• Coordination: Management Visit Count, Majority Source of Care (MSOC), Unique Provider
Count, Specialty Count, Generalist Seen, Risk of Poor Coordination, Care Density.
• Risk Models: Local Age-Sex Concurrent Risk, ACG Concurrent Risk (Adjusted Clinical Groups),
Concurrent Risk (Regression-based), Predicted Total/Pharmacy Cost Risk, Rank Probability High
Total/Pharmacy Cost, Reference Probability High Total/Pharmacy Cost, Probability of
Unexpected Pharmacy Cost/High Risk Unexpected Pharmacy Cost, Probability of Persistent
High User, Predictive Models for Hospitalization including: Probability IP Hospitalization,
Probability IP Hospitalization Six Months, Probability ICU Hospitalization, Probability Injury
Hospitalization, Probability Extended Hospitalization.
• Patient Need Groups: Patient Need Groups (PNGs), Care Modifiers, Total Cost Risk Level
Guidance on citations and reference: Publications shall reference the software as The Johns Hopkins
ACG® System and include the software version number used for the research. First occurrences of
terms shall be preceded by ACG® System. Example: ACG® System Rx-Defined Morbidity Groups (Rx-
MGs) may be shortened to Rx-MGs on subsequent occurrences. Redundant use of ACG® System may
be omitted where meaning is clear: Example: ACG® System Rx-Defined Morbidity Groups (Rx-MGs)
and Coordination metrics were used for identifying high risk individuals. In the interest of replicability,
we encourage academicians to incorporate as much detail as possible about which models and/or
data processing options were applied in their research. Example: Summary Statistics tab indicates the
ACG predicted total cost model DxRx-PM- total cost-lenient dx-> total cost could be described as
"Predicted total costs scores from the ACG System were based on both diagnoses(any occurrence)
and pharmacy information."

The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 1: Technical Considerations
Chapter 1:
Technical Considerations
The central element of The Johns Hopkins ACG System Version 13.0 is a Windows-based reporting
application intended to facilitate implementation of the ACG System within health care settings. The
Windows-based software is not only a flexible reporting application, but also provides the ability to
run the software in batch mode from the command line, allowing individuals to automate or to
queue up multiple jobs. This chapter discusses using and installing all versions of the software.
Tip: Input and output file requirements as well as batch mode processing are identical across all
supported Windows and non-Windows-based Linux platforms. This simplifies the use of all ACG
System applications within your organization (see Batch Mode Processing on page 570 of this manual
for details on batch mode processing).
System Requirements
The Johns Hopkins ACG System is built to handle relatively large data volumes and processing
requirements. The performance of the software is very much based upon the speed and memory of
your computer.
Operating System
The following versions of Windows are supported:
• Windows 10 (32-bit and 64-bit)

Memory (RAM)
2 gigabytes (GB) RAM is recommended. The application will immediately utilize 256 MB on startup
and expand up to 1 GB RAM as necessary.
The size and complexity of the analyses (spreadsheet-like reports) are limited by the amount of RAM
on your computer. If you experience "Out of Memory" errors while running an analysis, you should
close any other open applications or otherwise expand the amount of available RAM, and try re-
running the analyses. If this does not resolve the issue, refer to Memory on page 25.
Disk Space
The application itself consumes approximately 350 MB of hard drive space. The temporary space
required to build an ACG data file is approximately four to five times the size of the input data files.
An ACG data file can consume anywhere from five to 100 megabytes per 100,000 patients (depending
on the length of member ID, number of diagnoses, etc.). One to ten gigabytes of free disk space is
typically sufficient to handle one million patients.
Screen Resolution
Minimum screen resolution of 1024 x 768.
For screen resolution below 1280 x 720, scaling factors greater than 100% are not supported.
Desktop Installations
The ACG System may be deployed on an individual Windows desktop. The installation is guided by a
wizard that allows the user to define the installation location. More specific installation instructions
are provided by your software distributor with download instructions.
Server Installations
The ACG System may be deployed on a centralized server, on either Windows or Linux platforms. This
installation mode will provide a basis for batch processing or as remote (ex. RDP) access of the ACG
System and is not intended as a method for distributed desktop access. It is important to note that
certain functions of the ACG System are machine- and user- specific.
The ACG license file has the .acgl extension. This file contains the contract term and licensed modules
for the ACG System. The license file recognized by the ACG System is machine-specific and user-
specific. In a Windows environment, this is well suited to the most common use of a workstation. In a
server or other multi-user environment, this may require additional installations of the ACG license file
for each user. For batch processing that can be initiated by multiple users or by another application, it
may be beneficial to include the installation of the current license file within the batch script to
prevent license-related errors. This does not imply that the ACG application needs to be reinstalled in
its entirety for each user. The license file installation is a function that occurs after the installation and
registration of the application.
The ACG mapping file has the .acgm extension. This file contains the mapping files and clinical logic
for the ACG System. The mapping file recognized by the ACG System is machine-specific and user-
specific. In a Windows environment, this is well suited to the most common use of a workstation. In a
server or other multi-user environment, it is possible for one user to have the most recent mapping
while additional users continue to use initial or older mapping file versions. For batch processing that
can be initiated by multiple users or by another application, it may be beneficial to include a mapping
file update within the batch script to ensure consistent use of the most recent mapping file.

to executing the Linux installation. When the appropriate Java runtime is not available, the following

Disk Space
If an out-of-space message displays when there is adequate space for the ACG data file, review the
following information related to the use of temporary space. The ACG application will use temporary
space that is approximately four-to-five times greater than the input data files to sort and merge the
data files. This can lead to out-of-space messages because the ACG application is taking advantage of
the Windows TMP variable for these activities. This is typically on the client’s primary (C:\) drive. It
may be moved using the following actions in a Windows operating system: Start > Control
Panel > System > Advanced System Settings > Environment variables.
The TMP variable can be edited to a location with more available space; however, this will change the
Windows default behavior (i.e., logging statistics will be moved as well). This TMP variable is machine-
specific and user-specific. Alternatively, the desired temporary directory can be specified in a
configuration file.
To change the temporary directory for Windows, use the following procedure:
1. Locate the ACG application (standard location is C:\Program Files\Johns Hopkins ACG 13.0).
2. Open the jhuacgw.lax file in a text editor (e.g., notepad) for the Windows graphical user interface
or the jhuacg.lax file for the Windows command line.
3. Locate the section titled LAX.NL.JAVA.OPTION.ADDITIONAL.
4. Append an option to the end to specify an alternate temporary directory in this format:
-Djava.io.tmpdir=[directory]
Note that java references Windows directories with double "\\" characters (see following
for an example).
5. Save the LAX file.
After editing, the LAX.NL.JAVA.OPTION.ADDITIONAL section should look like this:
# LAX.NL.JAVA.OPTION.ADDITIONAL
# -----------------------------
# JRE command line options
lax.nl.java.option.additional= -Xms128m -Xmx384m -Djava.io.tmpdir=C:\\temp
In Linux, Java utilizes the temporary directory "/tmp." To change the temporary directory on Linux,
use the following procedure:
1. Locate the ACG application (standard location is /opt/jhuacg13.0).
2. Open the jhuacg.lax file in a text editor (e.g., vi).
3. Locate the section titled LAX.NL.JAVA.OPTION.ADDITIONAL.
4. Append an option to the end to specify an alternate temporary directory in this format:
-Djava.io.tmpdir=[directory]
(see following for an example).
5. Save the LAX file.

Memory
The size and complexity of the analyses (spreadsheet-like reports) are limited by the amount of RAM
on your computer. If Out of Memory errors are experienced while running an analysis, close other
open applications or increase the amount of available RAM, and try re-running the analyses.
Out of Memory errors are often a result of an incorrect input file or a very extensive number of
categories in the report stratifiers. If the data had 20,000 individuals with costs greater than zero
organized into three lines-of-business AND the total cost and the line-of-business fields were
mistakenly inverted, a standardized morbidity ratio by Expanded Diagnosis Cluster (EDC) report would
potentially generate 5.72 million rows of output (286 EDCs x 20000 individuals) instead of 858 rows
(286 EDCs x 3 lines of business). Fields with high cardinality (large numbers of distinct values) are
generally not appropriate for the groups on analyses. Examples of fields with high cardinality are
patient ID, total cost, and pharmacy cost. In some instances, the provider ID, in combination with
additional fields (such as EDCs), could represent high cardinality in a data view.
Analyses such as the Comprehensive Patient Clinical Profile are intended to be generated for
individual patients, but an analysis such as the Utilization Profile Report was intended to be generated
at a group level. If the user attempts to generate a Utilization Profile Report for each patient, the user
will likely experience out of memory errors due to the large number of pages this will produce.
Null patient IDs can also generate Out of Memory errors. If patient IDs are null, then all medical
services records and all pharmacy records with a null patient ID are associated with each record in
the patient file with a null patient ID. This can quickly multiply across a whole data set to generate
significant resources for sorting and merging.
If the data source is very large, it is possible not enough memory is being allocated to the ACG
process. In this case, it may be appropriate to adjust the standard memory settings in the ACG
configuration. This action should not be necessary for data sizes below one million members. The ACG
application relies on the underlying Java runtime to allocate memory for the ACG processes.The Java
runtime will not automatically use as much memory as available on the computer; it must have a
hard minimum and maximum limit enforced. When Java runs out of memory, it displays an error
messageindicatingeither:"JavaHeapSpace"or "OutOfMemory". These error messages indicate that
Java requires more memory to complete the requested ACG process.
To increase the amount of memory Java will use from the default, use the following procedure:
1. LocatetheACGapplicationfolder(C:\ProgramFiles\JohnsHopkinsACG13.0 inWindowsor/
opt/jhuacg13.0 in Linux).
2. Open the jhuacg.lax file in a text editor (such as Notepad).
3. Locate the section titled LAX.NL.JAVA.OPTION.ADDITIONAL.
4. Modify the minimum and maximum memory constraints in the following line:
lax.nl.java.option.additional=-Xms256m-Xmx1024m
• In this command, 256m is the minimum amount of memory and 1024m is the maximum
amount of memory that Java will use.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

• On a 32-bit environment, Java cannot utilize more than two gigabytes (2 GB) of RAM. The
maximum value for the Java heap is closer to 1600m.
5. Save the LAX file.

Chapter 2: Basic Data Requirements
Chapter 2:
Basic Data Requirements
This chapter provides an overview of the general data requirements for the ACG System software and
its subsequent applications. The chapter is intended for the analysts and programmers who will be
planning and performing ACG System analyses.
The ACG System software is designed to operate using data typically retained in machine-readable
health insurance claims or encounter data files. In addition, member enrollment files detailing age,
sex, and other demographics for each unique patient (not just the subscriber to the insurance policy)
are generally required.
Once data are processed by the ACG System, a variety of data attributes are calculated for each
individual represented in the data. A layout of the standard patient summary file which could be used
to perform all of the available Windows-based analyses, is presented in Appendix B: ACG Output Data
on page 405.
Data Constraints
If insufficient data is provided to support a particular analytical method, the calculation of related
markers will be suppressed. The paragraphs below discuss the minimum data requirements for each
major analytical module. The Summary Statistics generated by the software provide an indication of
data presence for each of these attributes. Data presence is determined by a minimum of one non-
null entry in the field.
Diagnosis-based Markers
The following markers are derived from diagnosis codes provided on the Medical Services input file:
• Aggregated Diagnosis Groups (ADGs)
• Adjusted Clinical Groups (ACGs)
• Resource Utilization Bands (RUBs)
• Expanded Diagnosis Clusters (EDCs)
• Major Expanded Diagnosis Clusters (MEDCs)
• Chronic Condition Count
• Hospital Dominant Morbidity Types
• Frailty Flag/Frailty Concepts/Frailty Concept Count
• Compassionate Care Allowances (CAL-SSA)
• Pregnant
• Delivered
• Pregnancy without Delivery
• Low Birthweight
• Opioid Dependent
• Social Need Markers
Optionally, the ACG System will include diagnoses provided in the Supplemental Medical Services Data
file subject to the supplemental diagnosis method selected (See Analysis Time Frame on page 36). The
ACG System views diagnosis codes holistically for a patient, across all diagnosis code fields provided
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Data Requirements and Constraints
The Medical Services Input File on page 47 is used for all PNGs and Care Modifiers (CM). At least one
patient with non-null diagnosis code data in addition to the medical services file minimum
requirements is also required for the PNG and CM Applications.
If insufficient data is provided to support PNGs or Care Modifiers, the calculation of related markers

ACG GeoHealth Data Constraints
ACG GeoHealth, when licensed, is enabled by adding a patient-level geographic marker to the patient
input file, as outlined below. Users may use ZIP or FIPS codes. ZIP code is readily available within
patient address information, and should be entered as a 5- or 9-digit input. FIPS code should be
entered as an 11- or 12-digit input, is available in some data sources, and is an output of a geocoding
service. An 11-digit FIPS code represents census tract level, while a 12-digit FIPS represents census
block.
If insufficient data is provided to support the ACG GeoHealth module, the calculations will be
suppressed. Data warnings should be reviewed carefully. Note that some geo-codes may be valid but
not match in ACG GeoHealth. These include dummy zip codes (e.g., 99999) and zip codes that exist
only for administrative purposes without residents (e.g., post office boxes, government complexes,
etc). For ACG GeoHealth data warning codes, refer to Data Warnings on page 460.
The section below discusses the minimum data requirements for ACG GeoHealth.

General Data Considerations
Many of the analyses and several output variables in the ACG System are calculated relative to the
population presented to the software at a given point in time. It is important to consider the
implications of merging potentially dissimilar populations into a single ACG System process.
Analysis Time Frame
The recommended time period to provide to the ACG System is one year (twelve months) of data.
The ACG System is calibrated to use one year of data with an appropriate run-out period. For
example, the data required to perform a retrospective profiling analysis on calendar year 2021 should
include all diagnosis, prescription and demographic information collected between 2021-01-01 and
2021-12-31 after allowing for run-out/claims lag.
The ACG System enables the user to optionally specify the time frame of analysis when building the
ACG data file. The ACG System will utilize only the records within the specified time frame and based
on user selections may optionally calculate the summary cost variables that are provided on the
patient file.
Less than twelve months of data can be used effectively in predictive modeling applications. If an
individual is predicted to be high risk based on a limited amount of information, this is likely a true
assessment and worthy of intervention. However, using less than twelve months of data may not be
appropriate for retrospective applications, such as provider profiling. With limited time periods of
information, it is possible to identify an individual as low risk when really there is no information for
risk assessment. The percent of non-users may be artificially high with less than twelve months of
data.
Consistency Across the Enrolled Population
Many of the analyses and several output variables in the ACG System are calculated relative to the
population presented to the software at a given point in time. It is important to consider the
implications of merging potentially dissimilar populations into a single ACG System process. While it is
certainly possible to assign risk scores to all members with a single ACG process, in some instances,
individuals may have vastly different benefits and or enrollment periods all of which can lead to
differences in the quality of data capture, the service mix in encounters and the allowable cost paid
to providers.
Benefit Design
While it is certainly possible to assign risk scores to all members with a single ACG process, in some
instances, individuals may have vastly different benefits which can lead to differences in the quality of
data capture, the service mix in encounters and the allowable cost paid to providers. As an example,
for profiling purposes it might be highly desirable to aggregate data across product or benefit plan,
but some pre-work may be necessary to standardize costs for meaningful analysis. When aggregation
isn't a requirement, it is at times simpler to separate populations based on program eligibility. For
example, evaluate beneficiaries in private and government-sponsored programs separately where
assessments will be relative to each population since the benefits offered and underlying population
characteristics are significantly different.

Non-Users and Partial-Year Enrollees
Most ACG System applications involve the analyst viewing a snapshot of the utilization history of
population members during a particular period of time. If any members of the risk pool have been
eligible to use services for a period of time that is shorter than the in-scope period, both their
diagnosis history and their resource consumption profile may differ from members who were enrolled
for the entire period. For the most part, and as long as these new enrollees are randomly distributed
across the population (and population sub-groupings), their impact is minimal. However, if a large
number of enrollees are concentrated in one provider group that is profiled or in one employer group
for which rates are being set, the concentration of new enrollees may bias results to make this group
appear healthier than they otherwise might have been if complete diagnoses and claims information
had been available for them.
In general, when including individuals who are not eligible for the entire enrollment period, it is
recommended that results be scrutinized closely. One approach is to compare results excluding and
including these individuals to help assess whether their inclusion has introduced any systematic bias.
Another strategy for assessing their impact is to examine the ACG category distribution across the
various units of analysis, such as by provider. A disproportionate number of persons assigned to ACG
5110 and ACG 5200 (i.e., no diagnoses and non-user ACG categories) may indicate the enrollee cohort
entered the plan near the end of the analysis period and may lack sufficient contact with the provider
to allow accurate overall ACG category assignment. Such groups can, and perhaps should, be
eliminated from the analysis or be reported with appropriate caveats. The specific approach used will
vary for each analysis/organization based on the quality of the alternatives. Although the new
enrollees’ diagnosis codes may be incomplete, risk adjustment based on a limited pool of diagnoses
generally provides more accurate risk adjustment than do alternative demographic adjustments.
Most grouping methods and case-mix measurement tools that focus on episodes of care restrict their
attention to the subset of a population that actually consumes resources (e.g., those visiting a
provider or being admitted to the hospital). The most common applications of these tools, provider
profiling and other retrospective applications, are concerned exclusively with users of services since
only for these members can a meaningful profile be developed. However, for capitation rate
development and other prospective applications, non-users are of great importance since many, if not
most, of the enrollees who do not use services in the current period will consume services, to at least
some degree, in the future period. Since capitation payments are made regardless of whether the
member interacts with the capitated provider, the characteristics of non-users are important. For
profiling, consideration of the percentage of enrollees assigned to a physician who are non-users may
provide information on access issues or illustrate differences in provider practice patterns. In general,
population-oriented analysis will have more flexibility and be more comprehensive if both users and
non-users are included.
From the Provider Perspective
Many health systems may not only have multiple health programs with potentially different benefit
levels and/or serve patients of varying enrollment lengths, but they may also have clinics or provider
groups who serve patients from the broader community who may not be part of the health system.
This may create a situation where there is complete claims detail for patients who are part of the
health system buy may create a situation of only partial or incomplete data for those members from
the community. Such a situation is most common with large teaching hospitals who may draw
populations from all over the world because of their specialization in treating highly complex cases.
Similar to suggestions above for patients under various benefit programs, it may be advisable to
consider analyzing groups with complete detail on all patient physician encounters (and pharmacy),
separately from those for whom only detail on visits at the clinic are available.

Additional Data Elements/Inputs
While the ACG System is built on typologies relying primarily on diagnoses and pharmacy codes, there
is a wealth of additional data available which can help to understand patient need or complexity and
which can help support population health analyses or provide additional details for drilling down to
population subgroups of interest. While currently details from health risk assessments or geo-social
data do not influence any risk assessment variables or scores, such detail may be provided as part of
the patient file to support population health analytics and/or to create custom variables combining
such detail with ACG System Output.
Input File Layouts
Before using the ACG System, source data text files must be extracted from the claims or
administrative system. This document lists the recommended source data files required as input for
ACG System processing, as well as general extraction rules that apply to all source data files. Source
data files are text files and can be assigned any filename. Text files extracted from the claims system
must follow pre-determined formatting requirements. The requirements are specific to the type of
data each table will contain, and are outlined in the following section.
General Extraction Rules
The source text files must be in ASCII text format. Each row must contain a line feed indicator (CRLF
in Windows, LF in Linux). The default data file format is a tab-delimited, optionally quote enclosed,
text file (sometimes called a tab-delimited data file) with the columns in order as described in the
following tables. An optional, comma-delimited, quote-enclosed text file can also be used. These
formats are directly supported by Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Access, and a variety of other tools. The
organization is required to select whether or not the file contains a header record with column
names. Each file should follow source text file rules with respect to formatting and data type. For
most fields, the ACG System does not require fixed field lengths and can adapt most columns to the
length of the data provided. Any exceptions to this are noted in the specific file requirements.
Accommodating Data Sets with Limited Information
As noted previously, the ACG System is designed to operate on the data typically retained in machine-
readable health insurance claims or encounter files. Recognizing the limitations of administrative data
sources in common usage, users may augment the claim or encounter information by entering
additional, relevant information about their patient populations on the patient file.
If you feel your claim or encounter data is complete, there is no need to calculate the utilization
metrics in the patient file format below, and the software will calculate the patient file markers from
the detailed claims and encounter data. However, if fields are missing from the medical services or
pharmacy file layouts or if payment arrangements limit the availability of certain types of codes, the
patient file provides a means to override the ACG System software calculations for limited data sets.
Using Supplemental Data
The ACG System has long made it possible for a user-defined look back period to pick up potentially
fugitive diagnoses but this risks indicating as active, acute conditions that have been resolved.
Supplemental data is intended to augment data for chronic conditions for the current time period and
can be based on historical claims, EHR data or disease registry data.

Selecting Relevant Diagnoses for Input to the ACG System
In the United States and elsewhere, healthcare providers of all types record diagnostic codes on
insurance claim forms and other types of administrative records. These diagnoses are generally
accurate and have proven quite useful in understanding the case-mix of various populations.
However, the user can maximize the accuracy of the ACG assignment by allowing the ACG System to
filter the medical services used to assess morbidity.
Excluding Lab and X-Ray Claims
Most health care organizations collect claims information from clinical laboratory, diagnostic imaging,
and durable medical equipment providers that include diagnosis information. These claims should not
be used to determine morbidity. The diagnoses on these claims often, and perhaps even primarily,
represent rule-out, suspected, or provisional codes. The inclusion of such diagnoses could result in
many false positives. For example, all women receiving a blood test for pregnancy will likely be
classified as pregnant if the assignment is based on this lab service claim. When identifying claim or
encounter records to input to the ACG System, selecting all service claims within a specified time
frame is the recommended approach. If the user provides procedure codes and place of service in the
input files, the software will automatically exclude these types of claims in accordance with the
following definitions.
If detailed procedure and place of service is not made available, it is recommended that the input
files be pre-screened and lab, x-ray, and other provisional diagnoses be excluded in accordance with
the following rules. The Typical Place of Service Codes to Exclude and Procedure Code Ranges to
Exclude table provides a listing of the typical place of service codes and procedure code ranges to
exclude.

Extracting Diagnoses from Electronic Health Records (EHR) Data
Published research indicates that EHRs and claims often contain independent information from each
other and can supplement each other in providing more complete population health outputs.5 When
both medical services and EHR data are available, diagnoses from both may be provided as input to
the ACG System.
Encounter Filtering from EHR
Diagnoses from encounters that are typically recorded by non-clinical staff or are primarily for record
keeping purposes should be excluded. The list of encounter types to exclude will vary by EHR system,
but a sample of common encounter types to exclude is as follows:
• Canceled or Voided Encounters
• No Shows
• Encounters generated as abstract requests or as outgoing letters
• Encounters generated by patients (through a patient portal or email as examples)

• Telephone encounters
• Encounters generated from clerical orders

Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) can also serve to indicate the status of a diagnoses
(see http://www.hl7.org/fhir/valueset-condition-ver-status.html). It is recommended that only
confirmed diagnoses be included.
Problem List Diagnoses
Usage of EHR problem lists vary greatly from one health system to another and sometimes even
within a single health system. If there is confidence that the problem list represents current active
conditions it is recommended that diagnoses from the problem list be included. If the problem lists
represents recent history a viable option may be to include these diagnoses as part of the
Supplemental Medical Services file. For example, if the problem list contains the date of initial
diagnosis or a date of confirmation for a diagnosis, the dated problem list may be appropriate;
whereas an undated problem list may be less relevant. If the problem list represents morbidity
recorded two or more years ago, it is suggested that this detail be ignored.
Medical Services / Supplementary Medical Services Data
Format
This file should contain all diagnosis codes that were experienced (incurred) for each patient during
the observation period. The format is the same if using supplementary medical services to confirm
the presence of chronic conditions or if a supplemental disease registry is supplied. Supplementary
data usage is discussed under the heading Tracking Chronic Conditions on page 154.
There can be zero, one, or more rows per Patient ID. The patient_id, dx_version_1 and dx_cd_1
columns are required. Although patient ID, dx_version_1 and dx_cd_1 are the only required fields, the
presence of dates of service, place of service, provider ID, provider specialty,
provider_standard_specialty, procedure code, and revenue code may be required to generate specific
output data (See Data Constraints on page 28). The organization can optionally provide diagnosis
codes 2 through 5 for each row. If there are more than five diagnosis codes per record, the
organization may implement a custom format file to capture the additional diagnosis codes (see
Loading Data on page 58). Duplicating diagnosis codes to accommodate multiple procedures is
expected and will not influence the output of the ACG System. Likewise, the standard format provides
one ICD procedure code per record, but the organization may implement a custom format file to
capture additional ICD procedure codes. Exercise caution if providing cost in the medical services file
layout that costs are not duplicated from a header record across each detailed service line.

Tip: The ACG System accepts a variety of coding systems which must be identified using the
dx_version fields. The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is maintained by the World Health
Organization (WHO). If you are using WHO standard ICD-10 coding, the dx_version should be "10".
Many countries develop minor modifications to the ICD coding. In the US, these modifications are
referred to as clinical modifications (CM); therefore, the dx_version in the US should be "10CM". The
dx_version for SNOMED CT is "S".
Tip: Inpatient hospitalizations are defined based on inclusion of room and board revenue code, as
defined by the National Uniform Billing Committee (NUBC), in the range of 0100 to 0219 along with
either place of service code 21 or type of bill 011x, 012x or 018x. Alternatively, an inpatient
hospitalization can be defined by a place of service code of IP by itself.
Tip: If the user is interested in understanding the morbidity within the inpatient setting, a drg_cd
may be provided and can be used to produce the Analyze->Frequency Distributions->DRG by RUB
Distribution on page 512 with or without the use of a drg_version. In the absence of complete detail
from the inpatient setting, DRGs may also be used to inform risk assessment variables. If such detail
is to be extracted from the DRG, a drg_version must also be provided and referenced in your license
file.
Tip: The Supplemental Medical Services data is intended to provide better tracking of chronic
conditions on page 154 and for calculating newly diagnosed conditions on page 156. Options for how
these diagnoses are used by the software is determined by processing options explained in advanced
options on page 72. Users may provide the full file layout for the medical services file, or choose to
limit the supplementary file to only patient ID and diagnoses from a historical period.

Pharmacy Data File Format
This file should contain all pharmacy codes that were experienced for each patient during the
observation period. Special care should be used to provide only the final action claim with no activity
for voided or replaced claims. There can be zero, one, or more rows per Patient ID. The patient_id
and rx_cd columns are required.
Although patient_id and rx_code are the only required fields, the presence of rx_fill_date,
rx_days_supply and rx_quantity may be required to generate specific output data. See Data
Constraints on page 28. The organization may implement a custom format to re-order and/or pass
through variables in this file format (see Chapter 4: Loading Data on page 58).

HHS-CMS Enrollment File Format
The optional HHS-CMS enrollment data file format should contain all eligibility segments for each
patient during the observation period. There can be zero, one or more rows per Patient ID. If patients
have dual coverage, it is possible to have multiple records with overlapping enrollment dates.
Overlapping enrollment dates will trigger an HHS-CMS warning code but the records will be used as
provided.
This file is used to support the Hierarchical Condition Category models for risk adjustment applied
within the commercial Health Insurance Marketplace managed by the U.S. Department of Health and
Human Services and the Medicare Advantage program operated by the Centers for Medicare and
Medicaid Services (CMS). This file requires an additional license before the file may be processed by
the ACG System. An addendum to this documentation contains more information about these
models.
The patient_id, hhs_cms_benefit_begin_date and hhs_cms_benefit_end_date are required to generate
HHS-HCC and CMS-HCC risk scores. Other fields apply to either the HHS-HCC model applied within the
commercial Health Insurance Marketplace or the CMS-HCC model applied within the Medicare
Advantage program, denoted with the prefixes HHS_ and CMS_, respectively. The organization may
implement a custom format to re-order and/or pass through variables in this file format (see Loading
Data on page 58).

Using Local Allowable Rating Factors (ARF)
The HHS model includes an allowable rating factor for every age in the model based on the federal
age rating curve. Each state may develop its own age rating curve that complies with a maximum 3 to
1 age rating ratio. The ACG System can adapt to this requirement and utilize a local ARF file in the
HHS model calculations via the Tools > Options menu item.
A local ARF file must be a comma delimited file, containing a factor for every age from 0 through 65
inclusive, with the following columns:
• Age

Chapter 3: Loading Data
Chapter 3:
Loading Data
The ACG System is designed to handle custom file formats. You can add, delete, and relabel column
descriptions in each file layout. Any column name used in the ACG System algorithms must conform
to standard naming conventions. Additional custom names and descriptions may be provided to pass
through the system. Once you have added custom fields, these can then be used in the analyses for
filters and groups.
Custom File Formats
Using the chapter Basic Data Requirements on page 28 as a guide, prepare your own data to create a
Patient Data File, a Medical Services Data File, and a Pharmacy Data File according to the
specifications. If you choose to augment any of the file specifications with user-defined fields or re-
order the fields, you will want to create a custom file format which is recommended particularly for
the patient input file. If you create files following the file specification precisely, you will not need to
complete this step.
Creating a Custom File Format
You can add, delete, and rename fields in the patient, medical services, supplementary medical
services, pharmacy, lab results or HHS-CMS enrollment files. This chapter will walk through the
example of creating a custom patient file format. The steps for the additional custom file formats
would be the same.
1. On the ACG System for Windows desktop, click File > New. The New File window appears.
Figure9.NewFilewindow
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation

2. Select the Create Custom Patient File Format option, click Next, and click Finish. An untitled
tab displays on the ACG System for Windows desktop.
Figure10.FileFormatDefinition
3. Re-label, delete, or add columns as necessary.
• To relabel the column description, double-click the existing name and insert a new name.
• To delete a column, click the column name and then click the Delete button (or
click Edit > Delete).
• To add a column, click the empty column name and type the new column name, add data
type and column description, and press Enter. In order for a column to be recognized by
the ACG System software as a standard column, the column name must be precisely as it
is listed in the file format, described in Chapter 3: Basic Data Requirements on page 28.
The column name is case-sensitive and all standard column names must be lower case.
• To reorder columns use the yellow arrows to move columns up and down.
• Do not change the column names from the standard names provided. Alternate column
names will not be used by the ACG System algorithms but will be passed through the
system only.
• Do not utilize column names that equate to output generated by the ACG System. This
may create inconsistencies in the data type expected by the ACG System and your data
will not be preserved by the ACG System process.
4. Modify the column delimiter, quote enclosure, and row delimiter to match the file.
5. Click File > Save As The Save As window displays.
6. Give the file a unique name, and click Save. The file saves.

Expanding the Number of Diagnosis and ICD Procedure Codes Provided
You can also add, delete, and rename column descriptions in the Medical Services file. Patient_id and
dx_cd_1 are required fields. The Medical Services file can accommodate more than five diagnoses per
record using a custom file format. Any fields with the naming convention dx_cd_X will be used for
calculating morbidity in the ACG System. The data type for diagnosis codes should always be "string".
The Medical Services file can also accommodate multiple ICD procedure codes per record. The naming
convention is icd_proc_cd_X. There should be a corresponding dx_version_X or icd_proc_version_X for
each additional diagnosis and procedure code field or the ACG System will assume dx_version_1 and
icd_proc_version_1 apply to all subsequent diagnoses and procedures. Other non-standard fields will
be stored in the .acgd file and are exportable on the medical services export file type, but will not be
utilized by the ACG algorithms.

Risk Assessment Variables
One way the user can affect the output from the ACG System is with the selection of Risk Assessment
Variables. Risk Assessment Variables are inputs to the system provided by Johns Hopkins which
control the calculation of member-specific output variables.
The standard sets of Risk Assessment Variables delivered with the software are US-All Age, US-Non-
Elderly, US-Elderly and US-TANF. If an elderly model is selected, then all reference data and risk scores
will be calibrated against an elderly managed care population aged 65 or greater. The reference
population includes pharmacy benefits and expenditures so that pharmacy expense can be predicted
relative to a Medicare (United States federal program that pays for certain health care expenses for
people aged 65 or older)-eligible population. The US-TANF Risk Assessment Variables were calibrated
against a managed care population aged less than 65 funded through the medicaid program to low
income families with children. If a non-elderly model is selected, then all reference data and risk
scores will be calibrated against a managed care population aged less than 65. When the All age
model is selected, then coefficients are derived from pediatric (ages 0-17), adult (ages 18-64) and
elderly (ages 65+) populations, respectively, but expressed relative to the common adult mean.
As an example, to better understand the impact of selecting the US-All Age option, see Final ACG
Categories, Reference ACG Concurrent Risks, and RUBs on page 141 which shows the weights
assigned for each individual category separately for pediatric, adult and elderly populations.
Spreadsheets with additional detail on the US-All Age as well as similar distributions for the Elderly,
Non-Elderly and TANF reference populations may be found in the installation folder and Johns
Hopkins ACG Windows program group.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–71–

=== PÁGINA 72 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 3: Loading Data
The user is asked to select the Risk Assessment Variables to be used at the time that the input files
are specified. The Risk Assessment variables include:
• Reference ACG Concurrent Risk - An estimate of concurrent resource use associated with a given
ACG category based on a reference database and expressed as a relative value.
• Modeling Coefficients - The model parameter estimates associated with a given risk factor based
on a reference database. These coefficients are added for each member based on the risk factors
present to produce patient risk scores.
• Reference Prevalence Rates - RUB, ACG, ADG, MEDC, EDC, Major Rx-MG, and Rx-MG prevalence
rates for each age-sex cohort within a reference population. These rates are aggregated to form
the expected prevalence in the corresponding Standardized Morbidity Ratio and Distribution
analyses. Age-sex reference rates are also provided in the ADGs per patient, Diagnoses per patient,
and Ingredients per patient analyses. Reference percentages are provided for the ED Visit
Classification and the Laboratory Markers frequency distributions.
• Reference Utilization Metrics - Rates of services and conditions provided as comparison reference
rates in a variety of summary and distribution analyses.
• Resource Utilization Bands - Aggregations of ACG categories based upon estimates of concurrent
resource use providing a way of separating the population into broad co-morbidity groupings.
Several standard analyses use the distribution across RUBs.
• Frailty Marker - A dichotomous (on/off) variable that indicates whether an enrollee has a diagnosis
falling within any of the clusters that represent medical problems associated with frailty.
• Hospital Dominant Morbidity Types - Diagnoses that, based on expert clinical review, would be
associated with a high likelihood of hospitalization in the next year.
• CAL-SSA - Diagnoses that, when present, potentially identify a compassionate allowance condition
defined by the U.S. Social Security Administration.
Advanced Options
By default, the ACG System software automatically selects the best predictive model based on the
data found in the patient file (that is, whether or not total cost or pharmacy cost data is available for
each member) and the data found in the diagnoses and pharmacy input files (depending on whether
or not one or both are present). Optionally the user may request specific behavior from the software
by utilizing Advanced Model Options.
The selection of these options is controlled by clicking the buttons under the "Show Advanced
Options" section described in Loading Your Own Data on page 60.
Diagnostic Certainty - Stringent diagnostic certainty will apply an algorithm requiring more than one
instance of a diagnosis for a subset of chronic conditions that may be recorded provisionally prior to a
definitive diagnosis. The default for stringent diagnostic certainty is unchecked, meaning that a single
diagnosis code will be used unless more specific criteria are stated.
The recording of provisional diagnosis codes can falsely identify individuals for care management
programs and/or over-estimate costs. The goal of stringent diagnostic certainty is to provide greater
certainty of a given diagnosis for a subset of chronic conditions. When the Stringent Diagnostic
Certainty option is selected, the system may limit diagnoses used in calculating system markers. For a
subset of diagnoses that may be recorded provisionally, a second instance of a diagnosis is required
for the ACG System marker to be assigned. When first date of service is present in the medical
services file, the diagnosis must be present on two distinct dates of service. If date of service is not
present, the diagnosis must be present on two distinct medical services records.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–72–

=== PÁGINA 73 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 3: Loading Data
The processing selection related to diagnostic certainty will be identified in the model selection and
reported in the ACG Data File Summary Statistics and build options. Reference disease prevalence
may vary based upon this selection.
If the Apply option is selected for the Supplemental Diagnosis Method and the Stringent diagnostic
certainty option is selected, then a chronic diagnoses must appear twice across the Medical Services
and Supplemental services files. In all other instances selecting the Stringent diagnostic certainty
option requires two occurrences in the same time period, either the Medical Services or Supplemental
Medical Services or both files.
Diagnostic Filters - Using automatic diagnostic filters will exclude claims from certain places of service
or associated with certain types of procedures when the diagnosis is not associated with a face-to-
face encounter. The rules for excluding these diagnoses that may be recorded as rule-out, suspect or
provisional are provided in Typical Place of Service Codes to Exclude and Procedure Code Ranges to
Exclude on page 45. The default is checked to use automatic diagnostic filters to exclude potentially
rule-out, suspect or provisionally coded diagnoses from morbidity assessments.
The ACG System will exclude provisional diagnoses from morbidity assessments based upon Durable
Medical Equipment (DME), lab, and radiology procedures or place of service as described in Excluding
Lab and X-Ray Claims on page 45 in both Medical Services and Supplementary Medical Services files.
The automatic diagnostic filters will utilize data elements, such as procedure code and place of
service, defined in the Medical Services/Supplementary Medical Services file format. If not all data
elements are provided, consider if it is necessary to pre-filter the data to accommodate potentially
rule-out, suspect or provisionally coded diagnoses. The choice to apply automatic diagnostic filters will
be applied globally to both Medical Services and Supplementary Medical Services files.
The filtering of provisional diagnoses applies to ADGs, EDCs, Frailty, HOSDOM, CAL-SSA, Mechanical
Ventilation, Dialysis Service, Cancer Treatment, Pregnancy, Delivery, Low Birth Weight, Chronic
Conditions, Complications of Diabetes, and Condition Markers.
Pharmacy in CRI - Using pharmacy fills and procedures in concurrent models determines whether
medication data will be used in the determination of the unscaled and/or rescaled Concurrent Risk.
The Concurrent Risk is derived from a linear regression and may optionally consider pharmacy data
when available. It is the default and strongly recommended that this option remain unselected. When
left at the default setting, concurrent risk assessment will use age, sex and diagnosis only. The option
to include pharmacy data is provided to assess potential biases in the diagnosis data that might be
reflected in the pharmacy data. However, due to the circularity in defining morbidity based on
prescribing, it is not recommended that pharmacy data contribute to risk for any profiling or payment
applications.
All Models - Calculating all valid predictive models produces a separate output file where the rows
are the patients and the columns are all possible predictive modeling scores. This file is useful for
analysts wishing to compare the suite of ACG System predictive modeling tools looking to contrast the
diagnosis, pharmacy, and diagnosis + pharmacy-based predictive models. By default this option is not
selected, and the ACG System will not produce an all model export file.
Note: Selecting the option to calculate all valid models may cause substantial processing delays. This
is a data-intensive activity producing hundreds of scores for each individual.
Utilization Markers (calculate utilization markers) - Calculating utilization markers determines whether
the ACG System will calculate utilization markers from the detail provided in the medical services file.
The default is for the ACG System to automatically calculate dialysis service, nursing service, major
procedure, cancer treatment, psychotherapy service, mechanical ventilation, CAL SSA, emergency
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–73–

=== PÁGINA 74 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 3: Loading Data
department visits, inpatient hospitalizations, inpatient days, all cause inpatient hospitalizations,
unplanned inpatient hospitalizations, readmissions 30 day, unplanned readmissions 30 day, and
outpatient visits from the medical services file. When the calculate utilization markers option is
checked, the calculated field will overwrite data provided in the same field in the patient file.
Utilization Markers (ignore minimum requirements) - When the ignore minimum data requirements
to calculate utilization markers option is selected, the ACG System software will loosen the criteria
needed to generate individual risk markers, pharmacy adherence, and the hospitalization risk models.
Under the default behavior, the data required to populate the utilization markers, including dates of
service, place of service, revenue codes and procedure code must be present on at least one record.
Additionally, at least one patient must meet the criteria for having an inpatient hospitalization. If
these criteria are not met, the hospitalization risk scores are suppressed. This behavior is intentional
because under normal circumstances the failure to calculate hospitalization risk alerts the user to a
data problem. However, there are circumstances when very small populations or populations with a
bias may be fed through the software which do not meet these data requirements. The ignore
minimum data requirements allows the user to override this behavior once data validation has
occurred.
If columns such as place of service, revenue code, and procedure code are not available in the
medical services file, the user may optionally supply this information, calculated manually, in the
patient file. If utilization measures are provided in the patient file, uncheck this box. It is possible to
implement a mixed model where selected fields are presented on the patient file while others are
calculated from medical services. To employ this mixed model, uncheck the calculate utilization
makers option. A column that is not populated (i.e., 100% of the values are null) will be calculated
while any columns with values provided on the patient file will be maintained as provided.
Note: The exception is that when at least one inpatient hospitalization marker is provided on the
patient file, it is assumed all six markers of hospitalization will be provided. The inpatient
hospitalization markers are the all cause inpatient hospitalization count, inpatient hospitalization
count, inpatient days, unplanned inpatient hospitalization count, readmission within 30 days and
unplanned readmissions within 30 days.
Pharmacy Procedures - The default option is to use both medical services procedures and drug codes
provided on the pharmacy file for assessing pharmacy morbidity. Selecting this option excludes the
imputation of pharmacy use from procedure codes on the medical services file. The source of
pharmacy morbidity will be identified in the Rx-MG export files. Pharmacy data is a minimum
requirement for the system to calculate Rx-MGs; without the pharmacy input file, Rx-MGs will not be
calculated from procedures in medical services alone.
Low Birthweight Status - The ignore low birthweight status for ACG splitting option will aggregate
infant ACG categories together when the morbidity level is similar. For example, this option would
produce ACG category 5310 for infants: 0-5 ADGs, no major ADGs instead of producing ACG
categories 5311 and 5312 for low birthweight and normal birthweight infants, respectively. Based on
the improved explanatory power of splitting the ACG categories based on birthweight, the default is
for this option to be not selected.
Delivered Status - The ignore delivered status for ACG splitting option will aggregate pregnancy ACG
categories together when the morbidity level is similar regardless of delivery status. For example, this
option would produce ACG category 1710 for pregnancy: 0-1 ADGs instead of producing ACG
categories 1711 and 1712 for delivered and not delivered pregnancies, respectively. Based on the
improved explanatory power of splitting the ACG categories based on delivery status, the default is
for this option to be not selected.

=== PÁGINA 75 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 3: Loading Data
Prior Costs - In general, including prior costs will improve performance of the predictive model
performance. It is true, however, that including prior costs in the model makes it look more like a
prior cost model. Therefore, in certain instances, such as a federal agency interested in using
predictive modeling scores for payment, you may want to exclude prior cost from the model. The
user may want to check this option when cost data is incomplete or biased (e.g., a subset of claim
types are capitated or pharmacy data is unavailable). This option is also useful for certain disease or
case management applications by removing the influence of prior cost information from the
predictions. By default, this option is not selected, meaning that prior cost information will be used
when it is provided.
Cost Truncation Point - Individuals with extreme costs skew basic statistics such as the mean cost per
patient. This mean cost is used as the basis for many estimations within the ACG System software,
including Local ACG Concurrent Risk, Local Age-Sex Concurrent Risk, Predicted Cost Range, and Care
Density Cost Saving Range. Users can use this option to define a cost truncation limit to minimize the
impact of high cost outliers. The cost amount entered beside the "Cost Truncation Point” will be used
to truncate patient total cost amounts, thereby defining the column "total cost” as the maximum of
patient total cost and the cost truncation point. The remainder of cost calculations in the system use
this total cost field. The original provided or calculated total cost amount will be preserved in the
column "untruncated total cost.” If no cost truncation point is provided, the columns total cost and
untruncated total cost will be equivalent.
Total Cost Risk Level Quantiles - A fixed list of 11 quantiles available to users for selection, to define
the total cost risk level stratification. Users may choose between one and three quantiles, with the
default being 60 and 90. See definitions and detail in the topic Risk Stratification on page 255.
HHS-CMS Year - This indicates the model year published by CMS to be applied. In payment
applications, the HHS models are concurrent models so the model year represents the observation
period and the payment year. The CMS models are prospective models so the model year represents
the payment year. Although the user can select any observation period, for the typical CMS payment
cycle, the observation year is the year prior to the model year selected.

• File - Opening/closing/saving ACG System data, license or format files with .acgd, .acgl or .acgf

Opening *.acgd Files
After the input text files have been processed by the system, the results are stored in a *.acgd
format. Use File > Open to select a previously processed .acgd file.

Report Options
Many of the reports available through the Analyze menu may be customized at the user’s discretion.
Customization is controlled through the Report Options menu that includes up to six concepts:
• Filters
• Options
• Comprehensive Profile options
• Utilization Profile options
• Calculations
• Groups
Not all concepts apply to all analyses. When managing report options globally through the Tools
menu, all options are configurable. However, certain options may appear grayed out or may not be
visible when not applicable to a particular analysis.
Filters
Use filters to control the selection of patients from the active data file to be included in the analytical
view. If no filters are defined, all patients will be included in an analysis. A typical use for filters is to
run an analysis on a sub-set of a population, such as a single benefit plan, company, product, or line
of business. Filters can be defined on any available column in the patient data, which also includes all
ACG-calculated elements and additional custom fields imported as part of the data file. It is possible
to stack filters using Boolean "And" or "Or" operators. For example, to run an analysis on all patients
in the PPO Product that have Employer ID 2051 or all patients in the Benefit Plan POS_A, fill out the
filter as follows:

Note: The effect of an "Any" line is to apply the filter criteria on each side of the Or separately. In
the example used, a patient in the Benefit Plan POS_A would be included even if they didn't have
the Employer 2051 due to the "Any" condition. However, a patient in the PPO Product would only be
included if they have the Employer 2051 due to the "All" criteria at that level.
Filters can be saved and recalled for any future analysis. Filters are saved within a users’ Windows
profile so they are specific to a single computer and user.

Filters, and other report options, appear in multiple contexts. Filters may be managed globally, as in
the following example, or each analysis offers the ability to filter. Filter screens are used in the
calculation function described below. Filters may also be applied on import and export. The list of
available fields may change based on context. In some analyses there may be both patient filters and
patient warning filters. See usage of patient warning filters described in Warning List on page 500.

2. Click Add Criteria. The criteria options display.
Figure24.Filtercriteriaoptions
The list of fields available for filtering will include calculated columns that have already been
defined as part of the Report Option. See Calculations on page 86.
3. Select a column from the patient data (A).
4. Select the qualifier required to appropriately subset the data (B). The majority of the qualifiers
are self-explanatory; some exceptions are outlined following:
• Starts With, Does Not Start With, Ends With, and Does Not End With - These qualifiers
are often used with data-specific reporting dimensions such as benefit plan, company,
product, or line of business.
• Does Not Contain and Contains - These qualifiers are typically used when including /
excluding specific MEDC Codes, EDC Codes, Major Rx-MG Codes and/or Rx-MG Codes.
These codes are stored as single strings (codes ordered alphabetically, separated by
spaces), so one of these qualifiers must be used in order to ensure the entire string is
evaluated for the presence / absence of the specified code.
• Pregnant, Delivered, Low Birthweight, Dialysis Service, Nursing Service, Cancer
Treatment, Major Procedure, Psychotherapy Service, Mechanical Ventilation, and CAL-
SSA - These qualifiers are stored as binary markers, where 0=No and 1=Yes. While these
markers may appear as Y or N on the Comprehensive Patient Clinical Profile Report, they
are stored in the data as 0 or 1. Therefore, the filters must use the 0 or 1 designation. If Y
or N is entered as a filter value for one of these markers, an error message will state that
the value Y or N is invalid for the selected marker. This will be an indicator that 0 or 1
should be used instead. The remaining binary markers (Frailty Flag, High Risk Unexpected
Pharmacy Cost, and No Generalist Seen) are stored as Y/N.
5. Continue to add criteria until all filtering requirements have been satisfied. For each criteria
added, consider whether an additional All, Any, or None qualifier is required. If more criteria

Options
For some of the analyses, there is an additional Options tab. This provides the user the option to use
local ACG or reference ACG concurrent risks, local or reference prevalence rates, or total or pharmacy

=== PÁGINA 82 ===

Chapter 4: Operating the ACG System Software
hospitalization model or pharmacy adherence type to display. To summarize, the corresponding
options and analyses are:
• Concurrent Risk Type: Options include Local ACG Concurrent Risk, Reference ACG Concurrent Risk
or Reference Concurrent Risk. These options are visible in the analyses as the estimated
concurrent resource use in EDC by Resource Utilization Band (RUB) Distribution, MEDC by RUB
Distribution, Rx-MG by RUB Distribution, and DRG by RUB Distribution. Such comparisons allow
within group comparisons to be contrasted to external or reference comparisons. Additionally, the
user may select the concurrent risk score to display on the Comprehensive Patient Clinical Profile
and the Utilization Profile.
• Cost Model Type: Options include Total Cost or Pharmacy Cost. The cost model selection is used to
calculate Predicted Resource Use in Cost Predictions by Selected Condition, Cost Predictions by Rx-
MGs, Hospital predictions for Select Major Conditions, and Pharmacy Adherence for Select
Conditions. This option also affects the model displayed in the Utilization profile.
• Hospitalization Model Type: The options are specific to the hospital prediction model, i.e., IP
Hospitalization, IP Hospitalization within 6 months, IP ICU Hospitalization, IP Extended
Hospitalization, IP Injury Hospitalization, Readmission. The model selected is displayed in the
Hospital predictions for Select Major Conditions. This option also affects the model displayed in the
Utilization profile.
• Prevalence Type: Options include Local or Reference Prevalence Rates. The prevalence rates are
displayed as Age/sex adjusted expected rate/1000 in Standardized Morbidity Ratio by EDC,
Standardized Morbidity Ratio by MEDC, Standardized Morbidity Ratio by Rx-MG, and Standardized
Morbidity Ratio by Major Rx-MG. Additionally, prevalence type enables the user to select a
reference population for the ADG Distribution, ACG Distribution, and RUB Distribution from the
Analyze menu and the Ingredients per Patient, ADGs per Patient and Diagnoses per Patient
analyses from the Validate menu.
• Pharmacy Adherence Type: Options are MPR, CSA or PDC to reflect the pharmacy adherence
possession measure to display on the Utilization Profile.
• Logo file: Use the [...] to browse and select a logo file for inclusion on .pdf formatted reports (e.g.,
Comprehensive Patient Clinical Profile and Utilization Profile). Logos will display in the upper right
hand corner. Logo files can be in *.png, *.jpeg, *.jpg, *.gif, and *.bmp with dimensions of 60 pixels
by 60 pixels.
• Comments: Free text comments can be added to tabular analyses and the Utilization Profile
Report. The comments will display on the Report Options tab.

Calculations
Use calculations to incorporate new data attributes into your analyses. Columns defined in
calculations may be incorporated into filters or groups. Calculations can be defined on any available
column in the patient data, which also includes all ACG-calculated elements and additional custom
fields imported as part of the data file. More than one column may be added, each with their own
specification.
In the following figure, three calculated columns have been added: Program, Coordination and High
Risk Pregnancy. The definition for High Risk Pregnancy is displayed on the right hand panel. Using
combinations of the Pregnancy without Delivery marker, ACG Code, Hospital Dominant Morbidity
Types and Condition Markers, this calculation is exposing the specific risk for selecting the woman into
a high risk pregnancy program. Each of these statements operates in the order that they are
presented, so if a woman is defined under both the "Comorbid with 1+ Major ADGs" and "Hospital
Dominant Condition" definitions, she will be represented only in the "Comorbid with 1+ Major ADGs"
grouping.

Groups
The analyses in the ACG System are conceptually different from reports in other systems and are best
conceived as data views. The primary difference is that a single analysis can generate several
stratifications in one single session. The Groups define the stratifications that an analysis will produce.
The Groups tab is originally populated with the default population stratifiers for the selected analysis.
The underlying details of a group can be displayed by selecting it (i.e., clicking on it). The currently
selected group displays a Name, which is the title of the section on the analysis, and the categories,
which are the list of columns that define the stratifiers for that group. You can add new groups,
modify groups, or remove groups before an analysis is run. If custom fields have been created, you
can build groups on these columns as well.

Options and Option Sets
The Filters, Options, Calculations and Groups applied to an analysis are referred to collectively as
Report "Options". It is this set of attributes that are defined and stored together under "Saved
Options". The Report Options may be defined on any analysis or from the Tools menu.
Figure32.ManageReportOptionscommand
After Report Options are saved, they may be applied to any analysis. Report Options may also be
organized into groups called "Option Sets". Each Option Set may contain a number of saved Report
Options and is stored in a separate file. The user may direct the file location of their saved Option
Sets. The Option Set files will have a *.acgr extension. This allows users to easily backup and/or share
Option Sets. A robust set of example options are described in Clinical Screening on page 280 and
delivered in the ACG System software as "Example Option Set".
Tip: Saved Report Options may be used to generate analyses using the command line interface.

Exporting Analyses
From each analysis tab it is possible to click the Export Table button (or click Tools > Export) to
export the complete analysis results to Microsoft Excel or to export a single tab's data to a Delimited
Data File (like a CSV file). Choose the type of file to export to. The Export All Tabs To Excel File option
will export all data in the analysis, saving each tab to a separate Microsoft Excel worksheet. The
Export Current Tab To Delimited Data File will export the data in the currently selected tab to a single
data file (comma-delimited or tab-delimited text file). You can choose to write out a header row as
the first row in the data file. This row contains the names of the columns and is useful when
importing the data into another database.

Specifically for these two formatted reports, there is also an option to bulk export these analyses.

Chapter 5: Validating Results
Chapter 5:
Validating Results
This chapter is intended for the programmer/analyst who will actually be running the ACG System
software. This chapter outlines a series of steps that will help you assess the face validity of the
grouping process.
Basic Review Process
The first stage in the quality control process includes an initial review of the reports automatically
produced by the software. These include:
1. Review the Summary Statistics tab including verifying the input files, person counts, non-match
rates, and that the number of warning messages is reasonable. The rows identifying the data
present in the system should match expectations based on the data provided.
2. A second tab of Source Related Summary Statistics provides observation dates, unique codes and
non-matched codes for each source represented in the input files. This is intended to assist in
isolating potential data issues when multiple data sources are integrated.
3. Review the Patient Sample tab to confirm the population of each field within the .acgd file and
that the data results match the patient source file.
4. Review the Local Weights tab to validate the presence of most or all ACG categories. Of particular
interest is a relationship between the pregnancy and newborn ACG categories, as well as the
number of non-user and no Dx code ACG categories.
5. Review the Local Age/Sex Weights table. Small numbers of individuals in a category, e.g., less than
30 patients, may be a warning to exercise caution in applying age-sex weights. In general, age-sex
weights are expected to trend upward with increasing age.
6. Review the Age-Sex Distribution tab against the known age and sex mix of the population.
7. Review the Total Cost Risk and Hospitalization Risk Distribution tabs.
Note: Expect to see a large portion of the population with probability scores below 0.40.
8. Review the Utilization Summary tab to identify any large variations in the identification rate of the
utilization markers.
9. Review the ED Visit Classification tab for any large variations from anticipated counts for all ED
visit types and unclassified visits. Additionally, the ED Visit Classification option in the Analyze
menu provides reference population percentages.
10. Review the Build Options tab. Information on input files (patient, diagnosis, and pharmacy) as well
as reference weights (e.g., Risk Assessment Variables) and options selected for the ACG Risk
Models are easily summarized. 'Refer to Build Options in Build Options Tab on page 497.
The second stage in the quality control process includes producing and evaluating those reports
available in through the Validate and Analyze menus (reference the respective "Review of Reports"
sections following).
Review of Reports Produced Automatically by the Software

Summary Statistics Tab
The first tab that displays after processing the data or opening an .acgd file is the Summary Statistics
tab. This tab provides a summary review of the input file(s) that were processed, a summary person
count, information on risk models and options selected, as well as information on non-match rates
and the number of warning messages generated. Full detail for each tab may be found in Summary
Statistics on page 483.
A second tab displays a subset of summary statistics by user-defined source on each input file. These
Source Related Summary Statistics are intended to assist in isolating high rates of non-matched codes
or unexpected observation dates so that the source data may be corrected.
Tip: Summary statistics may be exported as a multiple sheet workbook using Tools > Export.
General Data Checks
The first check is to verify that the number of patients processed is consistent with the general
knowledge of the input data.
A separate patient count is provided for patients aged 65 and older. The first and last medical service
date and first and last pharmacy fill dates are provided. These dates should match user expectations
and should ideally represent the same 12 month period from each source.
If cost is provided in the medical services and pharmacy input files, review the summary statistics of
Total Medical Services Cost and Total Pharmacy Cost to ensure that complete cost information has
been provided.
The Risk Assessment Variables on page 71 should be aligned with the characteristics of the population
under consideration.
The mapping file version should be the most current. Update the mapping file on page 20 if
necessary.
Data Presence
The Summary Statistics tab also provides an indication about the inclusion of utilization data to
support the hospitalization prediction models, provider data to support care coordination markers and
pharmacy detail to support the calculation of pharmacy adherence measures. There are 45 individual
