Rx-MG Medication Assignment Methodology
A team of Johns Hopkins physicians and pharmacists evaluated each unique active ingredient / route
of administration combination in the international pharmacopeia. This review, wherever possible,
factored in U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved and common off-label uses of the
drugs. Each unique active ingredient/route of administration combination was assigned to a single Rx-
MG according to this clinical review, based on the clinical judgement regarding the primary use. In
some instances, dosage strength informed the final Rx-MG assignment, e.g., opiates may be
associated with differing pain categories based on strength. The biomedical literature was also
extensively reviewed for evidence of alternate and prevalent international use of medications. Finally,
current evidence-based clinical prescribing practices were also considered.
Each clinical reviewer was apportioned a group of drugs within major Rx-MGs with which they were
most familiar. Each reviewer was then trained in the review process (applying the four criteria
specified above) by the project's principal investigator, Dr. Chris Forrest (who also was responsible for
the original version of the Rx-MGs). Where data were available, the clinical reviewers were provided
with distributions and O:E ratios of EDCs within each ingredient-route. The reviewers decided whether
to retain the existing Rx-MG for the ingredient-route or assign it to a new Rx-MG based on evidence
described above. They were also asked to record the logic that led them to the assignment decision.
All of the drug assignments were reviewed by the principal investigator. Disagreements were
reconciled during one on one meetings between the principal investigator and the clinical reviewer.
The completed assignments were then sent out for external review. The process was repeated until
the assignments were stable.
The resultant ingredient-routes were then mapped to NDCs using the Multum/Cerner Lexicon. The
NDCs were linked to a subset of the Legacy PharMetrics Adjudicated Claims Database licensed from
IQVIA, formerly QuintilesIMS. The focus was on patients under 65 years of age who had two years of
full enrollment for both medical and pharmacy benefits. The resultant database was the basis for
extensive analysis to test and validate the new Rx-MG assignments. There was an iterative process
whereby the results of the analyses were fed back to the reviewers who made changes. The analyses
were then repeated. Ingredient-routes were coded to highest level of specificity as needed. The
primary goal was to achieve comparable, if not improved, predictive performance. When the
assignments reached final form, the principal investigator wrote descriptions that summarized the
clinical logic behind each Rx-MG.

the table below.

Chapter 7: Pharmacy-based Markers
The NDC number is a United States-based 11-digit numeric identifier for each drug product on the
market. In the ACG System, NDC numbers are included on the pharmacy input file, and from there
are grouped and used to assign Rx-MGs. Creating of Rx-MG groupings from NDCs involves collapsing
nearly 240,000 unique NDC codes to about 4,050 ingredient/route of administration combinations
which are then assigned to an Rx-MG.
NDC code mappings are updated quarterly within the ACG System mapping file updates. Typically,
1,500 - 2,500 new NDC codes representing 50 - 75 new ingredients are assigned Rx-MG codes each
quarter. Newly-mapped NDC codes are inclusive of new products, manufacturers, drug routes and
package size.
The assignment of NDC codes to Rx-MGs uses the first nine (9) digits of the NDC less the last two
digits identifying package size where feasible (beginning with V11.1). If there is any ambiguity
regarding the active ingredient or route of administration based on the first nine digits, the
assignment of the Rx-MG relies on the full 11-digit code. This practice allows the ACG System to more
quickly assign NDCs that are in common use, reducing the number of non-matched pharmacy codes.
Most NDC codes representing drugs are assigned to a single Rx-MG, and just 2% are mapped to
"Other/Other." NDC codes representing medical supplies, exclusively over-the counter medications,
and other non-pharmaceutical items are not assigned to an Rx-MG but are included in the map for
completeness.
Ensure your ACG System implementation pulls in these quarterly mapping updates to capture new
medications/NDC codes with the most current crosswalks. System users may check the number of
non-matched NDC codes in the Summary Statistics report, and may export non-matched NDC codes.
It is possible that a small frequency of NDC codes to not match to ACG System inherent codes, due to
unique manufacturers or introduction of new package sizes not yet available in commercial drug
databases.
HCPCS
If HCPCS pharmacy codes are available in the Medical Services input file, the Rx-MG assignments will
also consider medications administered (typically injections and intravenous) in the physician's office
and hospital outpatient clinics. The HCPCS sometimes use brand names instead of generic ingredients
that needed to be identified. Further, the HCPCS sometimes use the route "injectable" very broadly to
include intravenous drugs.
ATCs
The Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification system (ATCs) are an international drug taxonomy
that is curated by the World Health Organization. The nomenclature uses non-proprietary names, and
is a hierarchical classification. There are 5 levels in the classification: Main Anatomic/Pharmacology
group (14); Sub-group Pharmacology/Therapeutic; Sub-group Chemical/Pharmacology/ Therapeutic;
Chemical Substance. Only one ATC code is assigned per route of administration, but single ingredients
can have multiple assigned ATCs.
The ACG System team regularly updates the assignment of new drug codes to Rx-MGs.
High, Moderate, and Low Impact Rx-MGs
Within the Patient Rx-MG Assignments on page 441 as well as in the Comprehensive Patient Clinical
Profile Report, the Rx-MGs associated with an individual are categorized as High, Moderate, or Low
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Chapter 7: Pharmacy-based Markers
impact. The definition for these categories is based on the individual contribution of the condition to
the predictive modeling score. The specific criteria are as follows:
• High Impact Rx-MG: Coefficient >1 in the pharmacy derived predictive model without prior cost
predicting total cost
• Moderate Impact Rx-MG: Coefficient between 0.1 and 1.0 in the pharmacy derived predictive
model without prior cost predicting total cost
• Low Impact Rx-MG: Coefficient < 0.1 in the pharmacy derived predictive model without prior cost
predicting total cost
The specific impact for each Rx-MG category is documented in the Rx-MG Codes and Descriptions on
page 382.
Active Ingredient Count
An active ingredient count is calculated as the count of unique active ingredients encountered in the
patient 's drug claims. Generally, each individual ingredient from a combination drug (multiple active
ingredients assigned a single rx code) where an Rx-MG is assigned that does not begin with 'ZZZ' is
counted as an active ingredient. If HCPCS codes are available in the Medical Services input file, the
active ingredient count will consider medications administered (typically as injections) in the
physician's office in addition to drugs identified in the pharmacy file.
Drugs categorized into the "Other" major Rx-MG (ZZZxXXX) will not contribute to the active ingredient
count. This marker is a proxy for identifying poly-pharmacy members and contributes independently
and significantly to the prediction of cost. This marker is incorporated into all pharmacy-based
predictive models. Members with an active ingredient count of 20 or greater get additional weight in
the predictive models.
Proximal Active Ingredient Count
A proximal active ingredient count is calculated in the same way as the Active Ingredient Count
described in the last section, except that only fill dates in the last 120 days are considered. In the case
of drugs designated by HCPCS procedure codes and provided in the Medical Services input file, the
service begin date must be in the last 120 days. Looking back 120 days (approximately 4 months) is
intended to give a more accurate picture of the active ingredients in the currently prescribed drugs
for an individual patient. In order to be able to ascertain the correct 120-day period, this measure will
use the build options "observation begin date" and "observation end date" when provided (see
Analysis Time Frame on page 36 and build options on page 497) or will impute an observation period
from the last fill date. When calculated, the Proximal Active Ingredient Count value will always be less
than or equal to the Active Ingredient Count.
Novel Rx Scores
Along with existing ACG markers, new claims-based pharmacy markers can be applied to help health
care providers and organizations identify patients with higher likelihood to encounter adverse drug
events or non-adherence. There are two new concepts, each of which have three new markers.
Version 13.0 introduces two new sets of Pharmacy based markers for "Medication Complexity" and
"High Caution Medications". These new markers can help organizations identify patients suitable for
medication review.

Medication Complexity Scores
Medication Complexity Scores highlight medications with complex instructions for use, including
routes of administration, frequency, or those which require devices.
The set of Medication Complexity markers is designed to quantify the overall complexity of a patient's
drug regimen.
Each drug claim is scored in two ways:
1. Number of doses taken each day extrapolated from data in the prescription claim
(ComponentB). For example, two tablets taken three times a day would give a score of 6.
2. Difficulty of administration (ComponentA). For example, an oral tablet would score 1 and a
subcutaneous injection 3.
Once each drug claim is scored, three new markers are calculated:
• Medication Complexity Score (medication_complexity_score) is an overall score based on
summing the complexity scores (ComponentA + ComponentB) for a patient's individual
prescriptions.
• Complex Medication (complex_medication) is a binary marker triggered if any one individual
medication is considered complex (defined as a Component A score >= 3 AND a ComponentB
score >= 3), where 1 indicates a complex medication.
• Number of Medication Complexity Score claims (number_mcs_claims) is the number of
pharmacy claims, after data cleansing, that have a positive ComponentA score AND a positive
ComponentB score.
In order to activate the Medication Complexity Scores, a pharmacy input file is required with
Pharmacy code, Rx Fill Date, Rx Days Supply, and Rx Quantity present in the file.
High Caution Medication Scores
High Caution (or "risky") Medication Scores highlight medications with inherent risk of adverse drug
events (ADEs) which include life threatening complications, or those that require therapeutic drug
monitoring for safety.
• High Caution Rx Score (high_caution_rx_score) is an overall score based on the count of the
number of distinct categories of high caution medications a patient is receiving.
• High Caution Medication (high_caution_medication) is a binary marker triggered if the patient
is receiving any high caution medication, where a 1 indicates a high caution medication.
• High Caution Rx Categories (high_caution_rx_categories) is a list of high caution categories,
separated by spaces. The categories have a space delimited list of all unique three-character
high caution categories triggered for the patient which is specified during the computation of
high caution Rx scores.
In order to activate the High Caution Medication Scores, a pharmacy input file is required with
Pharmacy code, Rx Fill Date, and Rx Days Supply present in the file.

It is not uncommon for there to be claims for the same patient, where the drug code and fill date are
the same. For the purposes of the novel Rx scores these claims are considered duplicates. Only one
claim in a set of duplicate claims will contribute to the novel Rx Scores. The number of patients with
duplicate pharmacy claims found is given in the Warnings Distribution report (warning 25: Patient has
potentially duplicate pharmacy records).
The presence of duplicate claims will affect the novel Rx score computations, especially in the case
where two claim lines are submitted where one is a modification of an original and where the
quantities may have changed. If Medication Complexity Score or High Caution Rx Score cannot be
computed for any of the set of duplicate claims, then all claims in the set of duplicates are invalid for
calculation of these markers. Likewise, if Medication Complexity Score cannot be computed for any of
the set of duplicate claims, the claim with the highest Rx Days' Supply may be chosen to calculate the
High Caution Medication concepts. If Rx Days' Supply is null or 0 for all claims in a set of duplicates,
then all claims from the set of duplicate claims are invalid for calculation of High Caution Medication
concepts.
Refer to the Patient and ACG Results file on page 405 for the new novel Rx Scores outputs.
Applications of Novel Rx Scores
These two new markers can also be incorporated into ACG risk adjustment models to explain health
care costs and utilization. One study using real-world data showed that in a large commercially
insured population, individuals with 1+ complex or high caution medication marker had higher
comorbidity, health care costs and utilization than their counterparts, both concurrently and
prospectively.
Adding all claims-based pharmacy markers separately or together into the risk adjustment models
with various degrees of baseline information provided the greatest improvement in explaining
concurrent and prospective pharmacy costs, compared with medical (non-medication) costs; however,
these pharmacy markers did not have much added value in explaining health care utilization beyond
the base models.
An individual's medication use derived from pharmacy claims can be used to populate markers of
medication risk. Evidence suggests that these complex and high caution pharmacy markers can be
used as markers of added risk, especially when predicting pharmacy-related health care outcomes.
Additionally, these markers may also be used to efficiently identify patients with specific
characteristics related to medication use who could benefit from pharmacist intervention to reduce
health care costs, utilization and/or adverse events.

Chapter 8: Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based Markers
Chapter 8:
Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based Markers
The ACG System outputs a number of markers derived from a combination of the patient's diagnosis
code history and medication fills from all encounters during the observation period. These markers
provide a unique, patient-level lens into combined diagnostic history and medication use, highlighting
opportunities to improve clinical care and optimize medication use.
Broadly, markers described in this chapter include:
• Condition Markers identify the presence or absence of 22 chronic diseases in an individual
patient. If the condition is present, the condition marker describes the modality by which the
condition was identified. The additional "Untreated" column indicates if the condition may be
diagnosed but untreated by relevant medications.
• Pharmacy Adherence Markers measure adherence to medication for 17 specific conditions
using Medication Possession Ratio (MPR), Proportion of Days Covered (PDC) or Continuous
Single-Interval Availability (CSA) metrics. Adherence markers also calculate and display
meaningful gaps in medication supply.
• High Risk Opioid Use markers of risky use of physician-prescribed opiate medications.
As described in the Clinical Screening chapter on page 280, Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based markers may
be used alone, or in combination with other disease and risk markers, to identify patients with
opportunity to improve medication use, areas for improvement in coding and documentation, and to
support pharmacist clinical care.
Condition Markers
The ACG System uses condition markers to highlight select chronic conditions that are commonly
tracked by ACG System users, focus for disease management programs, or warranting ongoing
medication therapy. This marker set contains 22 individual conditions, listed later in this chapter.
Condition markers indicate the presence of the disease in each individual patient and, if present, the
relevant data source through which the condition was identified. Conditions may be identified through
medications (pharmacy criteria), diagnosis codes (treatment criteria), or both sources.
Condition markers are output at the patient-level from the ACG System in the "Patients and ACG
Results" export as "XX_Condition"; for example, Diabetes_Condition or Glaucoma_Condition. The
condition marker column can have one of 5 mutually exclusive values, listed in order of precedence:

The "TRT" marker is designed to show treatment of a condition and requires a minimum of two fills
on separate dates not more than 210 days apart for a relevant drug. The "TRT" marker is only
considered for 17 of the 22 chronic conditions. 9 of these 17 conditions require a diagnosis also to
trigger TRT, whereas 8 conditions can be given the TRT marker based on pharmacy data alone.
There are three sets of criteria required to calculate the Condition marker:
1. Diagnosis criteria - a specified EDC; required for ICD and BTH, and for some conditions for TRT.
2. Rx pharmacy criteria - a specified Rx-MG, or a drug from a specified drug class.
3. TRT pharmacy criteria - a drug from a specified drug class.
Drugs within each specified drug class that are relevant to each condition marker, are limited to drugs
with a documented indication for treatment of the condition.

Pharmacy Adherence
Significance of Pharmacy Adherence for Effective Care
There is a considerable literature on pharmacy adherence and a substantial body of evidence that
high levels of medication adherence yield improved therapeutic outcomes and more cost effective
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–183–

=== PÁGINA 184 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 8: Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based Markers
treatment. Medication adherence represents an important dimension of effective disease
management.
Medication adherence is one dimension of patient compliance with therapy. Optimally, medication
adherence means taking the correct drugs, for the correct indications, at the correct times, at the
correct dose, and under the proper conditions for safe and effective use (storage, shelf life, avoiding
substances that could affect efficacy, etc.)
The only way to accurately assess medication adherence on all of these dimensions is through direct
patient observation, a highly impractical approach. Researchers have developed a number of less
intrusive strategies for assessing medication adherence including patient logs, periodic assessments of
the patient’s medication supply, and electronic sensors in the medication bottles that record when
the bottle was opened. These approaches constitute indicators of medication adherence, but none
fully address all of the dimensions of medication adherence defined above.
A significant amount of medication adherence research relies on information that is reported on
pharmacy claims. Claims data provide an indicator of medication possession. The pharmacy claim
captures the date that the medication prescription was filled and the number of days supply. There is
substantial literature on medication possession that detail a number of widely used metrics. For an
excellent review, see Hess et al. (Annals of Pharmacotherapy, 40:1280-1288, 2006). The ACG System
pharmacy adherence markers were developed in line with these existing methodologies.
Development of Possession/Adherence Markers
Generally, measurement strategies have targeted specific possession events (i.e., gaps) or average
time of possession expressed as a ratio (supply over prescribing period).
The ACG System employs both of these strategies as they address different dimensions of adherence.
Gaps in filling medication prescriptions capture acute occurrences and may represent a therapeutically
significant event that could be overlooked if only averages were considered. Gaps, if captured on a
timely basis, are amenable to care management intervention. Averages represent how well
medication is supplied over a span of time (i.e., one year). They are a good summary indicator of
possession that can assist in assessing the overall compliance of a patient, but are less amenable to
immediate clinical action.
Both approaches follow the same conceptual model. The following figure depicts a gap event:
Figure46.GapinMedicationPossession
The analysis begins with a prescription for a targeted medication during the time period of interest.
The prescription covers a span of time that is defined by the associated days supply. The interval
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–184–

=== PÁGINA 185 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 8: Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based Markers
between the end of the days supply of the first prescription and the onset of a new prescription for
the same medication represents a gap.
A common approach to gap measurement is to include a grace period at the end of the days supply
to ensure that the reported gap is clinically significant. Thus, a patient could be reported as having no
gaps in possession, but actually have a number of small gaps that fall within the grace period. In this
example, the grace period is 15 days. In most instances, a 15-day grace period has been employed
within the ACG System. A 30-day grace period is used when the impact of a longer gap is considered
to be minimal or it is necessary to accommodate attributes of dispensing.
Certain events which can complicate the measurement of gaps and potentially introduce false
positives are addressed as follows. The first scenario in which a patient renews a prescription before
their current supply has been completely exhausted, is presented in the following figure.
Figure47.GapinMedicationPossessionFollowingOversupply
Under this circumstance there is still supply on hand when the prescription is refilled. This surplus is
added to the days supply of the refill. The assessment for a gap considers both the surplus and the 15
day grace period.
Pharmacy Adherence Defined
Four markers have been adopted for inclusion in the pharmacy adherence module. Each marker
represents a slightly different perspective on adherence, with a unique application and use case.
Calculations include:
• Number of gaps counts significant intervals during the observation period where there is no
medication supply
• Medication Possession Ratio (MPR) counts the total number of days for which medication is
dispensed, divided by the total number of days between the first and last prescription
• Continuous Single-Interval Measure of Medication Availability (CSA) is the ratio of days
supply to days until the next prescription, averaged across all prescriptions
• Proportion of Days Covered is the ratio of total days supply from the first prescription fill to
the end of the observation period
Medication possession can have different implications for various conditions and medications. The
ACG System focuses on 17 disease states for which chronic administration of medication is critical to
successful condition management in most patient scenarios.
Given the complexity of medication treatment, the presence of a treated condition may be inferred
from use of some chronic medications, but not others. For that reason, the ACG System requires
confirmatory diagnoses to trigger calculation of adherence markers for some conditions, but not all.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Adherence markers are only calculated for conditions for which the patient has the "TRT" Condition

Detailed definitions for adherence marker inclusion are detailed in the table below.
Unique situations exist in which patients may not have adherence markers calculated, as data and
prescription patterns are inadequate to make a valid assessment. For example:
• The patient may be prescribed a medication that falls within a relevant drug class, but is not
eligible for adherence calculations i.e., short-acting insulins for diabetes.
• The patient may have 2 very-short medication fills which do not sum to at least 60 days total
supply
• The patient may fill multiple medications to treat a specific condition on a single date, but
never refill
• The patient may have very infrequent fills or switch between drug classes within a condition
• The patient had two prescriptions within the same drug class, but not for the same active
ingredient.

The measurement of adherence is confined to only these condition-drug class pairings. It is possible
for patients to take multiple ingredients within the same drug class and/or temporarily substitute one
ingredient for another within the drug class. To prevent the appearance of oversupply, when multiple
ingredients are prescribed, calculations are performed at the ingredient (not drugclass) level.
Pharmacy adherence calculations can be complicated by the multitude of ways that patients access
medications and by the patient's eligibility (or lack thereof) for prescription benefits. When using the
adherence markers, it is important to understand the completeness of the pharmacy data file input
into the ACG System and any associated limitations. Examples of scenarios which may complicate
adherence marker calculations include:
• Pharmacy benefits outsourced or absent
• Enrollment gaps or discontinuation of eligibility
• Samples provided in the physician's office or in-office dispensing
• Discount drug programs
Number of Gaps
The Number of Gaps measure is a count of occurrences where the time interval between the end of
supply of one prescription and the onset of the next prescription for the same medication (active
ingredient) is more than the grace period. To be significant, the gap must extend beyond a grace
period (currently 15 or 30 days depending on the condition and drug class pair).

days supply available, but there are 4/18/21 - 2/18/21 = 60 days to cover. Allowing for a 15-day grace
period, there is a gap of 60 - (39 + 15) = 6 days. So, for this set of Rx claims the number of gaps is 1.
Medication Possession Ratio (MPR)
Medication possession ratio, or MPR, is a standard measure for calculating medication adherence
from pharmacy administrative data. This marker contains the calculation of the ratio of days supply to
total prescribing days. MPR is calculated as the total number of days for which medication is
dispensed (excluding the final prescription) divided by the total number of days between the first and
last prescription.
Medication possession ratio is calculated for patients taking at least one chronic medication within the
condition-drug class pairings listed in the Condition-Drug Class Pairings table. For each condition, there
is a marker with the naming convention of the specific condition appended with _MPR. If a person is
taking multiple medications (active ingredients) for a single condition, the days supply and total
prescribing days are totaled across all medications and then averaged. In general, MPR is more
sensitive to large gaps than to frequent gaps.
In common usage, an MPR of .80 or higher is considered good adherence. MPR can be greater than
1.0 if the member consistently refills prior to exhausting supply on hand and consistent MPR values
substantially greater than 1.0 may be investigated for potential over-use. Note that for the MPR
calculation, patient inpatient hospitalization days are not excluded from the prescribing days
denominator. Additional patient-level detail at the active ingredient/drug class level for each
prescription evaluated in the adherence calculations is available in the Pharmacy Spans Export File. on
page 464
The MPR Example 1 table, MPR Example 2 table, and MPR Example 3 table provide examples of MPR
calculations.

Continuous, Single-interval Measure of Medication Availability (CSA)
Continuous, Single-Interval Measure of Medication Availability (CSA) is the ratio of days supply to days
until the next prescription, averaged across all prescriptions. CSA is calculated for patients taking at
least one chronic medication within the condition-drug class pairings listed in the Condition-Drug Class
Pairings table. For each condition, there is a marker with the naming convention of the specific
condition appended with _CSA. CSA considers adherence over discrete prescribing events, equally
weighting each prescribing event.
Like MPR, CSA does not exclude inpatient hospitalization days from the denominator. The CSA, since
it is an average, shows more sensitivity to extremes and thus is more suited to identifying frequent
gaps in medication possession. CSA can be greater than 1.0 if the member consistently refills prior to
the exhausting supply on hand. In general, this measure is more sensitive to frequent gaps than to
large gaps.
Additional patient-level detail at the active ingredient/drug class level is available in the Pharmacy
Spans Export File on page 464.
The tables below provide examples of CSA calculations:

Proportion of Days Covered (PDC)
The proportion of days covered (PDC) is the ratio of the number of days supply divided by days
between first prescription fill and end of observation period, averaging medication possession over
the observation period. PDC indicates the rate of possession from the first dispensing event in the
period through the observation period end date. Within the US, PDC is the most common measure
for adherence calculations of medications that require chronic administration.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–191–

=== PÁGINA 192 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 8: Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based Markers
While MPR and CSA measure the distance between fills, PDC will consider the time period from the
first prescription through the end of the observation period, regardless of the timing of the last
prescription fill. The ACG System does not consider length of eligibility, so exercise caution when
interpreting PDC.
PDC has a maximum value of 1.0 and, unlike MPR and CSA, does consider inpatient hospitalization
days in the calculation. PDC is measured at the drug class level only. PDC calculations do include days
supply from the final prescription.
The PDC Example 1 and PDC Example 2 tables provide examples of PDC calculations.

10/14/2021 11/17/2021 30
11/17/2021 12/18/2021 30 3
The final fill on 12/18/2021 is for 30 days, but because of earlier over-supply and the observation end
date of 12/31/2021, only 3 days of this final fill is used in the observation period.
PDC = (10 fills x 30 days supply + 3 days supply from final fill) /
(Observation End Date 12/31/2021 - First Fill date 1/21/2021) = 303 / 344 = 0.8808.
The PDC is less than 1.0 because there are some days not covered early in the observation period
(between 1/21/2021 and 5/3/2021).

Pharmacy Spans
Pharmacy spans are the starting point for the calculation of the Gaps, MPR, CSA and PDR measures. A
pharmacy span is the period between two fills for the same ingredient. For example, four Rx claims
for one ingredient will generate three spans. Pharmacy spans contain the information required to
calculate the Adherence measures, such as the days between fills, the carried over supply etc. and are
described in more detail in Pharmacy Spans on page 464. ACG System users can export the pharmacy
spans generated by the ACG system to review the intermediate steps in the calculation of the
Adherence measures.
In some cases, a pharmacy span may be excluded from adherence calculations and flagged
accordingly in the Rx Eligible for Adherence column within the Pharmacy Spans Export File, which is
described in more detail in Pharmacy Spans on page 464. A span may be classified as not (N) included
in the adherence calculations, may be included in possession (P) calculations only, or may be included
in gaps (G) calculations only. Examples include:
• N: The drug class is not eligible for adherence calculations, i.e., short-acting adrenergic
bronchodilators or short-acting insulins.
• N: There is an extended gap (greater than 60 days exceeding the grace period).
• N: The required minimum prescribing period (60-day supply) at the drug class level was not
met AND there were spans with at least one day exceeding the grace period, but the patient
has a fill for a different ingredient within the same drug class (potential substitution).
• G: The required minimum prescribing period (60-day supply) at the drug class level was not
met.
• P: Spans with at least one day exceeding the grace period, but the patient has a fill for a
different ingredient within the same drug class (potential substitution).
There must be at least one eligible span for adherence to be calculated.
Reporting of Possession
With the exception of PDC, reporting of possession is summarized at the condition level within the
Patients and ACG Results file. A number of conditions have only one condition-drug class pair (e.g.,
osteoporosis), while others have multiple pairs (e.g., persistent asthma). If a condition is associated
with multiple drug classes, all gaps associated with these drugs are reported. Further, if a gap occurs
for a combination drug, the gap is reported for each component that falls into a separate drug class.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–193–

=== PÁGINA 194 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 8: Diagnosis+Pharmacy-based Markers
Specific drugs and prescribing periods are stored and made available in the Pharmacy Spans on page
464 Export File.
In addition, reporting of possession (including PDC) is available at the drug class level within the
Comprehensive Patient Clinical Profile Report and the related Drug Class Summary Export which is
described in more detail in Drug Class Summary on page 467. The maximum gap (largest gap, in days,
for a medication within the specific drug class) is reported within this analysis. Gaps may differ greatly
in terms of duration and the duration has potential implications for care management. The
intervention for someone with an extended gap in possession may be different than for someone
experiencing a one-time shorter gap.
In some cases a span may not (N) be included in the adherence calculations, may be included in
possession (P) calculations only, or may be included in gaps (G) calculations only. Examples include:
• N: The drug class is not eligible for adherence calculations, i.e., short-acting adrenergic
bronchodilators or short-acting insulins.
• N: There is an extended gap (greater than 60 days exceeding the grace period).
• N: The required minimum prescribing period (120-day supply) at the drug class level was not met
AND there were spans with at least one day exceeding the grace period, but the patient has a fill
for a different ingredient within the same drug class (potential substitution).
• G: The required minimum prescribing period (120-day supply) at the drug class level was not met.
• P: Spans with at least one day exceeding the grace period, but the patient has a fill for a different
ingredient within the same drug class (potential substitution).
Excluded spans are flagged in the Rx Eligible for Adherence column within the Pharmacy Spans Export
File, which is described in more detail in Pharmacy Spans on page 464.
Note: There must be at least one eligible span in order for adherence to be calculated.
End-of-Period Possession
The pharmacy adherence methodology assesses gaps and possession ratios between the first
prescription fill and the last prescription refill. When assessing the last fill, it is helpful to differentiate
patients that have supply through the full observation period from patients that are without supply at
the end of the observation period. If a member is without supply at the end of the period, further
investigation may be needed to determine if the member has stopped therapy, if the member has
started an alternate therapy or if the member is non-adherent with the current therapy.
For each ingredient that is evaluated, the supply of medications is tracked through the Pharmacy
Spans Export File. By comparing the supply end date to the observation period end date, possession
at the end of the period can be calculated. The Drug Class Summary Export File captures an End of
Period Possession field (Y/N) to indicate if there is still supply available as of the observation end date.
If more than 120 days have elapsed between the supply end date and the observation period end
date for all drug classes within a given condition, the individual is likely now untreated and the
untreated marker will be set to D for discontinued. The patient will still have the condition marker set
to TRT if all other criteria are met.
Validation and Testing
Pharmacy adherence has strong face validity among clinicians. If patients fail to comply with therapy
then there are likely to be consequences downstream. For some conditions these will be felt
immediately while for others years may pass before serious adverse events are experienced.

Medication possession is a complex issue that will require a close partnership between analysts and
clinicians. There are subtle distinctions in the significance of gaps depending upon the condition.
Further, gaps may potentially be indicative of good management. For persons with persistent asthma,
gaps in adrenergic bronchodilators could mean that the asthma is under good control and over-supply
could mean the converse, poor control.
High Risk Prescription Opioid Use
The abuse of prescription opioids is a serious health problem that is international in scope. Opioid use
at high levels is associated with increased mortality, frequent emergency department use and a higher
utilization of health care services. To facilitate the identification of this high risk group, three markers
are available. The focus of these markers is primarily on high risk users of physician-prescribed
opioids. Each marker captures a somewhat different dimension of opioid use as follows:
Chronic User : The Chronic User marker captures high risk use abased on morphine milligram
equivalents (MMEs). Based on prescribing data, calculates persons with 100+ MMEs per day for 90+
consecutive days over an observation period. This pattern is indicative of high risk of opiate
dependence.
Concomitant User : The Concomitant Use marker captures high risk use as the contiguous use of
opioids and benzodiazepines, which is a combination increasing risk of overdose and death. Based on
prescribing data, identifies persons with 30+ days of concomitant opioid and benzodiazepine use (may
or may not be continuous) over an observation period.
Opioid Dependency : The dependency marker is an indicator encompassing both licit and illicit use.
This diagnostic based marker identifies persons who are diagnosed with an opioid dependency. This
diagnosis is generally regarded as under-diagnosed and under-reported. Patients may have a diagnosis
but be in active treatment/recovery or may be diagnosed based on illicit drug use. In our research,
we found that about a quarter of the patients with a diagnosis of opioid dependency did not have
any opioid prescription. Included diagnoses cover opioid abuse, dependence and poisoning.
MMEs are a standard way to assess levels of opioid use. Evidence suggests that prescribing above a
daily MME of 90 -120 should be avoided to the extent possible, and patients at this level should be
carefully monitored. Multiple sources were used to establish MME conversion factors for the
prescribing-only metrics including U.S Centers for Disease Control, U.S. Center for Medicare &
Medicaid Services, and Multum. Where sources disagreed, we consulted the literature and with Johns
Hopkins physicians and pharmacists on current best practices.
The MME calculation includes medications used in outpatient settings only, including oral, sublingual,
buccal and transdermal formulations. Inpatient medications, those used in the surgical setting only,
compound ingredients, injectable products, and intravenous products are excluded from the
calculation. Buprenorphine-containing products used for treatment of substance abuse are excluded
from the calculation, while buprenorphine products labeled for pain management are included. For
methadone, our calculation is based on use for pain management indications; high-dose use for
substance abuse should be calculated using locally prevailing clinical guidance.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Benzodiazepines are widely used for the treatment of anxiety (and to a lesser extent to control
seizures). It is, therefore, not uncommon for patients to take opioids and benzodiazepines
simultaneously. In combination, these drugs both sedate and depress breathing, increasing the chance
of difficulty breathing, other serious side effects, and death. Concomitant prescribing should be
limited to the extent possible and, if these medicines are prescribed together, dosage and duration
should be limited. Any instance of overlap during the observation year is counted to arrive at 30-day
plus threshold, as an indicator of drug safety risk.

Chapter 9:
Laboratory-based Markers
This chapter describes markers that are derived from laboratory data input. Laboratory-based markers
enable refinements of diagnosis- and medication-based morbidity profiles for individuals and patient
populations. The markers are compatible with the international LOINC19standard and are intended for
outpatient laboratory results that are generated in laboratory environments and physician clinics.

Diabetes
The diabetes laboratory markers adhere to the American Diabetes Association guideline of 6.5%
hemoglobin A1c to identify diabetes in an individual. When the diagnosis- and pharmacy-based

analyzed. The HEDIS® 20 Comprehensive Diabetes Care A1c threshold of 9.0% indicates inadequate
glycemic control in our clinical logic. Alternatively, a 2-hr 75-g oral glucose tolerance test - not given
during pregnancy, a pair of random glucose tests, or the combination of one random glucose and one
A1c result provide additional lab indication for diabetes.
Impaired glucose tolerance (hyperglycemia) is sometimes referred to as pre-diabetes. When the two
most recent A1c results are below 6.5% and above 5.7%, or any of the A1c's are above 6.5% and the
most recent A1c is below 5.7%, we identify impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) based on laboratory
data.
Dyslipidemia
The dyslipidemia clinical logic assesses low-density lipoprotein (LDL) control among individuals who
have a disorder of lipid metabolism condition marker present (not "NP") and any high-risk condition,
defined as any diabetes, aortic aneurysm, CAD/CHD, cerebrovascular disease, or peripheral vascular
disease. An LDL value greater 100 mg/dL indicates inadequate LDL cholesterol control. Among
individuals with unrecognized dyslipidemia, pairs of total cholesterol (>240 mg/dL; >6.22 mmol/L), LDL
(>100 mg/dL; >2.59 mmol/L), and HDL (<40 mg/dL male; <60 mg/dL female or <1.04 mmol/L male;
<1.55 mg/dL female) provide a lab indication of dyslipidemia.
Deficiency anemia
Among individuals for whom the deficiency anemia condition is not present ("NP"), the condition is
identified based on hemoglobin (Hb) values at following thresholds: Hb < 14 g/dL (<140 g/L) for males
and Hb < 12 g/dL (<120 g/L) for females.
Kidney disease
Among individuals for whom chronic kidney disease is not present ("NP"), kidney disease is identified
by pairs of recent blood urea nitrogen and creatinine values. Out of these four results, three values
must exceed the following thresholds: creatinine (Cr) > 1.3 mg/dL (>115 mmol/L) for males; > 1.1
mg/dL (97 mmol/L) for females and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) > 20 mg/dL (> 7.1 mmol/L).
Impact of diagnosis filtering and using stringent condition identification options
The ACG System offers filtering of rule-out diagnoses and optional stringent diagnosis requirements.
Removing diagnoses thru filtering and stringent requirements may result in a condition to become
unrecognized, and this change will impact the assignment of laboratory markers.

Chapter 10: Utilization and Resource Use Markers
Chapter 10:
Utilization and Resource Use Markers
Utilization markers identify unique markers of risk and are specifically used in the hospitalization risk
models. There are a variety of utilization measures that are usually captured from dates of service,
place of service, type of bill, diagnosis codes, revenue codes and procedure codes. As there are
variances in coding systems, the following are intended to fully explain how the software calculates
the associated utilization variables. Optionally, these variables may be manually calculated and
provided on the patient file (see Patient Data Format on page 39).
Business Rules for Utilization Markers
All Cause Inpatient Hospitalization Count
The intent is to count acute care inpatient hospitalization stays, regardless of cause.
To count inpatient visits, count as one event each inpatient confinement with either: (a) IP in place of
service, or (b) room and board revenue codes on contiguous dates of service and either the number
21 in the place of service or 11x, 12x or 18x in the type of bill. The sum of these events represents
the number of inpatient visits.
The criteria for identifying an inpatient confinement are:
• Inpatient hospital place of service (IP); or Inpatient hospital place of service code (21) or type of
bill 11x, 12x or 18x, along with a revenue code (three-digit version) for room and board: 100 to
219.
• If interim claims are submitted, identify a single inpatient confinement for claims with contiguous
begin and end dates of service.
• If a patient is transferred within or between facilities without a gap in service dates, count as a
single inpatient visit.
Inpatient Hospitalization Count
For the hospitalization risk dependent variable, exclude from the All Cause Inpatient Hospitalization
count, inpatient admissions with a primary discharge diagnosis of:
ICD-10
Pregnancy and delivery: O00-O99, Z37
Newborns: Z38
Injury: S00-T98 (except T80-T88)
V01-Y98 (except Y40-Y84)
The ACG System will use the last service line and additional services with the same begin and end
date to determine inclusion in the inpatient hospitalization count. If there are records that both
include an injury diagnosis along with records which do not include an injury diagnosis, the ACG
System will include the hospitalization in the inpatient hospitalization count. If all records for the
confinement include a diagnosis of injury, the hospitalization will not be included in the count. If any
record includes a delivery segment, the ACG System will categorize the hospitalization as a delivery
and will not include it in the inpatient hospitalization count.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

=== PÁGINA 204 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 10: Utilization and Resource Use Markers
Unplanned Inpatient Hospitalization Count
The unplanned inpatient hospitalization count is a subset of the inpatient hospitalization count with
exclusions for planned admissions. A planned admission is defined as either:
• A definitively planned procedure, identified by either ICD procedure code or diagnosis code.
Definitively planned procedures includes items such as rehabilitation services, chemotherapy and
transplants.
• A potentially planned procedure, identified by ICD procedure code. Potentially planned procedures
are more common surgical procedures, such as hip replacements, cardiovascular procedures and
other inpatient surgical treatments without evidence of acute complications such as infections,
burns or injuries.
Any inpatient hospitalization that cannot be identified as definitively or potentially planned is
considered unplanned.
Readmission 30 Day Count
The readmission 30 day count is a subset of the all cause inpatient hospitalization count. The
presence of this count indicates, regardless of cause, the identified admission occurred within 30 days
of a previous inpatient hospitalization (including a prior readmission).
Unplanned Readmission 30 Day Count
The unplanned readmission 30 day count is a subset of the inpatient hospitalization count. The
presence indicates the identified admission meets the unplanned inpatient hospitalization criteria and
occurred within 30 days of a previous inpatient hospitalization (including a prior readmission).
Inpatient Hospitalization Days
Inpatient hospitalization days count the days between the minimum service begin date and the
maximum service end date associated with each inpatient confinement in the inpatient hospitalization
count.
For confinements with the same service begin and end date, count a minimum of one inpatient day.
Observation Stay
The observation stay marker identifies the presence of observation services that are not precursors to
subsequent observation stays and inpatient hospital stays in the same time period. Observation stay is
a binary marker where 1 indicates that the patient experienced at least one encounter in an
observation unit that did not convert to an inpatient admission.
The criteria for identifying an observation stay are any of the following:
Revenue code: 0760 or 0762
Procedure code: G0378-G0379, 99217-99220 or 99224-99226
Service Place: OBS
Observation Days
Observation days count the days between the minimum service begin date and the maximum service
end date associated with each observation stay that is not associated with an inpatient admission. A
minimum of one day is counted for each observation stay. Observation days represent the total
observation days during the measurement period, potentially summarizing multiple encounters.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Emergency Visit Count
The intent is to count emergency room visits that are not precursors to subsequent observation stays
and inpatient hospital stays in the same time period. Those emergency room visits that are
immediately followed by an observation stay or inpatient hospital stay are included as part of the
observation stay or hospitalization, respectively, and are not included in the emergency visit count.
The criteria for identifying an emergency room record are any of the following:
Revenue code for emergency room 0450, 0451, 0452, 0456, 0459, 0981
CPT code for evaluation and management in emergency room23 99281, 99282, 99283, 99284, 99285,
99288
Emergency room place of service code (23) with a CPT code for surgery 10021 to 69990
Emergency room place of service (ED)
Emergency room records identified with either 1) a revenue code for emergency room above or 2)
with any of the emergency room criteria above in conjunction with a type of bill code, will anchor an
emergency visit that may span over consecutive dates. Additional emergency services that occur the
day prior through the day following the service end date of an anchoring service are counted as a
single emergency visit event; otherwise, each unique patient/day with an emergency room record is
count as an emergency visit.
Tip: Emergency department visits that result in either an observation stay and/or an inpatient stay
are counted separately as output fields ‘ed visits leading to observation’ and ‘ed visits with all cause
ip hosp’, respectively, and are not mutually exclusive. A single emergency department visit may result
in BOTH an observation stay and an inpatient hospitalization.
ED Visits Leading to Observation
The intent is to count emergency department visits that resulted in an observation stay. Emergency
department visits that resulted in an observation stay are excluded from the Emergency Visit Count.
ED Visits with All Cause IP Hospitalization
The intent is to count emergency department visits that resulted in an inpatient hospital admission.
Emergency department visits that resulted in an inpatient hospital admission are excluded from the
Emergency Visit Count.
Outpatient Visit Count
The intent is to count instances where patients receive ambulatory care in outpatient settings.
To count outpatient visits, count as one event each unique record of a patient id, provider id and date
of service. The sum of these events represents the number of outpatient visits.
The criteria for identifying an outpatient service record are the following:
Physician office (11), outpatient hospital (19, 22), and other (02, 24, 25, 26, 50, 53, 60, 62, 65, 71,
72) place of service codes; type of bill 13x or 14x; or outpatient (OP) place of service code,
excluding services meeting the criteria for an emergency department visit.

service code (21 or IP). There are approximately 3,000 procedure codes on the major procedure list.;

Emergency Department Visit Classification
This section describes a method to classify emergency department (ED) visits. The classification is
intended for retrospective analysis and making inferences about the level of appropriateness of ED
utilization within a population of interest.
The Johns Hopkins Updated Expansion of the NYU Emergency Department
Algorithm
A team of Johns Hopkins emergency medicine physicians and health services researchers updated and
expanded the New York University Emergency Department Algorithm (NYU-EDA), a method that is
widely used to classify ED visits, using their best clinical judgment and building on diagnosis
aggregations from the ACG system. This new algorithm typically classifies 99% of visits and enables
valid retrospective inferences about ED utilization, and is termed the Johns Hopkins Emergency
Department Algorithm (JH-EDA).
The original NYU-EDA classifies visits based on the primary discharge diagnosis with probabilities
attached to four categories: (1) non-emergent; (2) emergent, primary care treatable; (3) emergent, ED
care needed, and potentially preventable or avoidable with timely and effective ambulatory care; and
(4) emergent, ED care needed, and not preventable. Injuries, psychiatric conditions, and alcohol and
drug use add four more categories, and unclassified visits comprise the ninth category of the
classification.
The JH-EDA adds three modifications to the NYU-EDA. First, rather than making probabilistic
assignments, the JH-EDA classifies each visit into one of eleven categories. Second, rather than placing
all injuries into one category, it categorizes injuries in three severity levels: non-severe injuries, severe
injuries, and severe injuries that are likely to require inpatient admissions. To assess injury severity,
the team used coded data on physician evaluation and management services in the emergency
department and identified a subset of severe injury visits as likely to require inpatient hospitalization
based on a greater than 50% empiric likelihood of subsequent inpatient admission. Third, the JH-EDA
classifies a larger number of ICD codes and a higher percentage of visits compared to the NYU-EDA.
Emergency Department Visit Class Assignment Methodology
Emergency department visits are identified in the medical service input file. The rules for identifying
Emergency Department visits are defined with the Emergency Visit Count on page 205. Input records
that satisfy any of the criteria for inclusion will be examined as emergency visits for this methodology.
While the emergency visit count focuses on emergency department visits that do not lead to
inpatient admission or observations stays, the emergency department visit classification includes all
emergency department visits, regardless of disposition. The details associated with each emergency
department visit on page 468 will include an indication when the visit led to inpatient or observation
care.
To ensure that the ACG System provides consistent assignments when there is more than one
qualifying record, the System gives preference to hospital facility input records and prioritizes these
records by type of bill and revenue code. In cases where there is no clear indication of facility billing
based on bill type or revenue code, conflicts resulting in more than one emergency visit classification
will be resolved by assigning the first applicable classification out of the following ordered list:
• Injury, severe and inpatient hospitalization likely
• Injury, severe
• Drug use
• Alcohol use
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Chapter 11: Coordination
Chapter 11:
Coordination
The Johns Hopkins ACG System introduced ACG Coordination Markers in order to identify populations
that are at risk for poorly coordinated care. Used by themselves or in conjunction with other risk
markers, this set of markers adds another dimension so as to enhance the clinical screening process.
The basic premise behind the creation of ACG Coordination Markers is that individuals receiving
poorly coordinated care have worse clinical outcomes and have higher medical expenses than
individuals who are being provided coordinated care.
Assessing Care Coordination
Care coordination has traditionally been assessed using instruments that have been unable to use
administrative claims information. These coordination assessment approaches have been survey
based, and have targeted the patient's, family member’s, or provider's perceptions of care
collaboration. Chart reviews have also been used to assess the information exchanged between
physicians, teamwork processes, and performance. Finally, resources and structures that support care
coordination have also been used to indirectly evaluate coordination. Surveys, chart reviews, and
resource information are not readily available for coordination assessment, making it challenging to
incorporate this dimension of care into the clinical screening process.
Using only administrative claims information, ACG Coordination Markers are able to assess whether
an individual is at risk for receiving poorly coordinated care. Five patient markers make up ACG
Coordination Markers:
• Management Visit Count: The number of face-to-face physician visits with an eligible specialty.
• Majority Source of Care (MSOC): An assessment of the level of participation of those providers that
provided care to each patient.
• Unique Provider Count: A count of the number of unique providers that provided care to the
patient.
• Specialty Count: A count of the number of specialty types (not the same as number of specialists
seen) that provided care to the patient.
• Generalist Seen: A marker indicating a generalist’s participation in an individual’s care.
A coordination risk measure combines these markers to determine whether a person has a "likely,"
"possible," or "unlikely" coordination issue.
A care density ratio quantifies patient sharing based on outpatient face-to-face visits with eligible
physicians.
Each of the ACG Coordination Markers limit their evaluation to outpatient face-to-face physician visits
as defined by procedure code.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Management Visit Count
The Management Visit Count represents the total number of face-to-face visits with an eligible
specialty.
Generalist Visit Count
The Generalist Visit Count represents the total number of face-to-face visits with a generalist
specialty during the observation period. This count is a subset of management visits representing
primary care.
Majority Source of Care (MSOC)
The Majority Source of Care marker will determine the percent of the outpatient face-to-face visits
provided by eligible physicians that saw the member most over the measurement period. For each
patient, the ACG System determines the following:
• The percentage of visits provided from the largest source. The Management Visit Count is the
denominator for this percentage.
• The provider ID(s) that is responsible for the majority source of care. In the event that more than
one provider is assigned the same MSOC percentage, the ACG System will identify all the providers
as being the majority source of care.
The following figure shows two patients. The patient on the left saw three eligible providers and
received eight of his ten outpatient face-to-face visits from the geriatrician. In this case, the
geriatrician is identified as the MSOC provider with a score of 0.80 (80%.) The patient on the right
saw four eligible providers and received four of her outpatient services from the endocrinologist. The
endocrinologist provider is identified as the MSOC with a score of 0.40 (40%.)

Care Density
Myriad formal and informal referral relationships among clinicians lead to varying levels of patient
sharing. Higher levels of patient sharing are often credited with higher intensity of care, better care
coordination, and greater potential cost opportunities.
The care density ratio is a patient-level measure of the extent of patient sharing among the
physicians that a patient saw during face-to-face encounters over a period of time. The numerator is
the total number of instances of patient sharing among a patient’s eligible physicians. Every relevant
instance of patient sharing contributes to the numerator, whereby the contributions of instance range
between 1 and 10 maximally. The denominator is the total number of unique pairs of the patient’s
physicians. A patient who visited at least two physicians receives a care density ratio.
Figure57.CareDensityRatios
The distribution of the care density ratio typically varies by the unique provider count, whether a
patient saw a generalist, and a patient’s resource utilization band (RUB)27. Among patients with
complex morbidity who seek care from multiple physicians one often finds a higher frequency of low
care density ratios, compared to healthier patients who seek care from a small number of physicians.
Hence the lower and upper quartile care density cutoff values vary among patients.
The care density ratio distributions are characterized by three “care density quantiles,” the bottom
quartile (LOW), the middle half (MID), and the top quartile (TOP). The ACG System outputs the care
density bottom and top quartile cutoff values.
A finding from research is that greater patient sharing and higher care density are associated with
lower resource utilization28. As a consequence one may form expectations about cost savings relative
to the top quartile of care density that is achieved by members. The expected savings associated with
high care density are greater for members in the bottom quartile of care density compared to
patients in the middle half. The care density cost saving ratio considers the same factors that have an
impact on the care density ratio and additionally the patient’s current care density quantile. The care
density cost saving ratio is derived by calculating the difference between the average reference total

Conclusion
The ACG Coordination Markers provide a meaningful way to identify members at risk for poor
coordination. The coordination risk marker provides a means for identifying those members most at
risk of coordination issues. Members with poorly coordinated care are more likely to have excess
utilization as a result of redundant testing, potentially harmful drug-disease interactions and overall
lower quality care. The care density ratio provides a means for quantifying the strength of possible
relationships among a member's network of physicians. A network with greater density is expected to
have greater potential cost savings. These markers complement the ACG System risk scores and
additional system markers in further defining the “at risk” population.
A file quantifying provider pairs is being made available for exploratory purposes. We look forward to
engaging with users on potential applications for this additional network output.

Chapter 12: Risk Modeling
Chapter 12:
Risk Modeling
The innovation that the ACG risk models present is their unique clinical logic coupled with their
excellent statistical performance. Each model employs risk factors that were created using clinical
frameworks that make sense to health professionals and medical managers.
This chapter describes the application of the diagnosis and pharmacy based markers in the
determination of patient risk. The chapter includes an overview of the methods used and validation of
the various scores produced by the ACG System.
Elements of a Risk Model: Five Key Dimensions
The structure of a risk model can be characterized in five dimensions: conceptual basis; reference
population; risk factors; statistical approach; and, modeled outcomes. Each of these dimensions is
discussed in more detail below in the context of the ACG System.
Conceptual Basis
The ACG System’s risk models are anchored in the same fundamental insight about morbidity that led
to the creation of ACG categories. This insight, conceived by Dr. Barbara Starfield in the 1970s, is that
morbidity clusters and multi-morbidity are the best indicators of health needs. Clinicians continue to
shape the ACG System to ensure that the models retain clinical cogency as improvements are made
to explanatory power. On very large datasets, it is possible to make improvements in predictive
power by just adding new variables, but there is an art to developing well-constructed risk factors to
support a parsimonious model.
In the application of risk models, it is important to define models that are less prone to strategic
manipulation. Again, statistical improvements may be gained by increasing the number of variables;
however, this makes the model susceptible to potential up-coding. The ACG System is robust and less
likely to appraise large shifts in risk assessment on the basis of a single diagnosis code.
Modeled Outcomes
The ACG System risk models can be used to predict or explain costs (annual total healthcare or
annual pharmacy costs) and to predict the likelihood of certain sentinel events (the likelihood of being
high cost, likelihood of inpatient hospitalization, etc). Optimal performance of ACG System risk models
occurs when the model is specifically calibrated to the outcome. A specialized model will be a better
fit than attempting to use a model focused on a different outcome (e.g., using a model built to
explain total cost to explain hospitalization, and vice versa). Some users of the ACG System have built
well-performing models on additional model outcomes (e.g. mortality)29; however, one of the criteria
for models presented in the ACG System is availability of reference data discussed in the following.
Reference Population
In order to provide a reliable standard model, the ACG System derives its risk models from a large,
representative reference population. The reference population is used as a control for a range of
factors known to affect modeled health risks such as age, sex, and morbidity burden.

A very large longitudinal claims database licensed from IQVIA, formerly QuintilesIMS, One IMS Drive,
Plymouth Meeting, PA, was used for the ACG System modeling efforts. The database is generally
representative of the U.S. commercially insured population. Multiple populations were used for
modeling: (1) commercial (all ages to 65 years old) and (2) Medicare Advantage (United States federal
program that pays for certain health care expenses for people aged 65 or older through commercial
managed care organizations). The ACG System also contains an all-age model that selectively assigns
risk scores based on the model appropriate to each patient: children (0-17 years of age), adults (18-64
years of age), and the elderly (65 and over years of age). There are also reference weights for specific
population subgroups such as Medicaid TANF (a health care support program for children and families
in the U.S.). The selection of reference population is made when processing the ACG System data file
with the selection of Risk Assessment Variables.
Various subsets of data for the period 2013-2015 were used for development and validation,
depending on the model requirements. The population was restricted to include enrollees that had
both pharmacy and medical eligibility. Additional eligibility requirements vary by model, but no less
than six months of eligibility is required for defining risk factors.
Risk Factors
As described in the previous chapters, the ACG System derives a wide range of risk factors depending
on available data.
The ACG System models make use of the comprehensive array of metrics available within the entire
ACG risk adjustment system. The risk factors that constitute the ACG System models are shown in the
following figure, and are discussed in detail following. The full list of variables used in the models are
available in Appendix D: Variables Necessary to Locally Calibrate the ACG System Risk Models on page
557.

Age and sex are included to assess age-related and sex-based health needs.
Overall disease burden is measured using the ACG categorization of morbidity burden. For more
information, see Patterns of Morbidity – Adjusted Clinical Groups (ACGs) on page 122. For predictive
models, 27 individual ACG categories that represent the most resource intensive morbidity groups are
included; for concurrent models, 30 individual ACG categories are utilized. All other ACG categories
are incorporated into the concurrent and prospective models as one of two groups. Individual ACG
Categories Included in the Risk Models on page 557 and ACG Categories Included in Three Resource
Groups on page 558 are derived from ACG category alone.
Disease markers. High-impact chronic conditions were selected for inclusion in the predictive model
because when they are present they have a high impact on resource consumption. They are common
chronic conditions that are associated with greater than average resource consumption, uncommon
diseases with high impact on both cost and health, complications of chronic disease that signify high
disease severity (e.g., diabetic retinopathy), or conditions that are a major biological influences on
health status (e.g., transplant status, malignancy). Only conditions for which the evidence linking
health care to outcomes is strong were included in the predictive model. A sub-set of the ACG
System’s Expanded Diagnostic Clusters (EDCs) is used to identify the high impact conditions in the
model. The Concurrent Risk models also include EDC conditions that are acute in nature. For more
information, see Disease Markers - Expanded Diagnosis Clusters (EDCs) on page 146.

Pregnancy without delivery is included in predictive models because of the high use of resources
associated with delivery that will occur in the subsequent assessment period. For more information,
see Pregnancy without Delivery on page 161.
This marker is not used in concurrent models because the delivery is a future event. Concurrent
models incorporate pregnancy using individual ACG categories.
Hospital dominant morbidity types are based on diagnoses that, based on expert clinical review,
would be associated with a high likelihood of hospitalization in the next year. All these diagnoses are
setting-neutral, i.e., they can be given in any inpatient or outpatient face-to-face encounter with a
health professional. The variable is a count of the number of morbidity types (i.e., ADGs) with at least
one hospital dominant diagnosis. For more information, see Hospital Dominant Morbidity Types on
page 156.
Frailty is a dichotomous (on/off) variable that indicates whether an patient has a diagnosis falling
within any clusters that represent medical problems associated with frailty. For more information, see
Frailty Conditions on page 157.
Rx-defined morbidity groups. All Rx-MGs are included in the predictive model, either independently or
as a complement to the diagnosis-based markers. For more information, see Rx-Defined Morbidity
Groups (Rx-MGs) on page 163.
The Concurrent Risk models may optionally consider pharmacy data when available. Due to the
circularity in defining morbidity based on prescribing, it is strongly recommended against using
pharmacy data to contribute to risk for any profiling or payment applications. The option is available
to assess potential biases in the diagnosis data that might be reflected in the pharmacy data.
Active Ingredient Count is considered in the predictive model when an individual has had medications
representing 20 or greater individual active ingredients. For more information, see Active Ingredient
Count on page 174.
Costs Percentiles can be added to the predictive model as a measure of demand and need for
services not captured by the treated morbidity information available in diagnostic codes. The model
uses either prior pharmacy costs or total health care costs as presented in the pharmacy cost band or
total cost band (see Resource Bands on page 214) depending on the outcome of interest. Cost
percentiles are not utilized in the concurrent model.
Utilization Markers are considered in the hospitalization and readmission models only. The
complement of utilization markers includes inpatient hospitalization, observation days, emergency
visits, outpatient visits, dialysis service, nursing service, major procedure, psychotherapy service, active
cancer treatment, mechanical ventilation and CAL-SSA. The readmission model also includes inpatient
days and unplanned readmissions within 30 days. For more information, see Predictive Models for
Hospitalization on page 246.
Combining these risk factors is clinically logical because the morbidity information obtained from
diagnostic codes complements that which is obtained from medication codes. In effect, the combined
model provides the most complete clinical picture of the patient’s health needs and demand for care
that is possible using administrative data.
While a model calibrated to look at diagnosis, pharmacy and prior cost information may yield the
highest statistical performance in theory, missing input data is a practical challenge that health care
organizations face. Rather than enforce the use of all risk factors, a number of model variants have
been developed to adapt to available data. The ACG System will apply logic to determine the model
that will make use of the most available data. This model will be identified in the summary statistics.

Statistical Approach
Three types of models are commonly used depending on the outcome variable:
• Actuarial cells are categorical variables that can directly explain variation in an outcome variable
(e.g., Age-sex or ACG categories are examples of actuarial cells used for explaining total cost).
• Linear regression models are used for continuous outcome variables (e.g., total cost or pharmacy
cost).
• Logistic regression models are used for binary/dichotomous outcome variables (e.g., probability of
high cost, probability of inpatient hospitalization or probability of readmission).
Actuarial cells provide an easily calibrated model for explaining the relative risk of an outcome.
Deriving a risk score from an actuarial cell requires only basic arithmetic. In use in the ACG System,
the actuarial cell determination of relative risk is calculated as the mean cost of all patients in an
actuarial cell divided by the mean cost of all patients in the population. This method is also referred
to as indirect standardization because comparisons are made by extrapolating a comparison of each
person to the average. This method is employed for age-sex concurrent risk, local ACG concurrent risk
and reference ACG concurrent risk. For more information, see Patterns of Morbidity – Adjusted
Clinical Groups (ACGs) on page 122.
Linear Regression using ordinary least squares parameter estimation is widely used and, when
calculated against a substantially large population, provides fairly stable estimates. The individual
predictions have an intuitive appeal, because they can readily be translated into monetary values.
While cost data do not fulfill the assumptions for these models (which are best suited for data
following a normal distribution with common variance across the variable range), the models are
sufficiently robust that some departures from the assumptions can be tolerated. Our work suggests,
for example, that generalized linear models using a log link function and a gamma distribution of
error terms provide PM estimates that are no better, and in many cases inferior to, standard linear
regression methods. Thus, ACG System uses a standard linear regression approach with ordinary least
squares estimation in order to provide risk factor weights (the beta coefficients from the regression
equations) with intuitive, real-dollar meaning.
Logistic Regression applied to dichotomous/binary outcomes events such as whether someone is
hospitalized or is in a high-cost group (e.g., in the top five percent of the highest cost persons in the
population). The output from logistic regression estimates the probability that the modeled event will
occur. The probability is expressed as a decimal number from 0 to 1. Logistic regression assumes a
specific functional form between predictors and the outcome (a logit relationship) that differs from
typical linear models of health care resource use.
Concurrent Cost Models
A concurrent risk model, also commonly referred to as a retrospective model, is an explanatory model
where the risk factors are derived from the same time period as the outcome variable. In the ACG
System, concurrent models are used to explain historical costs. For example, a concurrent risk model
may use patient experience from 2019 to derive risk factors (e.g., age-sex or ACG) in order to explain
variation in 2019 total expenditures. Concurrent risk models are often applied in the context of
performance assessment in order to derive the expected level of resource utilization. Learn more
about the application of concurrent cost models in Performance Assessment on page 334.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
