Example 10: Identify Patients with Severe and Persistent Mental Illness
ADGs provide a good foundation for identifying members with severe and persistent mental illness.
ADGs classify diagnoses into a limited number of clinically meaningful, but not disease-specific,
morbidity groups. Each ADG is homogenous with respect to specific clinical criteria and their demand
on healthcare services. ADGs are highly predictive of current and future resource use and take into
account the expected duration of the condition, the implied severity of the condition, the level of
diagnostic certainty, the etiology of the condition, and whether or not specialty care services are likely
to be used. Two ADG categories, ADG 24 (Psychosocial: Recurrent or Persistent, Stable) and ADG 25
(Psychosocial: Recurrent or Persistent, Unstable) can be used to assess the level of mental health
disease burden within the population. Using both ADGs together may result in the identification of a
large number of candidates for a behavioral health management program, but may not isolate the
group of members that would most benefit from program interventions. Typically, additional
stratification is required. A subset of the psychosocial EDCs (e.g., PSY07 - Schizophrenia and affective
psychosis, PSY12 - Bipolar disorder, PSY20 - Major depression, etc.), the predictive risk scores and/or
the Hospital Dominant Morbidity Types might be used to further stratify the population.
Tip: Refer to Morbidity Types – Aggregated Diagnosis Groups (ADGs) on page 115 for a detailed
discussion of ADGs and the clinical criteria used to define them, as well as a list of Major ADGs.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–305–

=== PÁGINA 306 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 16: Clinical Screening

The following figure demonstrates an example of how to differentiate the potential driver of the

Example 11: Using Calculations to Identify Disease Patterns
In addition to the various examples of filters discussed thus far, the use of calculations provides
additional flexibility within the ACG System. Demonstrated up until now, a typical use for filters is to
perform an analysis to identify a subset of the population that might benefit from care management
interventions. While filters can be used to control the selection of patients from the active data file,
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–309–

=== PÁGINA 310 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 16: Clinical Screening
calculations can be used to incorporate new data attributes into analyses. Columns defined in the
calculations can be incorporated into filters or groups. Calculations can be defined on any available
column in the patient data, which also includes all ACG-calculated data elements and additional
calculated fields imported as part of the data file. Multiple columns may be added, each with its own
specification. Examples of calculation use are the creation of a unique subset of RUBs (i.e., more or
fewer categories or correlated to different outcome), identification of a specific risk cohort (e.g., high
pregnancy risk, index condition, or disease pattern), or creation of a stratification algorithm to suit the
client’s specific analytical needs.
Tip: Refer to Report Options on page 77 for more information on report options and calculations.
An example of the benefit of using the report options feature to generate ad-hoc analyses can be
demonstrated using the Disease Patterns calculations included in the Example Option Set. The
provided disease patterns represent a novel view of EDCs. Rather than considering a single EDC, the
focus is on patterns of co-occurring EDCs. The notion of co-morbidity is a cornerstone of the ACG
System. There is clear evidence that diseases often occur together and that this co-occurrence is not
random. These combinations may have important implications for care and clearly influence resource
use. ACG categories were defined to explain resource use, but were not intended to guide care
management. The ability to identify members with commonly occurring combinations of conditions
(i.e., the identified patterns) allows care managers to segment the populations of persons with
particular index conditions of interest who are at high resource use risk due to specific comorbidities.
Three index conditions were chosen as the focus for the assessment of patterns:
• Persistent Asthma
• Diabetes
• Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD)
These conditions are often care-managed, have important cost impacts, and are accompanied by a
range of co-occurring chronic conditions. How the condition presents and is managed is typically
dependent on the associated comorbidities. The resultant patterns were built from a base of chronic
conditions on page 152 and include only those that occurred with a frequency of at least one percent
for the index condition.
Pattern selection can be a very complicated process. If, for example, patterns are to be drawn from a
dozen EDCs, there are thousands of unique combinations. To simplify the process of pattern selection,
factor analysis was performed. These EDCs were narrowed to include patterns that were significant,
occurred in high volume, and showed high costs and high utilization. The resulting patterns, although
developed empirically, were validated in the literature, and then incorporated into the Example
Option Set.
In practical usage, the patterns formation process need not be complex. Patterns frequently
encountered in clinical practice can be readily identified through interviews and built into reports
similar to those provided in the Example Option Set.
The following figure shows the three calculated columns included in the Example Option Set. These
can be used to identify members with Asthma Patterns, Ischemic Heart Disease Patterns and Diabetes
Patterns. The Ischemic Heart Disease Patterns is partially displayed below as an example.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

A review of the pharmacy adherence profile provides additional information regarding treatment for
specific chronic conditions and the adherence to that treatment regimen. In this example, there are
low medication possession rates (MPR) and multiple gaps (twelve) related to hypertension pharmacy
adherence.
The Continuous Single-Interval Measure of Medication Availability (CSA) is the ratio of days supply to
days until the next prescription averaged across all prescriptions. The Medication Possession Ratio
(MPR) is the total number of days for which medication is dispensed (excluding final prescription)
divided by the total number of days between the first and last prescription. The CSA and MPR are
generally quite similar. If a MPR is markedly lower than the CSA, then there could be one or more
large gaps that are influencing the results. In common usage, an MPR or CSA of .80 or higher is
considered good adherence.
The # Refill Gaps is the count of occurrences where the time interval between the end of the supply
of one prescription and the onset of the next prescription is more than the grace period (15 or 30
days depending on the drug class).
The Treated Condition Profile provides additional information related to the gaps. In this case, the
patient is taking four different hypertension medications, an ACEI/ARB, a Beta-blocker, a calcium
channel blocker and a diuretic. For each drug class there are three gaps in filling the prescriptions,
with a total of 94 gap days (exceeding the 30-day grace period).
The Pharmacy Spans export file (Tools > Export) can be accessed to see the prescription history
behind these calculations.
Tip: Refer to Pharmacy Spans on page 464 for a more detailed description of the Pharmacy Spans
file.
When developing a care plan for managing and educating this patient, the care manager might assess
the reasons the patient is non-compliant with his hypertension medications, determine if other co-
morbidities warrant intervention, and investigate what is driving the high number of outpatient visits.

Example 15: Identify High Pharmacy Users with Discordant Medical and Pharmacy Risk
The High Risk for Unexpected Pharmacy Cost Model is focused on predicting the subset of the
population who are consuming drugs beyond what might be anticipated based on their diagnosis-
based morbidity burden.
There are a variety of reasons why pharmacy utilization might be higher than expected. Sometimes
pharmacy costs are higher because of poly-pharmacy or the use of an expensive medication.
Unexpected high pharmacy utilization can also be a result of quality issues. These can range from
poor data (e.g., missing diagnosis codes), to poor or inadequate care and/or gaps in care. Other times
it is a matter of fraud, patient abuse or other inappropriate use.
Tip: The High Risk for Unexpected Pharmacy Cost Model is more fully described in Probability of

Medication Therapy Management Program (MTMP) Candidate Selection
Medicare (a United States federal program that pays for certain health care expenses for people aged
65 or older) Part D Drug Plans (PDPs) have unique challenges in that one of the regulatory
requirements of PDPs is that they implement Medication Therapy Management Programs (MTMPs).
MTMPs are designed to improve medication adherence, patient safety and quality. The programs
typically focus on promoting beneficiary education and counseling, increasing enrollee adherence to
prescription medication regimens and of detecting adverse drug events and patterns of over-use and
under-use of prescription drugs. These outreach programs should target individuals with multiple
chronic conditions, such as, but not limited to, diabetes, asthma, hypertension, disorders of lipid
metabolism, and congestive heart failure, who are taking multiple covered Part D Drugs and who are
identified as likely to incur annual costs above a specified threshold. Since PDPs may have access only
to prescription history under their program, meeting this criteria can be a challenge. The ACG System
pharmacy-based predictive models and the Rx-MG classifications provide an excellent means of
finding the population of individuals eligible for these programs. The Rx-MGs can be used to identify
members being treated for particular conditions while the pharmacy cost predicted risk, calibrated for
an elderly population, can be used to calculate an individual cost forecast. Using these tools for the
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–323–

=== PÁGINA 324 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 16: Clinical Screening
identification of candidates for MTMPs allows a PDP to screen the whole population with an objective
and reproducible method.
The U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) guidelines provide healthcare organizations
some flexibility in determining the eligibility criteria for their MTMPs and the ACG System can support
various selected methods. General CMS guidelines for 2014 MTM programs, as well as some example
filters, are presented below as a high-level summary for illustrative purposes. For a full explanation of
the MTMP criteria, refer to the CMS guidelines at https://www.cms.gov/medicare/prescription-drug-
coverage/prescriptiondrugcovcontra/mtm.html.
Multiple Chronic Diseases CMS has established both a ceiling and a floor for the minimum number
of chronic diseases that may be required. A healthcare organization can target beneficiaries with at
least two chronic diseases or at least three chronic diseases. Further, healthcare organizations may
target beneficiaries with any chronic diseases or limit enrollment in their MTMPs to beneficiaries
having specific chronic diseases. In the ACG System software, use the chronic condition count marker
to set thresholds for any chronic diseases, or alternately use the condition markers, EDCs and/or Rx-
MGs to identify members with specific chronic conditions.
Multiple Covered Part D Drugs CMS has also established both a ceiling and a floor for the minimum
number of drugs that may be required - two to eight. In the ACG System software, use the active
ingredient count to set thresholds for drug counts.
Likely to Incur $3017 A beneficiary must also be likely to incur an annual cost of at least $3,017
(2014 MTMP annual cost threshold) for all covered Part D drugs. In the ACG System software, this
criterion can be set based on actual pharmacy cost for the current 12-month observation period or
based on predicted pharmacy cost.

Example 17: Identify Patients at High Risk for Hospitalization
Hospital Dominant Morbidity Types represent a small subset of diagnoses associated with high rates
of admission in the following 12 months. The Hospital Dominant Morbidity Types contribute
significantly to the ACG System cost predictions. They have high Positive Predictive Value (PPV) but
lack sensitivity in identifying the full pool of patients at risk for hospitalization. The Hospitalization
Prediction models use hospital dominant morbidity types in addition to ACG-defined co-morbidity and
previous utilization to identify risk of hospitalization across the entire population.
Tip: The Hospital Prediction models are more fully described in Predictive Models for Hospitalization
on page 246

malignancy EDC also has a procedure code indicating radiation or chemotherapy services were

a patient with chronic renal failure has received at least one dialysis procedure during the observation

Example 18: Identify Patients at Risk for High Utilization
The ACG Coordination markers (Unique Provider Count, Specialty Count, Majority Source of Care and
Generalist Seen) can be used together to provide a comprehensive picture of coordination of care.
The ACG System assigns patients into three levels indicating the risk for coordination issues: Likely
Coordination Issue (LCI), Possible Coordination Issue (PCI), and Unlikely Coordination Issue (UCI). A
high unique provider count tends to be the major risk factor for potential coordination issues.
Tip: The Coordination markers are more fully described in Coordination on page 215.
To identify patients that are at risk for future high utilization, it might be reasonable to assess the
Coordination Risk in conjunction with previous utilization. Two utilization markers to consider are the
Unplanned Inpatient Hospitalizations count and the Readmissions 30 Day count. The Unplanned
Inpatient Hospitalizations count is a subset of the inpatient hospitalizations count with exclusions for
planned admissions. A planned admission is defined as either a definitively planned procedure, such
as rehabilitation services, chemotherapy and transplants or a potentially planned procedure, such as
hip replacements, cardiovascular procedures and other inpatient surgical treatments without evidence
of acute complications such as infections, burns or injuries. Any inpatient hospitalization that cannot
be identified as definitively or potentially planned is considered unplanned. The Readmissions 30 Day
count is a subset of the All Cause Inpatient Hospitalizations count. The presence of this count
indicates, regardless of cause, the identified admission occurred within 30 days of a previous
admission.
Tip: The Utilization markers are more fully described in Utilization and Resource Use Markers on
page 203.

Chapter 17: Performance Assessment
Chapter 17:
Performance Assessment
Performance assessment is commonly accomplished through profiling, a technique for comparing the
activities of one or more health care providers. Typically, profiling involves examination of resource
utilization: dollars spent on overall patient care or discrete services such as laboratory, pharmacy or
inpatient care. In profiling, the principal underlying question is "How does a provider's pattern of
practice compare to that of other providers once case-mix is accounted for?" By taking into account
the differences in illness burden among different providers' patient populations, the ACG System
allows one to determine whether variations in practice are a result of providers having sicker patient
populations or whether these variations are potentially attributable to differences in the way
providers practice medicine.
These evaluations have historically been used for the purpose of providing physician feedback or for
peer review. The goals here may be to stimulate voluntary changes in behavior, to identify potential
fraud and abuse issues, or to improve the quality of care delivered. However, efforts to extend the
use of these evaluations are rapidly emerging. Increasingly, cost of care measures are being used to
assign physicians to network tiers, to differentiate fee schedules, or to incentivize providers through
shared savings programs.
Technical Considerations
Profiling usually implies the comparison of performance across groups once differences in case-mix
are accounted for. A set of indicators is derived for each group in order to assist in identifying those
groups which deviate from the norm or average. The output from the analyses used to measure
efficiency should be actionable by the healthcare organization and the providers, enabling them to
assess relative performance when compared to others and to identify opportunities for improvement.
Further, the methods used in calculating efficiency should reflect the overall, true cost of care and the
appropriate areas of control (e.g., providers should not be held accountable for the impact of benefit
design). There are many considerations to be made when undertaking a profiling activity.
Data Quality A profiling analysis requires complete and accurate administrative claims data, as well as
member eligibility and demographic data. An appropriate analysis period must be chosen. Most
frequently this will be the most current 12-month period for which there is accumulated claims data,
after accounting for an appropriate run-out period.
Length of Enrollment To preserve accuracy, most profiling analyses will set a minimum enrollment
threshold (e.g., six months or more) for inclusion in the analysis in order to reduce the impact partial-
year enrollment may have on cost of care patterns. Further, it may not be reasonable to hold
providers accountable for impacting care if the member’s eligibility timeframe is very short. Assessing
the distribution and stability of the partial-year (and potentially non-user) populations over time may
provide insights into an appropriate threshold to be used. Also refer to the discussion on Partial-Year
Enrollees below.
Dollar Basis It is necessary to address variations in payment rates across providers, and to remove
biases that may be introduced by differences in fee schedules or contracted discounts. Standardized
prices are useful for benchmarking and for decomposing the service mix from contracted discounts.
This approach is also more equitable to providers, who have little or no control regarding their
patients’ use of higher-priced hospitals or specialists because of location or other constraints.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–334–

=== PÁGINA 335 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 17: Performance Assessment
Handling of Outliers/Catastrophic Cases Generally speaking, the rationale behind using an outlier
threshold is to prevent skewing the average cost of the provider due to a catastrophic case over
which the provider has little control. Excluding outliers completely is not the recommended approach,
as it removes the accountability for complications and manifestations that might lead to an outlier
case, and may cause meaningful information for evaluating the best and the worst examples of
physician cost of care performance to be lost. Truncating at a specified dollar limit, percentage basis
or standard deviation threshold, so as not to over-inflate cost comparisons, tends to be a more
consistent and equitable approach.
Provider Attribution The goal is to attribute provider costs commensurate with the degree of actual
or desired influence or control that the provider has on the total cost of care delivered. The challenge
is that multiple providers is the norm for patients with chronic conditions. In a “gatekeeper” model, a
patient must select a primary care physician (PCP), and attribution tends to be unambiguous;
however, one must decide how to account for the non-user population and whether additional
criteria should still be considered. For example, minimum eligibility criteria and/or at least one office
visit to the attributed provider during the measurement year will ensure the provider had an
opportunity to affect the overall care of the patient. While this approach provides for direct
accountability by the PCP, and strives to create awareness and opportunity for better coordination of
care, it may also test the administrative accuracy of the PCP data collection. When a PCP is not
selected or assigned, logic must be employed to determine one. This typically involves selecting the
provider who had the most opportunity to impart care and could be selected based on number of
visits, percentage of total professional costs, etc. This approach ensures the provider has had
management contact with the patient, but may result in the exclusion of members from the analysis
when the desired threshold is not reached. A secondary decision must be made regarding the level of
attribution, for example individual provider versus provider group (e.g., practice, clinic, health system,
etc.) In instances where care is delivered by a group of physicians rather than a single physician, it is
important to understand the relationship between the providers and its impact on the delivery of
patient care. While attributing at the group level may account for appointment coverage within the
group and improve sample sizes, a limitation of measuring performance at the group level is that the
more data is aggregated across physicians, the more the results will have a tendency to cluster
around the mean. This makes it more challenging to interpret and act on the results.
Peer Groups Peer groups should be defined based on the analytic purpose. In some analyses, all
providers are compared to each other. In other analyses, providers might be compared only to a
“like” subset of providers. Illness burden tends to vary significantly by provider specialty, even across
primary care specialties (e.g., Family Practice, Internal Medicine, Pediatrics, etc.), making provider
specialty a commonly used basis for peer grouping, but provider networks or geographically based
groupings might also be used.
Minimum Number of Observations/Panel Size Sufficient numbers of patients must be part of a
profiling analysis in order to generate an acceptable level of statistical validity and reliability. There is
not one standard for selecting the threshold; the intended use of the profiling activity and the data
available will likely inform this decision. The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
recommends a minimum of 25 patients, while the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA)
recommends a minimum of 30 patients, to estimate true provider cost of care. Likewise, to ensure
that a single provider is not skewing the comparison group, there should be sufficient numbers of
peers within each group to produce a reliable peer comparison.
Risk Adjustment There may be substantive differences in the distribution of risk characteristics in the
relatively small subset of a population that has contact with a single physician. In order to
systematically examine the pattern of practice or expenditure related to that group, adjustment must
be made to allow for the patients’ characteristics to be taken into account. Rather than looking solely
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–335–

=== PÁGINA 336 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 17: Performance Assessment
at charges the provider incurred, a global view of the overall risk-adjusted utilization of service
incurred by the provider’s panel gives a perspective on that provider’s contribution to the whole.
One approach for addressing the above issues is the HealthPartners Total Cost of Care, or TCOC,
methodology endorsed by the National Quality Forum (see www.healthpartners.com/tcoc). The TCOC
framework, which uses the ACG System as its risk adjustment tool, is a population-based approach for
standardizing cost measurement and assessing efficiency across provider practices.
Risk Adjustment Approaches: ACG Categories vs.
Regression-Based Concurrent Risk
It is important to note that there are different ways to apply risk-adjustment within the ACG System.
Two approaches, use of ACG concurrent risk, based on actuarial cells, and use of regression-based
concurrent risk, are discussed in the following sections.
ACG Concurrent Risk
In this chapter, the term “risk” is used to represent a relative value for resource use with respect to
some population average and is generally expressed as a numeric value with a mean of 1.0 (i.e.,
where the resource use is the same as that of the reference population). Relative risk scores can be
applied to mean resource use for a population to arrive at expected resource use. A fixed set of
concurrent ACG risk scores based upon the Risk Assessment Variables selection is available as part of
the software output file. An individual risk score is associated with each ACG actuarial cell. The
actuarial cells represent a fixed number of discrete categories into which individuals are placed based
on their expected use of resources.
The software-supplied reference ACG concurrent risk scores are available in two forms: unscaled and
rescaled. The unscaled reference ACG concurrent risk is simply the value of the reference ACG
concurrent risk score applied to a population of interest. The mean value of the unscaled reference
ACG concurrent risk provides a rudimentary profiling statistic. If the mean of the unscaled reference
ACG concurrent risk is greater than 1.0 it indicates the population being profiled is sicker than the
reference population (the software-provided national reference database). If the mean is less than
1.0, it indicates the population being profiled is healthier. To ensure that dollars in the system are not
over or under-estimated, an adjusted or rescaled reference ACG concurrent risk score that
mathematically manipulates the unscaled reference ACG concurrent risk score to have a mean of 1.0
in the local population is also provided. Refer to Rescale and Assign Monetary Values Process on page
235 for more details on the rescaling process.
If local cost data are available, the ACG System also calculates local ACG concurrent risk scores. These
local ACG concurrent risk scores more accurately reflect local benefit levels and area practice patterns.
In general, it is recommended that the population upon which the concurrent risk scores are
developed should be as similar as possible to the assessment population to which the concurrent risk
scores are applied. However, in the absence of local cost data, the reference concurrent risk scores
may prove useful for calculating reasonably representative profiling statistics.
There are a number of advantages associated with using an actuarial cell-based approach to risk
adjustment and experience indicates that ACG concurrent risk scores, especially when expressed as
relative values, have remarkable stability.
Conceptually simple Once the population has been classified into ACG categories, it is possible to risk
adjust the population using a spreadsheet alone. Some organizations have chosen to simplify this
approach even further by collapsing the ACG categories into smaller homogeneous groupings called
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–336–

=== PÁGINA 337 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 17: Performance Assessment
Resource Utilization Bands (RUBs). Even when grouped into RUBs, studies indicate that the ACG
System retains much of their explanatory power.
Stability The conceptual elegance and underlying simplicity of ACG categories have made the system
very stable over long periods. The underlying clinical truth captured by ACG categories does not
change dramatically with each new data set and each new application.
Ease of making local calibrations It is very easy to recalibrate ACG actuarial categories to reflect local
differences in patterns of practice, benefit structure, and provider fees. The same simplicity that
makes it possible to risk-adjust using a spreadsheet makes it equally possible to accomplish
recalibration using the same types of simple tools.
Less prone to manipulation Unlike some disease-specific risk adjusters, aggressive efforts to capture
additional diagnostic codes on the part of providers will have a more limited impact on ACG category
assignments. Where code creep associated with general increases in completeness and accuracy of
coding exists, the simplicity of the ACG System makes it very easy to identify this trend and to
implement appropriate action, such as recalibration of the underlying risk scores.
When differences in ACG concurrent risk scores occur across populations, it is often attributable to
differences in covered services reflected by different benefit levels, but may be due to highly skewed
populations as well (e.g., carve-outs, biased selection, etc.).
Regression-Based Concurrent Risk
The ACG concurrent risk scores are conceptually simple to understand and statistically validated in
numerous settings; however, they are a categorical measurement of risk which inherently allows for
less variability. While the stated risk is the same for all members within an actuarial cell, in reality
there is actually a continuum of risk within that cell that can be further differentiated using linear
regression. A regression-based model allows for:
Addressing within-cell variation The inclusion of additional risk factors to determine overall disease
burden helps to address within-cell variation and results in the assignment of individual risk scores.
Improved statistical performance A regression-based concurrent model tends to provide improved
statistical performance for the highest risk members of a given cohort and for skewed or biased
populations.
It is important to note that with this approach the user is constrained to the use of an external
reference population for model development and to the outcomes defined within the software. While
the inclusion of additional risk factors tends to improve the statistical performance, this explanatory
power is often confined to the data set and time period on which the model is based and may not
translate to the same statistical performance in another data set, a phenomenon referred to as over-
fitting. Further, the relatively large number of risk factors used in the regression model creates a
greater dependence on coding specificity. Finally, this approach may be difficult to explain and may
provide a false sense of precision due to the assignment of individualized risk scores.
Including Partial-Year Enrollees
When determining which members to include in the profiling analysis, the impact of including
members who have not been enrolled for the full 12-month analysis period should be assessed.
Two approaches for calculating ACG concurrent risk from local data are:
• PMPM (per member per month)
• PMPY (per member per year)

• PMPM = R /Months

• PMPY = R /N

Where R is calculated as the sum of resource use across all members assigned to a particular ACG

(ACG)

The primary difference between these two methodologies hinges on whether or not costs are
annualized to account for part-year enrollment; a PMPY approach tends to be preferred for risk
adjustment because of the way it handles part-year enrollees. Analysis has demonstrated that when
performing concurrent risk-based adjustment, a PMPM calculation of ACG concurrent risk for a
population that includes some number of part-time enrollees tends to over-estimate the expected
costs associated with 12-month enrollees and under-estimate the expected costs associated with
shorter-term enrollees. A PMPY calculation of ACG concurrent risk appears to provide a more
accurate measure of the expected cost.
Past work using data from multiple sites has demonstrated that persons who are enrolled for fewer
than 12 months in a healthcare organization during a given year tend to use more resources on a
PMPM or annualized basis than those who are continuously enrolled for the entire period. New,
previously uninsured enrollees may have higher costs as a result of previously unmet needs or they
could be switching insurers in the midst of a special healthcare episode (e.g., they could be
responding to a newly diagnosed condition).
Shorter-term enrollees as a group also exhibit higher costs in part because they include those who
leave an insurer either because they have special medical circumstances or, at the extreme, die. In
addition to these circumstances, as the following table illustrates, shorter-term enrollees have
seemingly higher PMPM costs in large part because the denominator of the PMPM calculation is
relatively smaller for those enrollees. By contrast, the average cost of 12-month enrollees tends to be
more stable. The following analysis illustrates the implications of this within the context of diagnosis-
based risk adjustment such as ACG categories.

Summary
Risk is not evenly distributed across populations. In order to systematically examine the pattern of
practice or expenditure related to a provider’s panel of patients, adjustment must be made to allow
for the patients’ illness burden to be taken into account. The ACG System provides a means for risk
adjusting profiles. Assuming the output is credible, reliable and actionable, healthcare organizations
and providers should be able to identify opportunities for improvement. As shown in the following
figure, the results of the profiling analysis can be used to focus scarce resources allocated to
education, peer review and performance improvement, identifying possible disparities, or for audits
focused on potential fraud and abuse. Further, results may be used to support contracting incentives,
tiered network design or panel balancing.

Financial Applications
Capitation and Rate Setting
The goal of risk adjusted payments as illustrated in the following figure is to allocate limited
healthcare dollars in a fair and equitable manner. The amount of money available for allocation is a
policy decision or budget matter; risk adjustment is typically one element of a comprehensive
allocation program.
Figure128.AllocatingtheHealthcareBudget
Considerations for Implementing Risk-Adjusted Payments
Method for Assessing Risk: Risk Categories vs. Risk Scores
The ACG System has made it possible to accomplish risk adjustment with fairly simple and
straightforward analytic strategies, and the ACG categories as actuarial cells have long been the
primary actuarial method for capitation and rate setting. Actuarial cells represent a fixed number of
discrete categories into which individuals are placed based on their expected use of resources.
There are a number of advantages associated with using an actuarial cell-based approach to risk
adjustment for capitation and underwriting.
Conceptually simple Once the population has been classified into a limited number of ACG
categories, it is possible to risk adjust the population using a spreadsheet alone. Some organizations
have chosen to simplify this approach even further by collapsing the ACG categories into smaller
homogeneous groupings called Resource Utilization Bands (RUBs). Even when grouped into RUBs,
studies indicate that The ACG System retains much of the explanatory power.
Stability The conceptual elegance and underlying simplicity of ACG categories have made the system
very stable over long periods. The underlying clinical truth captured by ACG categories does not
change dramatically with each new data set and each new application.
Ease of making local calibrations It is very easy to recalibrate risk based upon ACG categories to
reflect local differences in patterns of practice, benefit structure, and provider fees. The same
simplicity that makes it possible to risk-adjust using a spreadsheet makes it equally possible to
accomplish recalibration using the same types of simple tools.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–346–

=== PÁGINA 347 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 18: Financial Applications
Less prone to manipulation Unlike some disease-specific risk adjusters, aggressive efforts to capture
additional diagnostic codes on the part of providers will have a more limited impact on ACG category
assignments. Where code creep associated with general increases in completeness and accuracy of
coding exists, the simplicity of the ACG System makes it very easy to identify this trend and to
implement appropriate action, such as recalibration of the underlying risk scores.
There are some additional items to be considered when using actuarial cells for risk adjusted
payments.
Small cell size Sufficient numbers of members must be assigned to each ACG category in order to
generate an acceptable level of statistical validity and reliability. There should be at least 30 members
assigned to each ACG category.
Length of enrollment When calculating ACG concurrent risk scores for payment purposes, it is
frequently recommended to include only those members with 12 months of eligibility, but if this
excludes too many members from the analysis, the eligibility cut-off could be lowered.
Outliers Often an upper cost threshold (set at the reinsurance threshold) is applied to limit skewing
of the most complex ACG categories. This does not impact the ACG category assignment, but rather
the calculation of the ACG concurrent risk (calculated as the simple average total cost of all individuals
assigned to each category divided by the average total cost of all individuals in the source data file).
Note that if the software-calculated ACG concurrent risk is being used, the cost truncation must be
done on the input file.
Carve-out populations Comparability across populations is essential; carve-out populations, such as
behavioral health, may need to be addressed separately and the methods for doing so should be
applied consistently.
Alternately, a regression-based concurrent model could be used to determine risk. The ACG
concurrent risk scores are conceptually simple to understand and statistically validated in numerous
settings; however, they are a categorical measurement of risk which inherently allows for less
variability. While the stated risk is the same for all members within an actuarial cell, in reality there is
actually a continuum of risk within that cell that can be further differentiated using linear regression.
A regression-based model allows for:
Addressing within-cell variation The inclusion of additional risk factors to determine overall disease
burden helps to address within-cell variation and results in the assignment of individual risk scores.
Improved statistical performance A regression-based concurrent model tends to provide improved
statistical performance for the highest risk members of a given cohort and for skewed or biased
populations.
It is important to note that with this approach the user is constrained to the use of an external
reference population for model development and to the outcomes defined within the software. While
the inclusion of additional risk factors tends to improve the statistical performance, this explanatory
power is often confined to the data set and time period on which the model is based and may not
translate to the same statistical performance in another data set, a phenomenon referred to as over-
fitting. Further, the relatively large number of risk factors used in the regression model creates a
greater dependence on coding specificity. Finally, this approach may be difficult to explain and may
provide a false sense of precision due to the assignment of individualized risk scores.

Timeframe for Analysis: Retrospective vs. Prospective
In a retrospective analysis, the actual cost during a given 12-month period is known, and a relative
risk based on each individual’s underlying morbidity during that same matching 12-month period can
be assigned.
Conversely, in a prospective analysis, the data from period one are used to predict the cost in period
two. This can be achieved using either an actuarial cell or regression-based approach. In the former,
the actuarial cell (ACG) assigned from Year 1 data is still used, but the costs from Year 2 are used to
calculate a prospective risk score (calculated as the simple average total cost of all individuals assigned
to each category divided by the average total cost of all individuals in the source data file). In the
latter, a regression-based predictive model could be used to determine the risk. In this approach, each
individual gets a unique relative risk score (unscaled or rescaled).
While various implementations exist, there has been a broader adoption of concurrently calibrated
models due to their higher explanatory power and because of their inclusion of acute conditions,
whereas prospective models rely heavily on chronic conditions. A prospective model might be chosen
if liability in the subsequent time period is of greater interest.
Data Appropriateness for Risk Adjusted Payment Models
When determining what data to use in the risk adjusted payment model it is important to consider if
certain information might provide incentive effects. For example, prior cost is very effective for
predicting next year’s expenditures. In fact, prior cost is the gold standard to which risk adjusted
payment methods are compared for evaluation purposes. Including prior cost in a risk adjusted
payment model provides explanatory power beyond what can be achieved by prior cost alone.
However, including prior cost in a risk adjusted payment model will build into that model pre-existing
biases (e.g., those based on past practices and not necessarily on medical need). Similarly, the
inclusion of pharmacy information can improve predictive performance, but is not recommended for
risk adjusted payment applications due to the potential harm of over/under-prescribing within a
patient population.
Prior cost and pharmacy data are available as optional inputs to the ACG System risk models. When
using the ACG System output for capitation and rate setting, the recommendation is to use a
diagnosis-based model, relying only on International Classification of Disease (ICD) input variables.
Level of Assessment: Plan-level Payments vs. Individual Payments
In a plan-level risk adjustment method, an overall case-mix index (CMI) is calculated by averaging the
risk scores of all members within the total population. Payments are then based on the relative case-
mix across plans, e.g., the number of enrollees in the plan times the overall case-mix of the plan
times the average amount of resources required to treat the average patient across the entire
population. If any one individual leaves (or joins) the plan, payment goes down (or up) by the CMI
times the average resource need across the population. The rationale here is that the entry (or exit)
of any one individual does not have a significant impact on the overall morbidity of the plan.
In contrast, an individual-level payment model has a similar net effect after summing across individual
members; however, a key difference between the two implementations is what happens when a
member joins (or leaves) a plan. Rather than an increase (or decrease) tied to the mean CMI of the
plan, the increase is tied to the individual’s risk profile. For example, if someone with a high risk score
joins a plan, the plan will receive more for this individual than someone with a low risk sore.
The ACG actuarial cells perform very well at a population level, but it is important to recognize that as
the ACG categories become more complex, there is more cost variation at the individual level. This
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–348–

Chapter 18: Financial Applications
should be taken into account when contemplating plan-level payments versus individual-level
payments. A regression-based model tends to perform better at the individual level.
Another consideration when adopting individual-level payment models is that there is a lack of
experience for new enrollees, and therefore, accurate risk scores cannot be determined. A separate
methodology must be employed to address payments for new enrollees.
Summary
The ultimate testimony to the value of using ACG categories as the basis of actuarial cells is the fact
that for nearly two decades, they have been used to facilitate the exchange of billions of dollars
within numerous private and public healthcare organizations in both the United States and Canada.
For a case study illustrating the use of ACG categories for prospective payment at the individual-level
see: “The Development of Risk-Adjusted Capitation Payment System for Medicaid MCOs: The Maryland
Model”, Weiner et al, Journal of Ambulatory Care Management, January, 1998.
For a case study illustrating a plan-level concurrently calibrated risk adjustment method, see: “Health-
based Capitation Risk Adjustment in Minnesota Public Health Care Programs”, Gifford GA, Edwards KR,
Knutson DJ, Health Care Finance Rev 26:21-41, 2005.
Underwriting
The ACG Predictive Models, calibrated for high-risk case-identification, provide underwriters with a
suite of tools to estimate future resource use based on the case-mix of the enrolled population, which
offers an improvement over more traditional prior utilization models. For example, in addition to
estimating future resource use, the models can also be used to help identify persons expected to
move from relatively low to relatively high resource use. This not only improves the quality and
accuracy of underwriting, but also provides opportunities for reducing costs for employers by getting
at-risk employees enrolled in timely case management interventions to help reduce both future
medical expenses and illness-associated absenteeism.
The ACG Predictive Models are especially useful for small group underwriting because the movement
of one or two high-risk individuals into or out of a healthcare organization can have potentially
dramatic effects on costs for a small group. Small employer groups are sensitive to price and have a
tendency to shop for a new carrier at renewal time. The initial rate process uses more data than is
feasible during a typical renewal; therefore, the initial rate process often produces the most
competitive rates. Small groups exhibiting low risk can often find rates lower than with their current
provider; however, small groups exhibiting a history of high expenditures may find going to a new
insurer prohibitively expensive. This type of selection bias can lead to a very high risk pool and a
future inability of an insurer to offer attractive rates to retain the healthy groups. In order to retain
the best business, insurers are faced with the difficult task of offering competitive pricing for these
small groups by trying to accurately match premium revenue to expected expense while complying
with existing rating regulations. The Johns Hopkins suite of Predictive Models provides insurers with
the necessary tools to leverage existing medical and pharmacy claims in order to better estimate risk
and better set premiums for small group renewal.
There are several benefits to using predictive modeling within the underwriting process:
• There is greater efficiency. Predictive modeling can provide an automated risk assessment on
every member; thereby reducing the medical underwriting effort. This reduction in effort, in turn,
reduces the elapsed time needed for analysis and consequently will reduce the lag between the
experience period and the rating period. Using a pharmacy-based model can reduce this lag
further. This leads to greater accuracy.

=== PÁGINA 353 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 19: Social Determinants of Health in the ACG System
Chapter 19:
Social Determinants of Health in the ACG
System
Population health analytics is a continually evolving field, and organizations need to adopt clinically-
relevant, actionable tools to succeed. To support our customers, the Johns Hopkins ACG System has
developed new features to help system users understand and address social determinants of health
(SDoH) and social need within their populations, with easy-to-use features that generate insightful
analytics.
Why focus on SDoH?
As part of value-based care models, healthcare providers and organization are being held responsible
for health outcomes and total cost of care of their population. This has provided impetus for
physicians and hospitals to increasingly focus on identifying and addressing social determinants of the
population that may be associated with overall health outcomes and spending. In addition to being
held accountable and reimbursed for collecting social needs and implementing social needs specific
interventions, many states have begun implementing programs in Medicaid populations.
For example, Vermont's Support and Services at Home (SASH)35 model uses SDoH data to connect
low-income seniors and adults with disabilities with community-based services, and to promote care
coordination. Twenty-eight data points are collected in SASH via a uniform assessment tool, which
participating housing organizations are required to administer on a periodic basis. The tool includes
validated screens and surveys for food insecurity, substance use, tobacco use, and social isolation.
With the launch of a new electronic shared care plan, SASH enrollees, in collaboration with care
managers, will be able to identify social risks and work toward meeting SDoH-related goals.
Increasingly, ACG System users are being asked to use Social Determinants and Social Needs data in
analyses to understand population needs, craft clinical improvement strategies, deploy resources and
measure health equity. These new ACG System features provide uses the tools and data points to
create these analyses using curated outputs and summary measures, in combination with pre-existing
risk markers and measures.
How are Social Determinants captured and reported?
The first important effort in the direction of capturing standardized information on SDoH is the 10th
revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) which includes a new set of "Z-codes"
(Z55-Z65) in addition to ICD codes- R, E, T, S and X to describe factors influencing health status and
health-related outcomes. The availability of SDoH codes may offer an opportunity to demonstrate the
impact of these social factors more broadly and could serve as a way to standardize documentation.
The ACG System leverages these codes that can be used by any provider in different health settings
and maps them to common social needs to consistently identify patients with social and geographical
factors affecting health. In addition to individual-level ICD codes, social determinants will be captured
35 AdditionalinformationontheVermontSupportandServicesatHomecanbefoundat: https://sashvt.org/
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

at a geographic-level through zip codes and FIPS (Federal Information Processing Series)36 codes at a
patient- and population-level, for users with the GeoHealth module available.
What is the ACG System Approach to SDoH?
ACG System measures and incorporates social determinants at both the patient-record and
geographic level. Essentially, patient-level measures capture the most pressing healthcare needs for an
individual where as Social Determinants are population level markers within a geographic, social
and/or political boundary. For example, a lack of educational attainment in given zip code is a social
determinant of health while illiteracy and low-level literacy is a patient-level social need that may not
apply to every individual within that geographic area. Understanding both of these concepts is critical
in population health. SDoH may impact the health of patients over a lifetime while social needs reflect
a documented pressing need or needs with an immediate health impact.
The ACG's System newest feature, ACG GeoHealth, incorporates SDoH risks related to geography, or
where the population being analyzed lives or is located. Building on ACG's whole-person approach to
health needs and predictive measures, ACG GeoHealth provides ACG System users with cleansed,
curated data providing in-system capabilities to:
• Describe population distribution, disease prevalence and utilization patterns by geographic
challenges
• Complete SDOH needs assessment and develop an improvement plan aligned with strategic
investments
• Support resource allocation, case manager and CHW case-finding activities aligned with high-need
geographies and a hotspotting approach
• Measure health disparities and program outcomes based on geographic variables
This feature provides many opportunities to enhance existing ACG System use cases and applications
enabling end users to integrate socio-environmental factors, in addition to clinical features, into the
management and understanding of patient populations.
The ACG System's new Social Need Markers consist of five critical domains of social need: Social,
Education, Health Care System, Economic and Physical Environment. Within those categories, 13 sub-
domains further dissect the environment to which a patient is exposed on a daily basis. These
domains are developed with the understanding that no single variable or code can fully describe a
patient's social needs. The overall goal is to combine individual attributes into meaningful categories
that are relevant for population health which gives users a full understanding of how populations are
impacted by geographically-driven factors. Social Need Markers figure prominently in this new release,
helping users understand patients' individual social and behavioral risk factors.
For instance, having access to health care is a clear social determinant of health. If a patient doesn't
have insurance, however, they are not able to access that care. They are more likely to have poor
health outcomes because of that lack of insurance. ACG GeoHealth has the precise ability to consider
the neighborhood in which the patient resides. This gives users a critical look at socio-environmental
factors. Users can also closely examine individual zip codes or census tr acts of a certain population.

=== PÁGINA 355 ===

Chapter 20: ACG GeoHealth Overview
Chapter 20:
ACG GeoHealth Overview
ACG GeoHealth measures were selected to add value to population health and risk-based analyses,
provide complete population data, and generate insightful output informing SDoH needs. ACG
GeoHealth v13.0 includes 17 unique variables with five metrics each resulting in a set of 85 total
variables that are associated with more than one geographical match level. The purpose of these
variables is to help users understand the accuracy of the point estimate seen an estimate value in
order to put them in context with state and national norms (i.e., if the margin of error is too wide,
then the estimate value may not be very accurate to capture the SDoH variable prevalence for a
geographic area. Similarly, national and state percentiles give users context on where the local data
point lies in comparison to the national level and state level respectively.
Below are the five metrics:
• Estimated Value: The estimated value of the SDoH variable for a geographical area such as Census
Tract FIPS11 or USPS ZIP5 based on U.S. Census tract estimates. This is typically a percentage,
median value (e.g., household income), or an aggregate score (e.g., ADI). This field should be
considered a raw output value.
• Margin of Error: The calculated error of the estimated value. Those based on U.S. Census
represent a 90% confidence internal. Geographic areas with low population density or low
questionnaire response rates may have high margins of error, which is important to consider in
advanced analyses and some research applications.
• National Percentile : The percentile ranking of the geographic area's SDoH variable estimated
value with respect to national estimates. The ACG System team recommends users apply national
percentiles when their populations cross state lines or include multi-state plans.
• State Percentile : The percentile ranking of the geographic area's estimated value within a U.S.
state. The ACG System team recommends users apply state-level percentiles when their
population occurs within a single state, to improve accuracy and granularity of measurements.
• National Category: An ordinal category based on the National Percentile value. For example, Low,
Medium, High based on the lowest 20%, middle 20%-80%, and the highest 20%. National
categories are assigned for ease-of-use in descriptive analyses.
The 85 discrete variable labels consist of the variable group prefix plus a three-character extension of
_est, _err, _nat, _sta, or _cat. Each set of 85 variables may have different field values that are
associated with more than one geographical match level. For example, variable values
pop_density_est, pop_density_err, pop_density_nat, pop_density_sta, and pop_density_cat may be
available for assignment at a census tract or zip level and where the geo_name is unique among sets
of geo_name + 85 geo variables.
Refer to ACG GeoHealth Codes and Descriptions on page for codes and description of these below
variables.

The US Census Bureau publishes FIPS codes which are geographical identifiers assigned alphabetically
by geographical name for states, counties, and other core statistical areas. These are known as census
tract levels.
The figure below indicates how FIPS codes are composed:
More often, Zip codes are found within patient data. Zip codes are generalized areal representations
of the US postal service areas specifically based on collections of USPS mail delivery routes.
Literature suggests that geographic analyses using FIPS at the census tract provide more accuracy and
relationship to health outcomes; however, not all ACG System users have FIPS available so we provide
ZIP-based mappings for ease-of-use.
Tip: There are a variety of geo-coder web applications that can convert Zip Codes into FIPS codes. If
using FIPS codes, avoid the use of decimals as this field is a string, not a number, and select 2019
geo-assignments if possible.

Chapter 21: Social Need Markers
Chapter 21:
Social Need Markers
The addition of ACG GeoHealth and Social Need Markers (SNM) will work alongside each other to
provide a comprehensive population and individual level view of social risk. In other words, Social
Need Markers are at a patient-level whereas ACG GeoHealth focuses on population level social
determinants.
Social Need Markers Overview
Social Need Markers within the ACG System were developed to give users a comprehensive view of
social needs in their populations: for use alone, or alongside other pre-existing ACG System features.
The ACG Social Need Marker module consists of five domains and 13 subdomains to capture some of
the most documented social needs of individuals coming in contact with health care systems. These
domains also overlap with the Accountable Health Communities model proposed by CMS which
requires health care providers and hospitals to screen and address them including food insecurity,
housing instability, utility needs, transportation needs, and interpersonal violence, and align with the
CDC's five critical SDoH areas of focus in Healthy People 2030 goals.
The ACG System will read the ICD-10 codes from medical services and/or supplemental files and
assign domain-specific social needs for each patient. Given the sometimes-low frequency of coding of
the social needs ICD-10 codes, only the overall Social Need Marker sub-domain and domain-specific
markers will be displayed in the frequency distributions report. Enhanced reporting will be developed
in future versions based on customer feedback.

The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Chapter 21: Social Need Markers
Combining ACG GeoHealth with Social Need Markers
within the ACG System
For ACG System users, the addition of the Social Need Markers to the ACG GeoHealth measures ,
which captures individual-level ICD10-CM codes related to social needs, adds a critical layer to
understanding both social risk and clinical risk, as well as their association with neighborhood level
characteristics and upstream SDoH.
An individual's patient profile is thus enhanced to better understand the potential impact social needs
are having on patient outcomes. As a starting point, adding in social needs variables to analysis of an
individual's patient profile provides a more person-centric view of the patient's needs and supports
critical decision making for providers and care teams; ultimately empowering care that is more
customized to whole-person needs and directing resources more appropriately. Social Need Marker
domains and sub-domains further their utility by providing a first step in understanding whether the
incorporation of social risk into risk adjustment approach is reasonable. By understanding these critical
domains across provider's patients, a particular organization (health plan, ACO, CIN, Provider Network)
can begin informing their consideration for how social needs could be leveraged in the development
of a risk adjustment approach for understanding provider performance for the purposes of value-
based contracting.
Based on the data provided through the ACG system with the addition of social needs, organizations
can quickly decipher which providers are operating above and below average of the whole and how
the social needs of their patients and complexity of their conditions is playing a role in the providers
performance. Organizations can also quickly identify what specific provider supports can enhance
provider performance, and empower providers with information about their patients. This information
supports the providers in making resource decisions and specifying their workflows and clinical care
plans. Incorporating this information provides an added benefit and perspective for not just the
overall organization (health plan, ACO, CIN, Provider Network) but additionally for the individual
providers and provider groups looking to enhance their reduction of adverse outcomes across a
population.

Chapter 22: SDoH Applications
Chapter 22:
SDoH Applications
This chapter outlines sample use cases using ACG GeoHealth and social needs measures.
Application 1
ACG GeoHealth Risk Factors by County
The ACG GeoHealth Risk Factors by County report is available under the Analyze > ACG GeoHealth
reports menu.
The ACG GeoHealth Risk Factors by County report outlines different geographical factors based on a
county. This report, available to users with the ACG GeoHealth licensed module, relies on FIPS-based
geocodes to quantify key geographic variables at the county level.
Using this analysis, an ACG System user wishes to examine the percentage of patients with a high risk
of using food stamps (SNAP) in certain counties. The user views the distribution of output variables
and sees the percentage of those is a high ADI (Area deprivation index), those in a densely populated
area, those living alone and those with a risk of SNAP benefits.
In this instance, the System user decides to dive deeper into Kane County given the low-density
population with a higher risk of SNAP given the organization is trying to address areas with potential
food insecurity.
Application 2
Measuring Geographic Health Disparities using ACG GeoHealth
Evidence indicates widespread disparities in chronic condition prevalence and health outcomes for
people based on where they liv The ACG GeoHealth tool can aid users in identifying these disparities
in their population.

• Adult patients with diabetes who lived in more deprived and rural areas were significantly less
likely to attain high-quality diabetes care compared with those in less deprived and urban areas.38
• Scant neighborhood resources compound the risk of heart failure above and beyond individual
socioeconomic status and traditional cardiovascular risk factors. 39

For a deeper dive, the ACG System user may identify a list of patients with select social needs, to

*These impacts are estimated. These new Rx-MGs do not contribute to predictive modeling.
Congruent EDCs and Rx-MGs
Congruent EDCs and Rx-MGs allow chronic diagnoses to be imputed when the supplemental medical
services option of "confirm with pharmacy" is selected (see Tracking Chronic Conditions on page 154).
Ideally congruence represents parallel concepts in both EDCs and Rx-MGs. For example immune
disorders (ALLx040) paired with disorders of the immune system (ALL06). This thinking extends to
situations where there are one to many relationships such as hypertension (CARx030) to both
hypertension without major complications (CAR14) and hypertension with complications (CAR15).

=== PÁGINA 405 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix B: ACG System Output Data
Appendix B:
ACG System Output Data
ACG System Output Data
The ACG System imports patient demographic and utilization data from the patient import file, all of
the diagnoses and pharmacy codes that a patient has experienced over the observation period from
the medical services and pharmacy import files, and adds a number of calculated data elements.
These data elements form the basis for all analyses provided in the ACG System. You can see each of
these data elements in the Patient Sample section of the ACG Data File (see the Column Definitions
for the Patients and ACG Results File table).
All of the ACG data components can be exported. Following are the data elements associated with
each choice under the Export ACG Data Options.
Patients and ACG Results
This data file contains all of the data elements from the original patient import file, with any missing
default columns added as blanks, and all of the ACG calculated fields. The columns in this export file
are the same columns (in the same order) as shown in the Patient Sample section of the ACG Data
File. The user can also elect to export a subset of available fields by clicking the Select Columns...
button and selecting/deselecting columns for export.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Patient MEDC Assignments
This data file contains one row for each MEDC code assigned to a Patient ID. An MEDC code is a
higher-level grouping for an EDC code. The MEDC code is also included in the Patient EDC
Assignments file. This file provides the added advantage of not duplicating MEDC codes for each
patient, whereas the Patient EDC Assignment file can contain duplicates for an MEDC code for a
patient. Patients may have more than one row in this table. Not all patients have diagnoses to assign
an MEDC. Patients with no MEDC assignments will be absent from this file. This file is organized in a

Utilization Summary
This data file contains summary statistics related to the utilization markers calculated by the ACG
System that are displayed in the ACG Data File screen. This data is calculated during the ACG grouping
process and summarizes the rate of specific services in the analysis population as well as derived from
reference data. The columns in this file are:
• Utilization marker
• Count
• Rate
• Reference rate
Model Markers
This data file contains a set of flags that are used during the ACG System grouping process for each
Patient ID. You will need to contact technical support for assistance in using this data. The categories
of markers in this file are:
• Patient ID
• Demographic Markers - Sex, age bands
• Dx-PM Covariates- Frailty, hospital dominant morbidity types, CAL-SSA, prospective RUBs,
pregnancy w/o delivery, ACG category markers, EDC markers
• Rx-PM Covariates - Rx-MG markers, active ingredient count
• Cost Percentile Groups - Total cost bands, Rx cost bands
• Utilization markers - Inpatient hospitalizations, outpatient visits, emergency department visits,
dialysis services, nursing services, major procedure, cancer treatment.
All Models
This data file contains all possible model scores for each patient. You will need to contact technical
support for assistance in using this data. The columns in this file are as follows. The MODEL_NAME
component is repeated for every model included in the ACG system. If a model does not apply to a
data set, it will be left blank.
• patient_id
• MODEL_NAME_pri
• MODEL_NAME_prir
• MODEL_NAME_cri
• MODEL_NAME_crir
• MODEL_NAME_prob
• MODEL_NAME_rprob
• MODEL_NAME_hosp
The naming convention for predictive modeling outputs is: Data source - Use of prior cost - diagnostic
certainty - dependent variable - score type. Possible values for each component of the model name
are presented in the following table.

information about these models.
HHS-CMS Warnings
Conditions that would affect the accurate calculation of a HHS or CMS risk score are flagged with the
warnings shown in the HHS-CMS Warnings table. Warnings should be reviewed carefully. All HHS-CMS
warnings are available in an export file format detailed below.
HHS-CMS Warnings

reports. The columns and descriptions for each available analysis follow.

the Filters, Groups, and Options capabilities, as described in Operating the ACG System Software on
page 76.

The Warning List is available through the Validate menu. The Warning List produces a list of all
patients that had ACG calculation warnings. The list layout is as follows:
ColumnName Definition
PatientID Auniqueidentifierforthispatient.

To identify a unique list of patients with a specific warning, enter criteria on the Patient Warning
Filters tab. To identify all warnings associated with patients meeting criteria, use the Patient Filters
tab. The Patient Filters and Patient Warning Filters tabs may be used in conjunction to isolate the
patients and warnings of interest.
Note: Reviewing data warnings is an important part of assuring data quality. Patients may be
represented more than once in this list if there are multiple warnings associated with the patient
data.

The Frequency and Cost Distribution analysis is available through the Validate menu and is a

MaximumTotalCost Themaximumoftotalcostacrosspatientswithinthisstratification.
Resource Utilization Band (RUB) Distribution
The RUB Distribution is available through Analyze > Frequency Distributions. ACG categories were
designed to represent clinically logical groupings for persons expected to require similar levels of
healthcare resources. However, enrollees with similar expected overall utilization may be assigned
different ACG categories because they have different epidemiological patterns of morbidity. For
example, a pregnant woman with significant morbidity, an individual with a serious psychological
condition, or someone with two chronic medical conditions may all be expected to use approximately
the same level of resources even though they each fall into different ACG categories. In many
instances users may find it useful to collapse the full set of ACG codes into fewer categories,
particularly where resource use similarity and not clinical cogency is a desired objective. Often a fewer
number of combined categories will be easier to handle from an administrative perspective. ACG
categories can be combined into Resource Utilization Bands (RUBs).
The software automatically assigns six RUB classes:
• 0 - No or Only Invalid Dx
• 1 - Healthy Users
• 2 - Low
• 3 - Moderate
• 4 - High
• 5 - Very High
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Calculating Statistical Significance
When comparing an observed distribution to a reference distribution, the use of statistical testing can
differentiate differences that might be attributed to chance from differences that are statistically
meaningful. For comparing distributions the ACG System is utilizing a Z test based on a normal
approximation to the binomial distribution.
Step 1: Assess validity of test
In order for the Z test to be appropriate there must be sufficient sample size to meet the
assumptions of normal approximation. There must be at least 5 individuals in the observation group
with the category and at least 5 individuals in the observation group without the category assigned
for a valid test. If an observation group and category do not meet this test, the significance test will
display as N/A.
Step 2: Calculate the Z-Score
The formula for the Z test for proportion is given by:
Step 3: Determine significance
The Z-score calculation can be compared to a standard normal distribution to determine a p-value. P-
values less than 0.05 will have a visual cue denoting statistical significance, either a "+" or "-"
depending on the direction of the variance between observed and reference rates.
ACG Distribution
The ACG Distribution is available through Analyze > Frequency Distributions. The foundation of the
system is the Adjusted Clinical Group algorithm. ACG categories assign persons to unique, mutually
exclusive morbidity groups based on patterns of disease and expected resource requirements. ACG
categories can be used in place of traditional age/sex categories when attempting to account for
variations in morbidity burden across two or more patient populations. A person falls into one
mutually-exclusive ACG health status category based on a combination of ADGs, age, sex and, if
available, birth weight for newborns and delivery status for pregnant women. The ACG Distribution
Analysis produces a frequency distribution by ACG code. The report layout is as follows:
ColumnName Definition
ACGCode EachACGcodethatwasassignedtoapatient.
ACGDescription ThedescriptionforACGCode.

ADG Distribution
The ADG Distribution is available through Analyze > Frequency Distributions. ACG categories are
based on building blocks called Aggregated Diagnosis Groups (ADGs). Each ADG is a grouping of
diagnosis codes that are similar in terms of severity and likelihood of persistence of the health
condition over time. All diagnosis codes assigned by clinicians over an extended period, such as a
year, are assigned to one of 32 ADGs. ADGs can be considered a type of morbidity marker. A person
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

MEDC by RUB Distribution
The MEDC by RUB Distribution analysis is available through Analyze > Frequency Distributions. This
analysis produces a frequency distribution by MEDC and by Resource Utilization Band (RUB). A patient
can be assigned to multiple MEDC codes, but only one RUB. This report is useful for case managers
because it helps to illustrate that not all individuals with a certain type of condition may be in need of
intervention or case management; rather, it is individuals in the far right of the table, those
individuals exhibiting a specific condition AND multiple co-occurring conditions who are most likely to
need high levels of health care services. This analysis has the option to report the estimated
concurrent resource use in terms of local ACG Concurrent Risk, Reference ACG Concurrent Risk, or
Reference Concurrent Risk. Using local ACG Concurrent Risk, each row is compared to the average of
the population while using reference ACG Concurrent Risk or Reference Concurrent Risk, each row is
compared to the reference data base described by the Risk Assessment Variables in the Summary
Statistics.
Tip: Selection of local versus reference concurrent risk is determined by the Concurrent Risk Type
value on the Options tab of the Report Options window.
The percent distribution is calculated across each row stratification. It is not likely, but possible, for a
row to have a total of less than 100% because RUB 0 is not included in the output. The report layout
is as follows:
