Calculating Age/Sex Adjusted Standardized Morbidity Ratios
Step 1: Form the sub-groups; obtain denominators for prevalence rates
Identify the subgroups based on an appropriate identifier such as a medical group, product-line,
employer group, or primary care practitioner identification number. Obtain a count of the number of
in-scope persons (e.g., selecting only those enrolled for six+ months) within each subgroup. These
counts will serve as the denominators for the subgroup prevalence rates.
Step 2: Calculate observed prevalence rates for the sub-groups
Obtain a count of the number of persons with a given MEDC (or other study category) within the
subgroup of interest. Divide this numerator by the denominator obtained in Step 1, and multiply the
quotient by 1,000. Repeat this procedure for each MEDC (or other study category) and subgroup in
the analysis. These calculations are the observed prevalence rates per 1,000 population.
Step 3: Obtain age-sex specific MEDC (or other study category) prevalence for the total
study population
The goal of this step is to calculate the average prevalence of each MEDC (or other study category)
for each age-sex cohort within the entire population (e.g., all subgroups combined). These rates will
be used in subsequent steps. We recommend dividing the population into the following age-sex
groups:
Males: 0-4, 5-11, 12-17, 18-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65+
Females: 0-4, 5-11, 12-17, 18-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65+
Calculate MEDC-specific prevalence rates (or other study category) for each age-sex group. The
numerator for these calculations will be the number of persons in the age/sex group who have the
MEDC (or other study category); the denominator is total number of persons in the age/sex group.
These rates will be used in Step 4. (These age-breaks assume a working age population. Therefore, if
a full age-range population or elderly population is being assessed, we suggest expanding the 65+ age
category as follows: 65-74, 75-84, 85 +).
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–519–

=== PÁGINA 520 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix C: Report Detail
Step 4: Calculate expected prevalence rates
By comparing prevalence rates that have been age/sex standardized, an analyst can rule out the
possibility that any differences in disease rates between two populations are due solely to differences
in age/ sex distribution. In this step, we outline how to calculate an expected prevalence rate that is
adjusted for the unique age-sex distribution of each sub-group.
Each member of the subgroup of interest should be categorized into one of the age-sex cells listed in
Step 3 above. The MEDC-specific expected prevalence rate (or other study category) for each
demographic cell is calculated as follows:
1. Obtain a count of persons within the subgroup falling into each age-sex cell.
2. For the MEDC (or other study category) of interest, multiply these observed counts by the age-sex
specific prevalence rates obtained from the total study population in Step 3 to get expected
counts.
3. Sum the cell-specific expected counts across all age/sex cells.
4. Divide this sum by the total number of persons in the sub-population being studied.
5. Multiply this quotient by 1,000 to get an expected prevalence rate per 1,000 population for that
particular EDC.
6. Repeat this process for each MEDC (or other study category) of interest.
This expected rate tells you how common the MEDC (or other study category) would be if the
subgroup had the exact age-sex disease rates as the total population. In epidemiologic terms, this
expected rate is obtained by indirect demographic adjustment. (For further information on this
adjustment process, readers are referred to the epidemiology texts listed in the footnotes.)43
Step 5: Obtain a Standardized Morbidity Ratio (SMR) for each MEDC (or other study
category)
To assess whether the observed (i.e., actual) MEDC prevalence rates (or other study category) are
different from the age-sex expected disease rates, a type of observed to expected ratio known as a
standardized morbidity ratio or SMR is calculated. To obtain the SMR for each MEDC (or other study
category), divide the observed prevalence rate for the entire subgroup (reference Step 2) by the
expected prevalence rate (reference Step 4). An SMR above 1.0 indicates that the subgroup has a
higher rate of disease than the total population, even after controlling for age and sex. An SMR below
1.0 suggests a lower than expected rate. For example, an SMR of 1.2 indicates that the MEDC (or
other study category) was 20% more common than expected; an SMR of 0.8 indicates that the MEDC
(or other study category) was 20% less common, and so on.
Step 6: Calculate Confidence Intervals (CIs) for the SMRs
Given that subgroup size will affect the statistical stability of the SMRs, this step suggests how a
confidence interval can be calculated. A 95% confidence interval (CI) provides a statistical measure of
how reliable the SMR is. If the CI includes 1.0 in the range, then we are 95% certain that the
observed subgroup prevalence is not different from the total population prevalence. Therefore, the
greatest attention should be paid to those MEDCs (or other study categories) where the SMR
confidence interval does not cross 1.0.
43 Kahn, H.A.,Sempos,C.T.(1989). "StatisticalMethodsin Epidemiology,"NewYork:OxfordUniversityPress;
MacMahon, B., TrichopoulosD.(1996). "Epidemiology:PrinciplesandMethods,"2nded.Boston:Little &Brown;Szklo,
M.,Nieto, F.J.(2000). "Epidemiology:Beyondthe Basics,"Gaithersburg,Maryland:Aspen.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Actuarial Cost Projections
The Actuarial Cost Projections analysis is available through Analyze > Predictive Analyses. This analysis
represents a summary of information relevant for actuarial purposes and for differentiating groups as
high, medium, and low risk. This analysis provides a number of aggregate measures for both current
and future costs expressed as a relative index (scores equal to 1.0 indicate average morbidity or risk,
greater than 1.0 indicate greater than average morbidity burden or risk and less than 1.0 less than
average).
There are additional rate-based measures provided to describe the factors contributing to group risk.
Groups with higher disease burdens will also generally tend to have higher prevalence rates of high
risk members who are more likely to have chronic conditions, higher rates of hospital dominant and
frailty conditions, and higher rates of psychosocial conditions. Comparisons can be made between the
group and the population mean by comparing the groups tab to the "overall" tab in the analysis
window.
The report layout is as follows: (The columns that are marked with a (D) only appear when diagnosis
data is present in the model.)

Pharmacy Adherence by Drug Class
The Pharmacy Adherence by Drug Class analysis is available through Analyze > Pharmacy Adherence.
This analysis describes the medication possession within the population for 17 chronic conditions and
the corresponding drug classes associated with chronic medication usage. Within each condition, the
Pharmacy Adherence by Drug Class Analysis identifies the population of members prescribed within
each drug class that have experienced a gap in medication possession in excess of a grace period. The
drug class level possession ratios are provided as metrics to measure characteristics of medication
adherence within the target population. By definition, this report shows only "treated" members.
Members may be represented in more than one drug class for a single condition.

Comprehensive Patient Clinical Profile Report
The Comprehensive Patient Clinical Profile Report is available through Analyze > Clinical Screening.
This formatted report presents a profile of an individual patient or group of patients including current
and predicted costs, relative predicted resource utilization, risk of hospitalization, coordination,
pharmacy adherence, and clinical indicators. This report assists clients with understanding member
level risk and resource needs. It is intended to assist with the clinical screening process. This report
employs a 1,000 patient maximum.

Transfer Payment Formula
When this analysis is exported to Excel, additional columns are added to capture assumptions about
the market the plan operates in. When the assumptions are entered, the spreadsheet will
automatically calculate the HHS payment transfer formula as presented in the HHS Notice of Benefit
and Payment Parameters for 2014, Final Rule.7 The formula applied is:
Where,
• = State average premium.
• PLRSi = Plan i’s plan liability risk score.
• AVi = Plan i’s metal level actuarial value (AV). AV is specified in the final rule as a function of
plan metal level.
• ARFi = Allowable rating factor (ARF). ARF is referenced in the final rule as an age rating curve
for ages between 0 and 65. The federal age rating curve is available from CCIIO.8
• IDFi = Plan i’s induced demand factor (IDF). IDF is specified in the final rule as a function of
plan metal level.
• GCFi = Plan i’s geographic cost factor (GCF). GCF is specific to the rating area; however, HHS
has clarified that all payment transfer will occur within rating areas, limiting the impact of the
cost differences across rating areas in the payment transfer formula.
• si = Plan i’s share of state enrollment.
The denominator is summed across all plans in the rating area in the risk pool in the market in the
state.
Local ARF File
The HHS model includes an allowable rating factor for every age in the model. The HHS model can
also utilize a local ARF file using Tools > Options.

markers. For reference, the independent variables used in the ACG System standard models are

Appendix E: Batch Mode Processing
Appendix E:
Batch Mode Processing
Batch Mode Processing
Windows/DOS
During the ACG System Windows installation process, a separate executable file (jhuacg.exe) is
loaded for command line use. The jhuacg.exe file is initiated at the command prompt in
Windows/DOS and utilizes the same input files as the Windows application. The command line
version produces an ACG Data File with the extension .acgd. The.acgd file is readable in the
Windows version. Click File > Open. Type the filename or use the Windows Explorer feature to
double-click the .acgd file of interest. You can also access the processed data using command line
functions explained in the "ACG Command Line Usage" section.
Linux
The Linux version of the ACG application supports command line use in both the installer and the
runtime version. The installer comes in the form of an executable for the Linux platform. To install the
software:
• Log in as root, move to the directory that the installation is located in, and run in
("./JHUACGSetup4Linux-13.0.bin").
• The software will install into "/opt/jhuacg{version}". The current version should install into
"/opt/jhuacg13.0".
To confirm the installation, run the help command: "/opt/jhuacg13.0/jhuacg -h".
Note: The software requires a Java® 11 Runtime.
ACG Command Line Usage
Command line usage of the ACG application works the same at the Windows command prompt and
at the Linux command prompt (shell). All examples given are provided in Windows format.
Syntax Help Example
"C:\ProgramFiles\JohnsHopkinsACG13.0\jhuacg.exe"-help

Guidelines
• All file names should be specified with an absolute pathname.
• All input files should be delimited by either commas, tabs, or a user-defined delimiter, using
optional quotes, with the platform specific end-of-line character(s) (CR/LF on Windows, LF on
Linux).
• By default export files will be exported as tab-delimited, quote enclosed, using the platform
specific end-of-line character(s). Use the delim option to select comma separated files or a user-
defined delimiter.
• To use a patient file or medical services file format that is different from the standard file format,
the user can either create a format file (*.acgf) in the Windows application and apply it within the
command line, or the user can create a custom format file for use with the command line.
The user needs to create a text file in the following format:
• property = value
• col name : data type : col desc
Column formatting rules are as follows:
• Column names should not contain spaces.
• Column descriptions may contain spaces.
• Data types are described in the documentation for file formats in the Windows application. The
most common values are "string," "integer," and "double."
Custom Format File Example

Interfacing to a Database using JDBC
The ACG System can interface directly with a database through a configured JDBC driver. This
configuration is normally performed by a DBA and is specific to the customer environment. Prior to
interfacing with the ACG System, the following steps need to be taken by the customer:
1. Download the appropriate JDBC driver for the customer database environment; this should be
a file with a .jar extension. The JDBC driver is typically offered by the distributor of the
database engine (e.g., Microsoft for SQL Server). There is no universal JDBC standard so there
is no guarantee of compatibility for every database and operating system. The ACG System
has been tested using SQL Server and Oracle.
2. The JDBC jar will need to be directly referenced on the class path. To add a JDBC jar file to
the class path:
• Open the JHUACG.LAX file in Notepad++ or another text editor.
• Locate the setting for "lax.classpath".
• Add the location of the JDBC jar file to the classpath, taking care to separate items on the
classpath with a semicolon (;), and using forward slashes (/) instead of backslashes, even in
a Windows operating environment.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–585–

=== PÁGINA 586 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix E: Batch Mode Processing
3. Determine the JDBC connection string. It is the customer responsibility to perform database
administration consistent with user requirements. The user denoted in the connection string
must have read/write access to the relevant ACG System tables.
4. Create source data tables or views within the database that match the ACG System input file
formats. Custom format files can be used, but the database column names must match the
ACG System expected column names exactly. Additional pass through columns must match
the format file column names exactly.
5. Create output data tables within the database that match the ACG System output file formats.
There are a few exceptions. For compatibility with the widest variety of database
management systems, longer field names are abbreviated for the JDBC interface only as
follows:
• inpatient_hospitalization_count > inpatient_hosp_days
• inpatient_hospitalization_days > inpatient_hosp_days
• all_cause_inpatient_hospitalization_count > all_cause_inpatient_hosp_count
• unplanned_inpatient_hospitalization_count > unplanned_inpatient_hosp_count
• readmission_30_day_count > radm_30d_count
• unplanned_readmission_30_day_count >unplanned_radm_30d_count
Note: pre-written table creation scripts are available for Oracle and SQL Server that can be
adapted to the customer environment. Request from your account representative.
6. Execute a command line script to create the ACGD file. With the exception of JDBC references
instead of file references, the options are the same as interfacing to text files. See example
syntax in Create a New ACG Data File from Database Tables on page 586.
7. Execute a command line script to export data to ACG System output database tables. With
the exception of JDBC references instead of file references, the options are the same as
interfacing to text files. See example syntax in Export Data from an ACG Data File to a
Database Table on page 587.

Additional Considerations
This interface is provided to support database integration and will improve the overall security of the
patient data by limiting the use of text files. This interface is not anticipated to improve performance
over text file integration due to the overhead imposed by the JDBC driver.
It is recommended that you keep intermediate data tables available to this process and load the ACG
output data into your own application tables for final use. Do not apply indexing or impose privilege
restrictions to the ACG output tables directly.
Using JDBC, an ACGD file is created as usual to support standard ACG System reporting. During the
creation of the ACGD file, the ACG System will still use local environment variables to determine
temporary space.
There are standard scripts that can be acquired from your primary support consultant to provide an
example based on standard ACG file formats. A database resource will be needed to modify and
execute these scripts in the customer environment.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Appendix F: Java API
Appendix F:
Java API
Java API
API Overview
The ACG® System includes a Java API which allows clients to process data one member at a time. This
may be useful when building applications that provide data to the system interactively (e.g., within a
workflow system). The client can utilize this API with a development environment that can interface
with Java. Because the API processes a single member at a time, some aggregate processes will not
be performed by the API and will be the responsibility of the developer.
In order to use prior cost as an input into the predictive model, the developer will be required to
calculate the total and pharmacy cost bands for input into the application. Furthermore, the Windows
application provides many ease of use features that are not present in the API. The most notable are
that local weights, rescaled indices, percentiles and probabilities are not implemented in the API.
ACG Java API Usage Details
The full usage detail for the API is extensive and is provided in HTML format. The HTML will help the
developer navigate through the ACG API Package classes, methods, and variables. This appendix
highlights common categories addressed in the API documentation but is not intended to be
exhaustive.
Demonstration
The API is packaged with a demonstration script to highlight usage for key functionality. The
demonstration generates all of the output from the API for a single member. The demonstration is
packaged with the API distribution. Common usage is highlighted in the sections that follow.
Create Input Data
The PatientData class is used to provide the input array to the API. This class further looks to the
MedicalService and PharmacyService class to complete the input data collection. PatientData may
include following parameters (listed in the Input Data Parameters table). Please review the
demonstration for specific usage.

Installing a Mapping File
The ACG System uses a mapping database to map ICD and Rx codes to ACG System categories. The
mapping provided in the release will be updated quarterly. Newer versions of the mapping database
will be distributed in a *.acgm data file. This file can be loaded by the ACGCodes class directly using
the syntax:
private ACGCodes createACGCodes() {
ACGCodes acgCodes = null;
try {
return new ACGCodes(new File("c:\acgmappingfile.acgm"));
} catch (ACGCodeFileException e) {
throw new RuntimeException("Failed to load ACGCodes from classpath",e);
}
}
See the demonstration script for example usage.
Tip: Contact your software vendor for specific documentation of the ACGCodes class.

Outside the Single Patient Context
There are several methods that apply outside the single patient context. In these instances, some
additional work needs to be performed outside of the call to the API.
Rank Probability
The Rank Probability High Total Cost and Rank Probability High Pharmacy Cost outputs are dependent
on ranking Predicted Risk scores for a population of members into 1000 quantile groups. The API is
designed to operate on a single patient at a time, so this ranking must be derived external to the API.
Once the rank is calculated for a patient, the Rank Probability High Total Cost and Rank Probability
High Pharmacy cost can be calculated using the ProbabilityHighCostModelCalculator.
Care Density
The Care Density Ratio and associated categories are determined based on the number shared
patients among providers derived from a collection of patient-provider pairs. The patient-provider
pairs are not specific to one patient, but represent a population measure and therefore must be
derived outside of the call to the API. There are three options implementing the determination of
patient-provider pairs:
• Memory-based implementation using MemoryProviderPairCounter
• Temporary storage implementation using DerbyProviderPairCounter (requires derby.jar not
distributed with API)
• External storage implementation using JDBCProviderPairCounter (requires JDBC driver and
connection string not distributed with API)
After the patient-provider pairs are accessible to the API, the Care Density metrics may be calculated
using getCareDensityRatio(), getCareDensityQuantile(), getCareDensityBottomQuartileCutoff(),
getCareDensityTopQuartileCutoff(), getCareDensityCostSavingRatio(), getCareDensityCostSavingRange().
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Appendix G: CMS-HCC Model
Appendix G:
CMS-HCC Model
CMS-HCC Model Overview
This document discusses the functionality related to the implementation of the CMS-HCC model
within The Johns Hopkins ACG System. With the required license, The Johns Hopkins ACG System
provides access to the CMS-HCC model used in the Medicare Advantage Risk Adjustment
methodology.
The model is updated annually and published in the Announcement of Calendar Year Medicare
Advantage Capitation Rates and Medicare Advantage and Part D Payment Policies and Final Call
Letter. Additional model details are provided in the form of SAS code published on the CMS website
at https://www.cms.gov/Medicare/Health-Plans/MedicareAdvtgSpecRateStats/Risk-Adjustors.html.
The ACG System used this documentation from the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services to
replicate the risk scoring algorithm to be used by the Medicare Advantage risk adjustment program.
In order to support transparency of the method, the ACG System provides several output files
described in the Appendices on page 479 detailing the exclusions, HCCs, risk scores and model
coefficients that support the CMS-HCC model.
Benefits of Combining the ACG and CMS-HCC
Methodologies
The ACG System will assign risk scores according to the CMS-HCC methodology, including the
component model variables and Hierarchical Condition Categories (HCCs), leveraging the same source
input files used by the rest of the ACG System. By releasing the CMS-HCC model within the ACG
System, the CMS-HCC model has been thoroughly documented to aid in the transparency of the
method.
The ACG System is identifying potentially problematic records that may be excluded by CMS from risk
adjustment. Medicare Coding Edits (MCE) are applied to specific claim lines where age and/or sex are
inappropriate to a diagnosis code. The ACG System will identify claims that would trigger CMS to
exclude records so that they may be corrected prior to submission to CMS.
In the Medicare Advantage risk adjustment methodology, the individual risk scores assigned by the
CMS-HCC model for one year are applied as an adjustment to the individual patient's premium rate
paid to a contracted managed care organization in the subsequent year.
The section Examples Combining the ACG System and CMS-HCC Models on page 610 demonstrates
several case-finding techniques that leverage output from both traditional ACG System markers and
the CMS-HCC model output. Monitoring cases with potentially poor data capture and addressing
issues of diagnosis accuracy is critical to optimization of revenue under any risk adjustment program.
The CMS-HCC is a prospectively calibrated model that utilizes a highly selective subset of diagnoses.
When identifying patients for care management, a more comprehensive model, such as the ACG
System Predictive Model (ACG-PM), is more appropriate for capturing patients with risk factors
indicative of high future costs. In particular, rapid assessment of risk is critical to identifying patients
with multiple chronic conditions for engagement in intervention programs. The ACG System predictive
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

=== PÁGINA 602 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix G: CMS-HCC Model
models include models calibrated to use pharmacy data only. Pharmacy data is typically adjudicated
at the point of sale and is, therefore, made available more quickly than medical claims. Dispensing of
medication also occurs with greater frequency than medical visits, giving greater insight for members
with limited claims experience.
Differences Between the CMS-HCC and ACG System
Methodologies
The CMS-HCC methodology is a prospectively calibrated model based on age, sex and diagnosis code.
In the ACG System, the most comparable output would be the unscaled_total_cost_predicted_risk.
However, there are several important differences between the CMS-HCC methodology and the ACG
System methodology.
• While the ACG System methodology makes risk score assignments regardless of length of
enrollment, enrollment periods are important to correctly apply the CMS-HCC methodology.
Since several eligibility categories are key determinants of the risk score, changes in CMS
factor type, medicaid status and long term institutional status need to be captured. The ACG
System has implemented these requirements by potentially assigning multiple CMS-HCC risk
scores for different enrollment segments.
• The ACG System methodology considers all diagnoses with the exception of external cause of
injury codes (ICD-10 Chapters V-Y) in the assignment of patient risk. The CMS-HCC model is
highly selective, currently assigning approximately 9,900 diagnosis codes to condition codes
that can influence patient risk.
• The ACG System methodology recommends excluding diagnoses from claims with certain
procedures and place of service codes as discussed in selecting relevant diagnoses for input to
the ACG System on page 45. The CMS-HCC methodology includes diagnoses from a selected
list of provider specialities, procedures and type of bill codes44. In general, the ACG System
methodology and the CMS-HCC methodology have the same intent. Of particular note, the
CMS-HCC methodology limits the specialties considered from professional claims, which is
likely to censor the diagnoses from more claims than the ACG System methodology.
• The ACG System methodology will generate warnings for unusual age, sex and diagnosis code
combinations. With the exception of males with pregnancy diagnoses, the warnings do not
impact the diagnoses used or the output of the ACG System method. The CMS-HCC
methodology applies a number of Medicare Coding Edits to exclude diagnosis codes.
• The ACG System methodology categorizes diagnosis codes into the building blocks of the ACG
System, such as ADGs and EDCs, uniformly across the population. The CMS-HCC methodology
will use demographic variables only for new enrollees, those with less than 12 months of
history in the Medicare program. CMS may merge diagnosis data from the Medicare Fee For
Service program with diagnosis data from the Medicare Advantage program. The health plan
may not have this diagnosis data to estimate their own risk scores.
• All patients in a population are included in the ACG System risk adjustment methodology.
Because the CMS-HCC model considers only claims paid under the Medicare program, there
are circumstances that will exclude members from risk adjustment. These records are
identified by the field exclude_from_risk_adjustment =Y. Most often, these records are
associated with problematic enrollment dates and no CMS-HCC risk score will be generated.
44 Thecode listisdownloadablefromhttps://www.cms.gov/Medicare/Health-Plans/MedicareAdvtgSpecRateStats/Risk-
Adjustors.html
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

=== PÁGINA 603 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix G: CMS-HCC Model
• The ACG System provides a measure of morbidity burden that is appropriate to use across the
population for applications such as provider profiling. The CMS-HCC model is calibrated to
correct under-payment for complex conditions and relies heavily on demographic categories
for lower quintiles. The CMS-HCC model would not be an appropriate risk adjustor for provider
profiling or other population-centric analyses.
Model Construction
The CMS-HCC model is an additive model that has been calibrated prospectively to predict total costs.
The methodology consists of multiple models, one for each eligibility category defined by contract
holder and risk adjustment factor type. A beneficiary may change their eligibility category mid-year
with a qualifying life event; therefore, an individual may have more than one risk score during an
observation period. Additionally, CMS applies the models prospectively so it is possible to apply the
model variables from one period to the eligibility characteristics in a subsequent period. For example
in 2021, a patient is elderly and living in the community with a diagnosis of congestive heart failure
and major depression. If in 2022 this patient moves into a nursing home, the ACG System will use the
diagnosis of heart failure and major depression with a 2021 observation period; however, the ACG
System may attribute demographic variables from the current enrollment information. See Example
Risk Score Calculation Based on CMS-HCCs on page 609.
In order to capture changes in benefit plan option, an enrollment file is required. The detailed
requirements for the enrollment information are discussed in Data Requirements on page 53.

Appendix G: CMS-HCC Model
Determine Diagnoses Used in Risk Adjustment
Historically, CMS provided recommendations for diagnosis inclusion via the Risk Adjustment
Processing System (RAPS) data collection process. The guidance, provided in the Medicare Managed
Care Manual, Chapter 7, included face-to-face visits with hospital inpatient facilities, hospital
outpatient facilities, and physicians. CMS provides some guidance about eligible facilities and eligible
provider specialties45. Plans create their own logic to determine these diagnoses prior to submission
via the RAPS process.
CMS announced in 2010 that the future of risk adjustment data submission will be a full encounter
record. The Encounter Data Processing System (EDPS) will receive all encounter data from managed
care organizations and EDPS will determine the diagnosis codes eligible for risk adjustment.
For payment year 2023, CMS will utilize EDPS and Medicare Fee for Service (FFS) as sources for the
Community, Institutional and ESRD models. Contracts operating under the Program of All Inclusive
Care of the Elderly (PACE) program will utilize diagnoses from EDPS, RAPS, and FFS. The provision of
medical services data to the ACG System is intended to support replication of this selection,
recognizing that organizations may not have access to FFS data.
The ACG System will apply diagnosis filtering as follows:
• Professional records are selected based on the presence of at least one acceptable CPT/HCPCS
46.
• Inpatient records are selected based on acceptable bill type code (011X and 041X).
• Outpatient records are selected based on acceptable bill type codes (012X, 013X, 043X, 071X,
073X, 076X, 077X, 085X) AND the presence of at least one acceptable CPT/HCPCS code.
Diagnoses excluded due to filtering logic are identified on the Medical Services export type on page
450 along with an exclusion reason.
The CMS-HCC model is explicit about using diagnoses from the claim header and does not address
diagnoses from the claim line. The ACG data model does not differentiate the source of diagnosis.
Therefore, to be true to the CMS-HCC model instructions, only diagnoses from the claim header
should be provided. The CMS-HCC model indicates the Medicare Coding Edits (MCE) that should be
applied. The MCE edits ensure that a diagnosis code is appropriate to the age and sex of the patient.
MCE edits are applied based on the patient’s age at diagnosis. Diagnoses that will not be used due to
a MCE edit are identified with a warning.
A patient may have multiple enrollment segments during the observation period. The ACG System will
determine a diagnosis begin date and diagnosis end date based on CMS enrollment records with
contiguous enrollment start and end dates. Further, the ACG System will define the correct age band
and model based on the last date of enrollment in a plan during the observation period.
Create Condition Categories (CCs)
The diagnoses selected for risk adjustment are grouped into condition categories. In the current CMS-
HCC model, just over 9900 diagnoses are included in the model and assigned to a condition category.

=== PÁGINA 606 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix G: CMS-HCC Model
In a few instances, a single diagnosis code may trigger more than one condition category. For
example, ICD-10-CM code I13.2 Hypertensive heart and chronic kidney disease, with heart failure and
chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease will trigger both CC 85 (Congestive Heart
Failure) and CC 136 (Chronic Kidney Disease, Stage 5).
Additional age and/or sex edits may also modify the assignment of a condition category. For example,
ICD-10-CM code J41.0 Simple Chronic Bronchitis is assigned to CC 111 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary
Disease, Including Bronchiectasis) for adults aged 18 and over, but the same diagnosis is assigned to
CC 112 (Fibrosis of Lung and Other Chronic Lung Disorders) for children aged 17 and under. Likewise,
ICD-10-CM code F34.81, Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, is assigned to CC 58 (Major
Depressive, Bipolar, and Paranoid Disorders) for patient aged 6 through 17, but does not get assigned
a CC for children under the age of 6 or adults 18 or older.
Condition categories are made available as a space-delimited string in the HHS-CMS Enrollment
Results output file.
Apply Hierarchies to Create Hierarchical Condition
Categories (HCCs)
In the event that a patient has multiple condition categories the CMS-HCC model imposes clinical
hierarchies such that a condition will not be counted if there are more severe conditions present in
the same hierarchy.
For example, a patient with diagnoses in both CC 84 (Cardio-Respiratory Failure and Shock) and CC 83
(Respiratory Arrest) will be assigned only to HCC 83, the more severe condition category in the
hierarchy. In the ACG System, the term HCC will be used to denote the terminal condition groupings
after hierarchies have been applied.
HCCs are made available as a space-delimited string in the HHS-CMS Enrollment Results output file
and in a separate CMS-HCC assignments output file with a record for each patient and HCC.
Determine the Correct Model
Separate models with different HCCs and interactions will be applied to each of the model types:
ESRD, Program of All-Inclusive Coverage for the Elderly (PACE), Institutional, Community and New
Enrollees. New enrollee risk scores are determined based on a number of demographic variables. The
relationship between CMS risk adjustment factor type and model is described in the table below.

Additional Adjustments
The ACG System calculates a raw risk score according to the specifications provided on the CMS
website. In practice, CMS further adjusts the risk scores based on a number of additional factors
before calculating a risk-adjusted premium.
Normalization factor - Normalization factors are published each year in the Medicare Advantage call
letter. The normalization factor is intended to adjust for changes to the underlying population since
the last model calibration to ensure that the CMS population risk score remains 1.0.
Coding intensity adjustment - The Medicare Advantage coding intensity adjustment is published each
year in the Medicare Advantage call letter. The adjustment is intended to correct for differences in
coding patterns between the Medicare Advantage population subject to risk adjustment and the fee
for service population used to calibrate the CMS-HCC models.
Both of these adjustments are intended to reduce risk scores. The normalized risk score, accounting
for both normalization factor and coding intensity factor, is calculated by the ACG System according to
CMS' guidance using the following formula.
When CMS introduces a new model calibration, the risk scores are typically blended proportionately
with prior model risk scores to mitigate the impact of model changes. The ACG System provides detail
on the primary and secondary models, including raw risk scores, normalization factors, coding
intensity factors and model proportions applied to determine the final risk score. In payment years
where no blending applies, all information about secondary models will be blank. These details are
presented for each enrollment segment in HHS-CMS Enrollment Results on page 470.
Frailty Adjuster - The Balanced Budget Act of 1997 (BBA) mandated that Medicare capitated payments
to Program of All-Inclusive Coverage for the Elderly (PACE) organizations be based on MA payment
rates, adjusted to account for the comparative frailty of PACE enrollees. The frailty risk score is
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Examples Combining the ACG System and CMS-HCC Models
In addition to the standard analyses produced by the ACG software, the components of the CMS-HCC
model are available for identifying patients of interest. Here are some ideas for filters that may be
meaningful for analysis.
Patients with High Morbidity and Low CMS-HCC Risk Scores
The concurrently calibrated components of the ACG System are defined with different filtering criteria
and a larger complement of diagnosis codes are used in defining morbidity. The group of patients
with low risk scores from the CMS-HCC model but very high morbidity as determined by the resource
utilization band (RUB) have claims that either have significant acute conditions or fail CMS’ claim type
assumptions. These patients should be reviewed to determine if there is any systemic error in a
particular claim type that might be corrected at the source.

Appendix H: CMS RxHCC Model
Appendix H:
CMS RxHCC Model
RxHCC Model Overview
This document discusses the functionality related to the implementation of the RxHCC model within
The Johns Hopkins ACG System. With the required license, The Johns Hopkins ACG System provides
access to the RxHCC model used in the Medicare Part D Risk Adjustment methodology.
The model is updated annually and published in the Announcement of Calendar Year Medicare
Advantage Capitation Rates and Medicare Advantage and Part D Payment Policies and Final Call
Letter. Additional model details are provided in the form of SAS code published on the CMS website
at https://www.cms.gov/Medicare/Health-Plans/MedicareAdvtgSpecRateStats/Risk-Adjustors.html.
The ACG System used this documentation from the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services to
replicate the risk scoring algorithm to be used by the Medicare Advantage risk adjustment program.
In order to support transparency of the method, the ACG System provides several output files
described in the Appendices on page 479 detailing the exclusions, RxHCCs, risk scores and model
coefficients that support the RxHCC model.
Benefits of Combining the ACG and RxHCC Methodologies
The ACG System will assign risk scores according to the RxHCC methodology, including the component
model variables and Drug Hierarchical Condition Categories (RxHCCs), leveraging the same source
input files used by the rest of the ACG System. By releasing the RxHCC model within the ACG System,
the RxHCC model has been thoroughly documented to aid in the transparency of the method.
The ACG System is identifying potentially problematic records that may be excluded by CMS from risk
adjustment. Medicare Coding Edits (MCE) are applied to specific claim lines where age and/or sex are
inappropriate to a diagnosis code. The ACG System will identify claims that would trigger CMS to
exclude records so that they may be corrected prior to submission to CMS.
In the Medicare Advantage risk adjustment methodology, the individual risk scores assigned by the
RxHCC model for one year are applied as an adjustment to the individual patient's premium rate paid
to a contracted managed care organization in the subsequent year.
The section Examples Combining the ACG System and CMS-HCC Models on page demonstrates
several case-finding techniques that leverage output from both traditional ACG System markers and
the RxHCC model output. Monitoring cases with potentially poor data capture and addressing issues
of diagnosis accuracy is critical to optimization of revenue under any risk adjustment program.
The RxHCC is a prospectively calibrated model that utilizes a highly selective subset of diagnoses for
forecast medication costs. The ACG System predictive models include models calibrated to use only
pharmacy data, age and sex as input to predicting medication costs. Access to multiple models
provides insight as to the quality of data capture based on diagnosis only.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–623–

Appendix H: CMS RxHCC Model
Differences Between the RxHCC and ACG System
Methodologies
The RxHCC methodology is a prospectively calibrated model based on age, sex and diagnosis code to
predict drug spend under CMS Part D benefits. In the ACG System, the most comparable output
would be the unscaled_pharmacy_cost_predicted_risk. However, there are several important
differences between the RxHCC methodology and the ACG System methodology.
• While the ACG System methodology makes risk score assignments regardless of length of
enrollment, enrollment periods are important to correctly apply the RxHCC methodology. Since
several eligibility categories are key determinants of the risk score, changes in CMS Part D
factor type, medicaid status and long term institutional status need to be captured. The ACG
System has implemented these requirements by potentially assigning multiple RxHCC risk
scores for different enrollment segments.
• The ACG System methodology considers all diagnoses with the exception of external cause of
injury codes (ICD-10 Chapters V-Y) in the assignment of patient risk. The RxHCC model is highly
selective, currently assigning approximately 4,500 diagnosis codes to condition codes that can
influence patient risk.
• The ACG System methodology recommends excluding diagnoses from claims with certain
procedures and place of service codes as discussed in selecting relevant diagnoses for input to
the ACG System on page 45. The RxHCC methodology includes diagnoses from a selected list
of procedures and type of bill codes48. In general, the ACG System methodology and the RxHCC
methodology have the same intent. Of particular note, the RxHCC methodology is likely to
censor the diagnoses from more claims than the ACG System methodology.
• The ACG System methodology will generate warnings for unusual age, sex and diagnosis code
combinations. With the exception of males with pregnancy diagnoses, the warnings do not
impact the diagnoses used or the output of the ACG System method. The RxHCC methodology
applies a number of Medicare Coding Edits to exclude diagnosis codes.
• The ACG System methodology categorizes diagnosis codes into the building blocks of the ACG
System, such as ADGs and EDCs, uniformly across the population. The RxHCC methodology will
use demographic variables only for new enrollees, those with less than 12 months of history in
the Medicare program. CMS may merge diagnosis data from the Medicare Fee For Service
program with diagnosis data from the Medicare Advantage program. The health plan may not
have this diagnosis data to estimate their own risk scores.
• All patients in a population are included in the ACG System risk adjustment methodology.
Because the RxHCC model considers only claims paid under the Medicare program, there are
circumstances that will exclude members from risk adjustment. These records are identified by
the field exclude_from_risk_adjustment =Y. Most often, these records are associated with
problematic enrollment dates and no RxHCC risk score will be generated.
• The ACG System provides a measure of morbidity burden that is appropriate to use across the
population for applications such as provider profiling. The RxHCC model is calibrated to correct
under-payment for complex conditions and relies heavily on demographic categories for lower
quintiles. The RxHCC model would not be an appropriate risk adjustor for provider profiling or
other population-centric analyses.
48 Thecode listisdownloadablefromhttps://www.cms.gov/Medicare/Health-Plans/MedicareAdvtgSpecRateStats/Risk-
Adjustors.html
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–624–

Appendix H: CMS RxHCC Model
Model Construction
The RxHCC model is an additive model that has been calibrated prospectively to predict drug costs.
The methodology consists of multiple models, one for each eligibility category defined by contract
holder and risk adjustment factor type. A beneficiary may change their eligibility category mid-year
with a qualifying life event; therefore, an individual may have more than one risk score during an
observation period. Additionally, CMS applies the models prospectively so it is possible to apply the
model variables from one period to the eligibility characteristics in a subsequent period. For example
in 2021, a patient is elderly and living in the community with a diagnosis of congestive heart failure
and major depression. If in 2022 this patient moves into a nursing home, the ACG System will use the
diagnosis of heart failure and major depression with a 2021 observation period; however, the ACG
System may attribute demographic variables from the current enrollment information. See Example
Risk Score Calculation Based on RxHCCs on page 632.
In order to capture changes in benefit plan option, an enrollment file is required. The detailed
requirements for the enrollment information are discussed in Data Requirements on page 53.
The RxHCC Risk Score Assignment Process shows the initial steps in assigning the RxHCC risk score.
Each step is discussed under its own heading below.
Figure138.RxHCCRiskScoreAssignmentProcess

Appendix H: CMS RxHCC Model
Determine Diagnoses Used in Risk Adjustment
Historically, CMS provided recommendations for diagnosis inclusion via the Risk Adjustment
Processing System (RAPS) data collection process. The guidance, provided in the Medicare Managed
Care Manual, Chapter 7, included face-to-face visits with hospital inpatient facilities, hospital
outpatient facilities, and physicians. CMS provides some guidance about eligible facilities and eligible
provider specialties49. Plans create their own logic to determine these diagnoses prior to submission
via the RAPS process.
CMS announced in 2010 that the future of risk adjustment data submission will be a full encounter
record. The Encounter Data Processing System (EDPS) will receive all encounter data from managed
care organizations and EDPS will determine the diagnosis codes eligible for risk adjustment.
For payment year 2023, CMS will utilize EDPS and Medicare Fee for Service (FFS) as sources for the
Community, Institutional and ESRD models. Contracts operating under the Program of All Inclusive
Care of the Elderly (PACE) program will utilize diagnoses from EDPS, RAPS, and FFS. The provision of
medical services data to the ACG System is intended to support replication of this selection,
recognizing that organizations may not have access to FFS data.
The ACG System will apply diagnosis filtering as follows:
• Professional records are selected based on the presence of at least one acceptable CPT/HCPCS
50.
• Inpatient records are selected based on acceptable bill type code (011X and 041X).
• Outpatient records are selected based on acceptable bill type codes (012X, 013X, 043X, 071X,
073X, 076X, 077X, 085X) AND the presence of at least one acceptable CPT/HCPCS code.
Diagnoses excluded due to filtering logic are identified on the Medical Services export type on page
450 along with an exclusion reason.
The RxHCC model is explicit about using diagnoses from the claim header and does not address
diagnoses from the claim line. The ACG data model does not differentiate the source of diagnosis.
Therefore, to be true to the RxHCC model instructions, only diagnoses from the claim header should
be provided. The RxHCC model indicates the Medicare Coding Edits (MCE) that should be applied. The
MCE edits ensure that a diagnosis code is appropriate to the age and sex of the patient. MCE edits
are applied based on the patient’s age at diagnosis. Diagnoses that will not be used due to a MCE
edit are identified with a warning.
A patient may have multiple enrollment segments during the observation period. The ACG System will
determine a diagnosis begin date and diagnosis end date based on CMS enrollment records with
contiguous enrollment start and end dates. Further, the ACG System will define the correct age band
and model based on the last date of enrollment in a plan during the observation period.
49 CMSpublishesthelist ofacceptablespecialtiesannually:
https://www.csscoperations.com/internet/cssc4.nsf/docsCat/CSSC%20Operations~Medicare%20Advantage%20Encounter
%20Data%20and%20RAPS%20Data~Resources
50 TheacceptableprocedurecodesareupdatedquarterlyandavailableontheCMSwebsite:
https://www.cms.gov/Medicare/Health-Plans/MedicareAdvtgSpecRateStats/Risk-Adjustors.html

Appendix H: CMS RxHCC Model
Create Drug Condition Categories (RxCCs)
The diagnoses selected for risk adjustment are grouped into condition categories. In the current
RxHCC model, just over 4500 diagnoses are included in the model and assigned to a drug condition
category.
In a few instances, a single diagnosis code may trigger more than one drug condition category. For
example, ICD-10-CM code I13.2 Hypertensive heart and chronic kidney disease, with heart failure and
chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease will trigger both RxCC 186 (Congestive Heart
Failure) and RxCC 262 (Chronic Kidney Disease, Stage 5).
Additional age and/or sex edits may also modify the assignment of a condition category. For example,
ICD-10-CM code F34.81, Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, is assigned to RxCC 131 (Bipolar
Disorders) for patient aged 6 through 17, but is assigned to RxCC 133 (Specified Anxiety, Personality,
and Behavior Disorders) for children under the age of 6 or adults 18 or older.
Drug condition categories are made available as a space-delimited string in the HHS-CMS Enrollment
Results output file.
Apply Hierarchies to Create Drug Hierarchical Condition
Categories (RxHCCs)
In the event that a patient has multiple condition categories the RxHCC model imposes clinical
hierarchies such that a condition will not be counted if there are more severe conditions present in
the same hierarchy.
For example, a patient with diagnoses in both RxCC 134 (Depression) and RxCC 132 (Major
Depression) will be assigned only to RxHCC 132, the more severe condition category in the hierarchy.
In the ACG System, the term RxHCC will be used to denote the terminal condition groupings after
hierarchies have been applied.
RxHCCs are made available as a space-delimited string in the HHS-CMS Enrollment Results output file
and in a separate CMS RxHCC assignments output file with a record for each patient and RxHCC.

=== PÁGINA 634 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
Appendix I:
HHS-HCC Model
HHS-HCC Model Overview
This document discusses the functionality related to the implementation of the HHS-HCC model
within The Johns Hopkins ACG System. With the required license, The Johns Hopkins ACG System
provides access to the HHS-HCC model used in the Federal Health Insurance Marketplace Risk
Adjustment methodology.
Beginning in January 2014, qualified health plans (QHPs) and non-grandfathered individual and small
group health plans operating inside and outside of the health insurance marketplace are subject to
risk adjustment. The risk adjustment methodology to be operated by CMS is referred to as the HHS-
HCC model. The requirements of the federal risk adjustment methodology were defined in the Patient
Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010 under the premium stabilization provisions. These
requirements were clarified in the Federal Register with the HHS Notice of Benefit and Payment
Parameters for 2014 that was finalized on March 11, 2013 and amended through Annual Payment
Notice communications.
The ACG System used documentation from the Center for Consumer Information &Insurance
Oversight (CCIIO) to replicate the risk scoring algorithm to be used by the federally operated risk
adjustment program. In order to support transparency of the method, the ACG System provides
several output files described in the Appendices on page 470 detailing the exclusions, HCCs, risk
scores and model coefficients that support the HHS-HCC model.
The HHS-HCC model is in the public domain with SAS code, sample datasets, diagnosis groupings,
model coefficients and implementation instructions52. The ACG System has been adapted to produce
the HHS-HCC risk scores in accordance with these instructions when some additional input data is
provided.
Benefits of Combining the ACG System and HHS-HCC
Methodologies
The ACG System will assign risk scores according to the HHS-HCC methodology, including the
component model variables and Hierarchical Condition Categories (HCCs), leveraging the same source
input files used by the rest of the ACG System. By releasing the HHS-HCC model within the ACG
System, the HHS-HCC model has been thoroughly documented to aid in the transparency of the
method.
The ACG System is identifying potentially problematic records that may be excluded by HHS from risk
adjustment. Medicare Coding Edits (MCE) are applied to specific claim lines where age and/or sex are
inappropriate to a diagnosis code. Additionally, HHS has a requirement that mother and infant claims
be separated into two distinct patient IDs or diagnoses will be excluded from risk adjustment. The
ACG System will identify claims that would trigger HHS to exclude records so that they may be
corrected prior to submission to HHS.
52 http://www.cms.gov/cciio/Resources/Regulations-and-Guidance/index.html#PremiumStabilizationPrograms
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

=== PÁGINA 635 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
In the Health Insurance Marketplace risk adjustment methodology, the individual risk scores assigned
by the HHS-HCC model will be aggregated to calculate an annual payment transfer across plans
operating within a market, rating area and risk pool. The ACG System will calculate the summary risk
information for the plan-specific portion of the payment transfer calculation. With a few assumptions
about the average state performance, you can readily estimate the impact of your current risk score
on the plan payment transfer. More details of this payment transfer calculation are provided with the
HHS Payment Transfer Summary Analysis on page 551.
The section Examples Combining the ACG System and HHS-HCC Models on page 641 demonstrates
several case-finding techniques that leverage output from both traditional ACG System markers and
the HHS-HCC model output. Monitoring cases with potentially poor data capture and addressing
issues of diagnosis accuracy is critical to optimization of revenue under any risk adjustment program.
The HHS-HCC is a concurrently calibrated model that utilizes a highly selective subset of diagnoses.
When identifying patients for care management, a prospective model, such as the ACG System
Predictive Model (ACG-PM), is more appropriate for capturing patients with risk factors indicative of
high future costs. In particular, for those previously uninsured, rapid assessment of risk is critical to
identifying patients with multiple chronic conditions for engagement in intervention programs. The
ACG System predictive models include models calibrated to use pharmacy data only. Pharmacy data is
typically adjudicated at the point of sale and is, therefore, made available more quickly than medical
claims. Dispensing of medication also occurs with greater frequency than medical visits, giving greater
insight for members with limited claims experience.
Differences between the HHS-HCC and ACG System
methodologies
The HHS-HCC methodology is a concurrently calibrated model based on age, sex and diagnosis code.
In the ACG System, the most comparable output would be the unscaled_concurrent_risk. However,
there are several important differences between the HHS-HCC methodology and the ACG System
methodology.
• While the ACG System methodology makes risk score assignments regardless of length of
enrollment, enrollment periods are important to correctly apply the HHS-HCC methodology.
Frequently asked questions (FAQ) released in April 2015 address mid-year changes in benefit
plan. Since metal level is a key determinant of the risk score, changes in metal level need to
be captured. The ACG System has implemented these requirements by potentially assigning
multiple HHS-HCC risk scores for different enrollment segments.
• The ACG System methodology considers all diagnoses with the exception of external cause of
injury codes (ICD-10 Chapters V-Y) in the assignment of patient risk. The HHS-HCC model is
highly selective, currently assigning approximately 10,700 diagnosis codes to condition codes
that can influence patient risk.
• The ACG System methodology recommends excluding diagnoses from claims with certain
procedures and place of service codes as discussed in selecting relevant diagnoses for input to
the ACG System on page 45. The HHS-HCC methodology includes diagnoses from a selected list
of procedures and type of bill codes53. In general, the ACG System methodology and the HHS-
HCC methodology have the same intent. Of particular note, the HHS-HCC methodology
requires CPT/HCPCS codes on outpatient facility claims, which is likely to censor the diagnoses
from more claims than the ACG System methodology.
53 Thecode listisdownloadablefromhttp://www.cms.gov/cciio/Resources/Regulations-and-
Guidance/index.html#Premium StabilizationPrograms
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–635–

=== PÁGINA 636 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
• The ACG System methodology will generate warnings for unusual age, sex and diagnosis code
combinations. With the exception of males with pregnancy diagnoses, the warnings do not
impact the diagnoses used or the output of the ACG System method. The HHS-HCC
methodology applies a number of Medicare coding edits to exclude diagnosis codes.
• The ACG System methodology categorizes diagnosis codes into the building blocks of the ACG
System, such as ADGs and EDCs, uniformly across all ages but the terminal groups, or ACG
categories, may vary based on age. The HHS-HCC methodology will potentially derive different
building blocks, or condition categories, for the same diagnosis code based on age.
• All patients in a population are included in the ACG System risk adjustment methodology.
Because the HHS-HCC model considers only claims paid for by a plan defined with metal level,
there are circumstances that will exclude members from risk adjustment. These records are
identified by the field exclude_from_risk_adjustment =Y. Most often, these records are
associated with problematic enrollment dates and no HHS-HCC risk score will be generated.
• The ACG System provides prospective risk scores to identify future risks. There are no
equivalent predictive risk score determined from the HHS-HCC model.
• The ACG System provides a measure of morbidity burden that is appropriate to use across the
population for applications such as provider profiling. The HHS-HCC model is calibrated to
correct under-payment for complex conditions and relies heavily on demographic categories
for lower quintiles. The HHS-HCC model would not be an appropriate risk adjustor for provider
profiling or other population-centric analyses.
Model Construction
The HHS-HCC model is an additive model that has been calibrated concurrently to explain total costs.
The methodology consists of multiple models, one for each benefit plan option described by metal
level, to account for variations in the beneficiary liability or actuarial value of the plan. A beneficiary
may change their benefit plan option mid-year with a qualifying life event; therefore, an individual
may have more than one risk score during an observation period. In order to capture changes in
benefit plan option, an enrollment file is required. The detailed requirements for the enrollment
information are discussed in Data Requirements on page 53.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.

Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
The HHS-HCC Risk Score Assignment Process shows the initial steps in assigning the HHS-HCC risk
score. Each step is discussed under its own heading below.
Figure139.HHS-HCCRiskScoreAssignmentProcess
Determine Diagnoses used in Risk Adjustment
The HHS-HCC model provides the methodology for selecting diagnoses to be used in risk adjustment.
The selection criteria vary by source of diagnosis as follows:
• Professional records are selected based on the presence of at least one acceptable CPT/HCPCS
• Inpatient records are selected based on acceptable bill type code
• Outpatient records are selected based on acceptable bill type codes AND the presence of at
least one acceptable CPT/HCPCS code
The HHS-HCC model is explicit about using diagnoses from the claim header and does not address
diagnoses from the claim line. The ACG data model does not differentiate the source of diagnosis.
Therefore, to be true to the HHS-HCC model instructions, only diagnoses from the claim header
should be provided.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–637–

=== PÁGINA 638 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
The HHS-HCC model indicates the Medicare Coding Edits (MCE) that should be applied. The MCE edits
ensure that a diagnosis code is appropriate to the age and sex of the patient. MCE edits are applied
based on the patient’s age at diagnosis. Diagnoses that will not be used due to a MCE edit are
identified with a warning.
The HHS-HCC model is explicit about the expectations for mother and newborn claims. The model
expects that the mother and newborn are two individuals in the plan and that all claims, including the
hospital stay for childbirth, are separated to the appropriate individual. Diagnoses appropriate to the
infant will be excluded from the mother’s risk adjustment and vice-versa. Claims that trigger these
exclusions will be identified with a warning. The ACG System will proceed to calculate a risk score for
the individual.
A patient may have multiple enrollment segments during the observation period. The ACG System
will determine a diagnosis begin date and diagnosis end date based on HHS enrollment records with
contiguous enrollment start and end dates. Further, the ACG System will define the correct age band
and model based on the last date of enrollment in a plan during the observation period.
Create Condition Categories (CCs)
The diagnoses selected for risk adjustment are grouped into condition categories. In the current HHS-
HCC model, just over 10,700 diagnoses are included in the model and assigned to a condition
category.
In a few instances, a single diagnosis code may trigger more than one condition category. For
example, ICD-10-CM code I13.2 Hypertensive heart and chronic kidney disease, with heart failure and
chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease will trigger both CC 130 (Congestive Heart
Failure) and CC 187 (Chronic Kidney Disease, Stage 5).
Additional age and/or sex edits may also modify the assignment of a condition category. For example,
ICD-10-CM code J41.0 Simple Chronic Bronchitis is assigned to CC 160 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary
Disease, Including Bronchiectasis) for adults aged 18 and over, but the same diagnosis is assigned to
CC 161 (Asthma) for children aged 17 and under. Likewise, ICD-10-CM code J43.9 Emphysema,
unspecified, is assigned to CC 160 for patient aged 2 and over, but does not get assigned a CC for
children under the age of 2.
Condition categories are made available as a space-delimited string in the HHS-CMS Enrollment
Results output file.
Apply Hierarchies to Create Hierarchical Condition
Categories (HCCs)
In the event that a patient has multiple condition categories the HHS-HCC model imposes clinical
hierarchies such that a condition will not be counted if there are more severe conditions present in
the same hierarchy.
For example, a patient with diagnoses in both CC 127 (Cardio-Respiratory Failure and Shock, Including
Respiratory Distress Syndromes) and CC 126 (Respiratory Arrest) will be assigned only to HCC 126, the
more severe condition category in the hierarchy. In the ACG System, the term HCC will be used to
denote the terminal condition groupings after hierarchies have been applied.
HCCs are made available as a space-delimited string in the HHS-CMS Enrollment Results output file
and in a separate HHS-HCC assignments output file with a record for each patient and HCC.
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–638–

=== PÁGINA 639 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
Assign RXCs
Beginning with the 2018 HHS-HCC model, a limited number of categories derived from prescription
drugs are incorporated into the adult model. The drug categories are called RXCs (see HHS-HCC RXC
Codes and Descriptions on page 396); RXCs can be determined based on either NDC or HCPCS code.
As with the diagnosis-based condition categories, RXCs are subject to a hierarchy such that only the
most severe condition inferred from the medication in the hierarchy will be retained. RXCs may
contribute to the risk score directly as well as with interactions with HCCs. RXCs will be presented
with the patient's list of HCC Assignments.
Enrollment Duration
Beginning with the 2017 model year, the HHS-HCC model includes enrollment duration in the adult
model. Based on the hhs_cms_benefit_begin_date and hhs_cms_benefit_end_date during the
observation period, the ACG System will calculate an enrollment duration (in months) to be used as
part of the model markers. The calculation is consistent with HHS-HCC documentation:
1 = 1–31 days enrolled
2 = 32–62 days enrolled
3 = 63–92 days enrolled
4 = 93–123 days enrolled
5 = 124–153 days enrolled
6 = 154–184 days enrolled
7 = 185–214 days enrolled
8 = 215–245 days enrolled
9 = 246–275 days enrolled
10 = 276–306 days enrolled
11 = 307–335 days enrolled
12 = 336–366 days enrolled
Determine the Correct Model
Separate models with different HCCs and interactions will be applied to each of the age groups:
infant, child and adult. For the definitions used in the HHS-HCC model adults are age 21 and over,
children are ages 2 through 20 and infants are younger than age 2.

Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
The final risk score is the sum of model coefficients associated with each model in the figure below.
Model coefficients also vary by plan metal level.
Figure140.ComponentsoftheHHS-HCCModels
Components of the HHS-HCC Models
Adult Model
Individual HCCs as well as some groups of HCCs (HHS-HCC Groups on page 651) contribute to the
adult model. The effect of HCC grouping is to limit the contribution of similar conditions. For example,
a patient with both HCC 117 (Muscular Dystrophy) and HCC 119 (Parkinson's, Huntington's, and
Spinocerebellar Disease, and Other Neurodegenerative Disorders) would get only a single model
coefficient from HCC Group G12.
Several HCCs are identified as severe illnesses (HHS-HCC Adult Severe Illness Conditions on page 650).
Severe illness HCCs may contribute individually but will only contribute additional model weight when
an interaction HCC (HHS-HCC Adult Severe Illness Interaction Groups on page 654) is present. Similar
to the HCC grouping above, severe illness interactions are grouped to limit the contribution of severe
illness in the event that a patient has multiple severe illness interactions. For example, HCC 2
(Septicemia, Sepsis, Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome/Shock) represents a severe illness.
HCC 2 in combination with HCC 68 (aplastic anemia) is in interaction group H. This combination has a
higher coefficient weight than HCC 2 in combination with HCC 154 (Vascular Disease with
Complications) which falls into interaction group M.
The final HHS-HCC risk score is the sum of model coefficients associated with age and sex, individual
HCCs, HCC groups and severe illness interactions. The model variables are made available as a space-
©2022TheJohnsHopkinsUniversity.Allrightsreserved.
–640–

=== PÁGINA 641 ===
The Johns Hopkins ACG® System Version 13.0 User Documentation
Appendix I: HHS-HCC Model
delimited string in the HHS Enrollment Results output file and in a separate HHS model variables
output file with a record for each patient and model variable.
Child Model
Unlike the adult model, severe illness interactions are not used in the child model. The final HHS-HCC
risk score is the sum of model coefficients associated with age and sex, individual HCCs, and HCC
groups (HHS-HCC Groups on page 651).
Infant Model
The infant model groups HCCs into one of five severity levels (HHS-HCC Infant Severity Groups on
page 655). If a patient is not assigned a severity level based on HCC, the infant will be classified into
severity 1 by default. Severity and sex are the only model coefficients for infants that are age 1 at the
end of the enrollment period.
For infants that are age 0, maturity (HHS-HCC Infant Maturity Groups on page 654) is assigned. If an
infant aged 0 is not assigned a maturity level based on HCC, the infant will be classified as term by
default. The severity/maturity interactions are the only model coefficients for infants that are age 0 at
the end of the enrollment period.
Additional Adjustment
There are several additional adjustments made to the risk score, either at the individual patient level
or in the aggregate payment transfer formula.
• Cost Sharing Reduction (CSR) Adjustment: The HHS CSR Indicator provided on the HHS
enrollment file is used to determine a multiplier that will be applied to the risk score for
recipients of cost sharing reductions. The HHS CSR is intended to lower the out-of-pocket
expenses for low income beneficiaries and Native Americans from federally recognized tribes.
The HHS CSR-adjusted risk score is the product of the HHS risk score and the CSR adjustment
factor. Missing or invalid values for HHS CSR Indicator will be treated as a HHS CSR Indicator of
0 (no cost sharing reduction adjustment).
• HHS Allowable Rating Factor (ARF): Based on an age rating curve that conforms with the 3:1
age rating restriction, the ARF factor is used in the payment transfer calculation to account for
differences in premium collected due to differences in the age-mix of the population. The ACG
System uses the federal age rating curve, but the ACG System also allows you to provide an
alternate ARF table by age.
• HHS Induced Demand Factor (IDF): Induced demand reflects differences in enrollee costs
attributable to differences in plan benefits. The IDF is a function of plan metal level used in
the payment transfer calculation.
• HHS Actuarial Value (AV): Actuarial Value reflects the amount of cost paid by the plan as
compared to enrollee out of pocket costs based on benefit design. The AV is a function of plan
metal level used in the payment transfer calculation.

Patients with Very High Risk Conditions
The HHS-HCC model assigns very large model coefficients for critical conditions. In the adult model,
for example, members with severe illness interactions get coefficient weight for the interaction
variable in addition to the individual HCCs. Patients assigned to INT_GROUP_H receive a very high
coefficient weight and represent an “at risk” population. The specific conditions associated with
interaction group H are identified in HHS Adult Severe Illness Interaction Groups on page 654. The
HHS model variables are presented as a space-delimited string and are accessible using filters with the
“contains” operator.
The more granular context of HHS-HCC model assignments is available in a separate filter tab title
HHS-CMS Enrollment Filters. Filters on this tab are applied to each enrollment segment.

In this example, Rx-MGs are used to indicate patients with diabetes. ENDx030 represents patients
taking medications for diabetes with insulin. ENDx040 represents patients taking medications for
diabetes without insulin.
The HHS-HCC codes in the diabetes hierarchy are:
18 Pancreas Transplant Status/Complications
19 Diabetes with Acute Complications
20 Diabetes with Chronic Complications
21 Diabetes without Complication
These HHS-HCCs are derived from diagnosis information and will increase the HHS-HCC risk score
when present. In this example, the absence of the HHS-HCC would be an indication that the individual
is taking medication for a condition that is not reflected in the risk score.
